#8637. Elizabeth Van Winkle Shares How Resilience Can Help Make the Military Better

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Ask someone who serves in the military or in a civilian leadership role within the government why they are doing what they do, and there’s a good chance you will hear an answer that references the “mission.”

While the specific mission varies by role, a common thread unites them: being part of something bigger than themselves in service to the greater good of America. Feelings of patriotism, pride, and purpose are powerful motivators. But on the toughest days, many of these same leaders carry themselves forward with a fourth ‘P’: pressure.

Dr. Elizabeth ‘Elise’ Van Winkle understands each of those motivators, and she knows firsthand how heavy that fourth one can become. During a pivotal chapter in her government career, that pressure took a severe toll on her health. Now when she speaks about her career, she offers advice for anyone who may be in a similar position. Regardless of the mission in question, your health will matter.

Van Winkle acknowledged that fitness wasn’t a priority when she was younger, but that changed when she went to college and majored in psychology and English.

“That was probably my foray into fitness and health, the psychological side,” she said. “That is an important part of fitness to me.”

Van Winkle’s original focus was to enter a career in criminology and trauma, and she started that pursuit in the Boston, Massachusetts public school system for behavioral and psychiatric issues. Seeing children dealing with adverse issues and life situations was a valuable learning experience for her.

“The kids taught me a lot about resilience and heartache, perseverance, rage, and emotional darkness.”

Once she became a mother, Van Winkle opted to return to school to get her Ph.D. in research psychology, with a focus on neuropsychology. During that time, she had her second child and landed an intern position with the Department of Defense.

“My plan was to do research and data analytics on health and resilience, stay a year, and then move into work at NIH or do something in neuropsychology.”

Sometimes the best-laid plans can go awry, and Van Winkle’s career would have a meteoric rise that she did not see coming. She stayed in the DoD and worked her way up to a Senior Executive Service (SES) level throughout the next several years. Then came the 2016 election. A combination of being in the right place at the right time and the incoming changes with the Trump administration meant Van Winkle was elevated from a one-star SES to a three-star SES equivalent within a couple of weeks. Then shortly after, she was named the Acting Assistant Secretary for Readiness.

“That propelled me into a level of political leadership that I had never really been in.”

It also led to a massive increase in responsibility. The self-described “data geek” went from leading a team of 25 people with a budget of $4 million to now leading upwards of 900 civilians, military, and contractors with a budget of $1 billion. Almost immediately, an executive order gave her team 45 days to develop a readiness recovery framework that measured the readiness of the entire Joint Force and what would be needed to recover that readiness as well as appropriation lines.

Van Winkle added, “Anybody in the Department knows that when someone says 45 days, they really mean 30 because it has to go through coordination.”

Van Winkle’s trajectory may have felt like a whirlwind, but she accepted what became her own mission. She committed every waking hour that she could towards her new role and responsibilities. That also meant putting other things on the backburner like time with her kids and her own personal needs. As a result, she became sick but was undeterred. Knowing her team would not leave until she did, Van Winkle even closed up her office so her staff would leave, then snuck back on her own to continue her work.

Finally, her team put a meeting on her calendar that led her to the Pentagon Health Clinic. The physician informed Van Winkle she had three different infections and asked her to consider going to the hospital, but Van Winkle knew there were scheduled advisor meetings and a commitment at the White House in her future. So, the physician gave her antibiotics and said something that Van Winkle said haunted her.

“She said, ‘I’ve heard it before. I imagine it’s the mission.’”

Van Winkle admitted seeing every flag along the way but opted to drive right through them for the sake of her own mission. She eventually recovered, was able to resume her duties, and a permanent assistant secretary was named later on, but Van Winkle learned a lesson that she shares openly today. Regardless of what the mission is or what challenges face you, you must make your health a priority in order to succeed. Her personal experience combined with what she learned in college and throughout her career has given her a more comprehensive perspective on what optimal health and fitness really looks like.

“I now truly see fitness as crossing the elements of physical, psychological, and spiritual.”

Today, Van Winkle serves as the Industry Executive for Federal Government at Oracle, helping translate complex military needs into technology solutions that support the Joint Force.

“My job is really to help Oracle understand that government perspective, the Department of War perspective, and really translate what can be some fairly complex elements within the federal government back to the technology venture at Oracle.”

Alongside her corporate role, she frequently speaks to military audiences about leadership and resilience: a message rooted in her Pentagon experience. Her core principle is that individual health directly dictates collective unit readiness. Van Winkle also shares her knowledge and experience from her time in the Pentagon and about resilience when she speaks. As she learned through her own experience, each person’s health and resilience matters because it impacts the readiness of the larger group.

“Every member of the unit must be performing at 100 percent for the unit as a whole to perform at 100 percent.”

As important as that is, Van Winkle noted that communication and transparency about a problem is just as important because if someone in the unit is under 100 percent and does not share that with leadership, it could lead to bigger issues for the entire unit later on.

“I think leaders often presume that members understand this, but what I would hear from military members is a focus on mission above and beyond all else. And that sometimes meant that they would step over those red flags in order to maintain this facade and that everything is okay.”

She concluded, “Ignoring the problem is just setting a timer. They may be able to hold it together for a while but not forever.”

Many members of the military have shared that they don’t bring up their personal problem because they don’t want to be the reason that the readiness of the unit is compromised. In Van Winkle’s opinion, the moment the problem is ignored, readiness is already compromised.

“If a leader knows someone is struggling or someone is injured or someone is going through a crisis, they can do something about it before it becomes a full-blown issue that impacts the unit and the mission. If the leader does not know about it, you are then creating a blind spot.”

Those in commander and leadership positions should also see addressing those problems and resilience as investments into readiness because programs focused on resilience can save time and energy for the sake of the mission.

“If you wait for it to become a readiness problem, you really lose before you even begin. So preventing these things is an incredible return on investment.”

Aside from advances in technology, the military’s emphasis on readiness and well-being of the service members in recent years is going to benefit many future recruits who decide to join the Joint Force. Van Winkle advises that there are other things leaders can do to make sure those who wear the nation’s uniform can be better both physically and psychologically and therefore, more capable of maximizing readiness.

“Look closely at yourself, and think of it like a maintenance check like you do for a weapons system,” she explained. “As humans, we tend to preserve stability over instability and we strive towards homeostasis, but this often means that we don’t see what’s in front of us, particularly if it doesn’t align with how we see ourselves.”

Van Winkle also noted that life can take unexpected turns whether you are ready for them or not, and being resilient means being able to adjust when needed as quickly as possible.

“Life is masterful at creating instability, and we are constantly adjusting to the experiences that we have. If done right, it can make us stronger and more resilient.”

Finally, she suggested not being afraid to have the tough conversations that come with service, readiness, or life. The willingness to speak about it not only helps the service member. It can help the leader as well, which can lead to service members focusing more on patriotism, pride, and purpose while being better prepared for the pressure.

“It does an incredible amount to maintain morale and cohesion in the unit, and it really does prevent those bigger problems.”

M&F Senior Military Editor Rob Wilkins contributed to this Fit to Serve article.

#8636. Frugal Man Buys $52,000 Car – Why??

As I type this, I’m jumping through the various hoops involved in buying a 2023 Tesla Model Y, a rather expensive, luxury “crossover” that is absolutely loaded to the gills with excess: all wheel drive, faster acceleration than a Lamborghini, enough space for seven people and enough computer gadgetry to function as a small Google data center.

Update: Looking for the ongoing tracker page? It’s here at “The Model Y Experiment“

The total net cost of this thing to me after all the taxes and tax credits* will be about $52,000, which is just a stunning amount higher than the Honda van it is replacing. That old classic cost me $4500 when I bought it off of Craigslist twelve years ago, and it had served me dutifully until just last month, crisscrossing the mountains and deserts of this country and also helping to rebuild a considerable swath of houses in my neighborhood.

I’m supposed to be a frugality-oriented financial blogger, and I’m also known for hating car culture – I think most people use cars about ten times more often than they need to, and most people drive cars they can’t afford. So why the hell am I buying a new one?

From those first three paragraphs, you can see I’m feeling plenty of self-mockery and ridicule over this new purchase. If you’re also a naturally frugal person, you can surely relate to the thoughts and you probably also agree with me that I’m off my rocker.

And indeed, I’m still on-board with frugality and healthy self mockery. After all, it was this overall life philosophy that earned me an early retirement 18 years ago, which provides all of the glorious freedom I enjoy now.

It was also the philosophy that allowed me to procrastinate on buying this expensive car for the last four years, even as countless people both close to me and out on the Internet egged me on and told me I should just loosen up and treat myself.

But there’s a classic slogan that applies to many areas of life, and it is something I like to dig up and ponder every now and then:

How does that piece of wisdom apply to frugal living and enjoying a long life of early retirement?

A quick story from a recent run to the grocery store will explain:

I was standing there in the bakery aisle, hoping to restock with a loaf of Dave’s Killer Bread for the next day’s breakfast with some visiting friends. But since this was in a standard grocery store rather than the Costco where I usually shop, the damned stuff was priced at an eye-watering $6.99 per loaf (instead the $4.50 or so I’m accustomed to paying, and even at the bulk store this stuff is about double the price of normal bread).

“WHO THE HELL DO YOU THINK YOU ARE, TRYING TO SELL BREAD FOR SEVEN BUCKS!!!”

Then I went through a whole mental battle of what I call Grocery Shopping With Your Middle Finger:

“Hmm I wonder if any of the other competing brands are any good?”

“What else is a good substitute for bread for this breakfast?”

And then thankfully, after exhausting all other mental options, I settled on the correct one:

“Because you are never going to wake up in the future and look at your bank account and think, shit, if only I had an extra $2.49 in there I would be a happier person.”

That night, I came home from the store and shared this funny tale with one of my guests. He understood perfectly because he too had earned his own retirement through a lifetime of grinding in tough jobs and disciplined frugality. And despite the fact that he has a net worth several times higher than mine, he admitted that he faces exactly the same mental battles over splurging on himself.

This same friend gives freely to charitable causes, has supported a local school for decades, and is always the first one to pull out the checkbook if a friend has hit hard times or is looking for a trusted business investor.

But he still has trouble bringing himself to take an Uber to the airport instead of riding the bus which takes an hour longer.

We both realized that we were being too cheap with ourselves, and we needed to work on it. And we came up with a set of three ideas that should hopefully work together to help us have more fun with our life savings, while we are still alive:

Principle #1: The Minimum Spending Budget:

Suppose you’ve done well over the years and amassed a pile of productive investments worth about two million dollars. Yes, this is a lot of money for most people, and that is the point: this hypothetical person truly has it made.

But as it turns out, most Mustachians I know with this level of wealth are still living very efficient lives, usually with a spending level of under $40,000 per year. On top of that, they typically live in a mortgage-free house and still have various forms of side income from a small business or two.

The 4% rule tells us that this person should be fairly safe spending up to about $80,000 per year from that cozy nest egg, even if they never earn any other money.

If this person wanted to be ridiculously conservative and set the spending rate at 3%, that still leaves about $60,000 of fun money every single year.. Plus, again, any side income, future inheritances, and social security income only add to the surplus.

Thus, a reasonable minimum spending level for this person might be $60,000 per year.

And in most cases, they know this, but still go right on living on $40k or less and claim they have everything they could ever want.

But if you watch carefully you’ll still catch them firing up the middle finger at things like $6.99 Dave’s bread or the $14.00 Cabernet at the restaurant or driving around in a gas guzzler even when they would prefer to have a proper, modern electric car.

And whenever these people do get extra money, their first instinct is to stash it away on top of the already-too-big pile.  In diagram form, their money flow looks like this:

Note that while this person is great at accumulating money through that big red arrow firing money back into the ‘stash, their “fun stuff” arrow appears quite flaccid and withered.

Principle #2 – the Dedicated Money Wasting Account

Lifelong habits are hard to break, and it’s sometimes hard to “waste” your own hard-earned money on things that seem frivolous, even when you know intellectually that you have way more money than you’ll ever spend.

But have you ever noticed that if you are spending somebody else’s money, preferably an anonymous corporation, it feels different?

For example, when you’re on a business trip and you just show up at the dining table to eat and drink and you never see the bill, you probably don’t fret about the prices, right?

The key is to make your own money feel like somebody else’s, and you can do it like this:

Principle #3 – The Splurge Accountability Buddy

Many of us frugal people tend to stick together. And most of us have different versions of the same problem: we know logically that money is plentiful these days, but our emotions keep us stuck in our old ways of optimizing too much.

But I find that when I team up with local friends who are actually trying to battle these same habits, we can question each other’s decisions, call out cheapness when we see it, and cheer on splurges when we know the other guy would enjoy it.

My super wealthy friend from above has become much better about treating himself (and his family) to quality goods for the home, amazing trips together, and just a general reduction in his stress over being “efficient with money”

My friend and HQ co-owner Carl (Mr. 1500 Days) has finally replaced his beaten-down minivan with a spiffy new Chevrolet Bolt electric car, and is loving that leap into the future.

And of course Mr. Money Mustache, after squeezing one final mountain road trip out of his 23-year-old Honda van, is finally allowing himself to get the Tesla he has been talking about for half a decade.

A recent life change (becoming a co-owner of a fixer-upper vacation rental compound in beautiful Salida Colorado) has reignited the travel fire in my heart and made me realize how much I do love getting out to distant places for visiting, mountain biking, gathering with groups of friends and my favorite activity of all: Carpentourism.

Running the Numbers: how ridiculously expensive is this car?

This is the perfect start to my experiment in spending more. Realistically, a $50,000 car is going to cost me about $10,000 more per year than my old van was burning.  With the biggest costs being these:

Since I personally had a spending deficit of several times more than $10k per year, I figure this is a solid first step. And, since the car’s primary purpose is things like epic camping trips, dream dates, and  long adventures around the country, it will definitely help me spend more on experiences, hotels, and go out to dinner a bit more often as well.

“This Privileged Rich Folk Talk is Making Me Sick, why don’t you give your money away to charity, or to me?”

In general, I agree: the world has problems and the richer you are, the more you should consider giving generously.

But also, to be honest, the whiny people who constantly send complaints like this out to strangers on the Internet really need to get a life. It’s great to encourage philanthropy through positive examples, but completely unproductive to send negativity to shame people you don’t even know for not following your own personal value system. The world has seen more than enough of this.

On top of that, this one-sided thinking can be counterproductive. Both of my friends have given generously throughout their lifetimes. In my own case, I have donated over $500,000 to the best causes I could find during the years I’ve been writing this blog, but I was still refusing to let myself replace that 23-year-old van.

And that overthinking was leading to even more of a scarcity mentality, as I compared my own meager spending to these bigger numbers of my donations, and found myself thinking things like,

“Damn, I’m spending $100 on this dinner date which sounds like a lot, but I also spent ONE THOUSAND TIMES more on donations last year, which sounds like even more. Maybe I am spending too much and need to cut back on EVERYTHING!”And then the fear side of my brain would illogically chime in: “Yeah and you’re going to make us run out of money and be poor forever! waaaah waaaah! Cut back and optimize and conserve!”

Yes – be a super, duper responsible steward of your life savings.

And yes, give generously with all your heart to charity.

But yes, it’s also okay to set aside a portion of the money you’ve earned, for frivolous spending on yourself and those closest to you. You’re not a bad person for having a few nice things.

It’s okay to pay that extra hundred bucks to sit a bit closer to the front of the airplane instead of the back if it helps you enjoy your vacation and spend a joyful half hour walking FREE at your destination while the 49 rows of people behind you fuss infuriatingly with their shit in the overhead bins.

It’s okay to buy the frozen berries at Whole Foods even though they cost eight times more than Costco charges, if it spares you from making a second unpleasant trip through parking lot hell.

And as for me, I am calling it okay to, at last, double flip the Autopilot stalk in my new Tesla and lean back as it it shoots me gracefully through even the highest mountain passes, forever leaving the desperately underpowered wheezing and gear shifting and noise* of the gasoline era behind, forever.

I ended up using an online car salvage service called Peddle*, at the recommendation of a friend. With about five minutes of entering the details of my old Honda, their system offered me $715, and then a towtruck came and took it the next day – and actually gave me the payment in cash, which I found kind of fun. I made a point of using all of that money for splurges like dinners out, in keeping with the theme of this article.

* I later signed this blog up for Peddle’s affiliate program so that link will benefit MMM if you use it.

* A useful tip for more effective splurging:Try to find the truly negative aspects of your life and focus any additional spending on improving those things. But it’s a subtle art so you have to get it right if you want lasting results in happiness.

You don’t want to just reduce hardship or challenge like hiring someone to take care of every aspect of your house, because overcoming daily hardships and having significant accomplishments provides the very core of our life satisfaction.

You also don’t want to just upgrade the things that are already good in your life. For example, a friend of mine is a gourmet coffee expert, and he suggested that I upgrade my setup at home to include on-the-spot roasting, and fancy grinding and brewing equipment. But I already love the good quality coffee I buy off the shelf from Costco, so it would be counterproductive to invest time or money into changing this part of my life.

But when you have something that causes you regular angst and stress, whether it’s a leaky roof that makes you dread rain, or a long commute that makes you dread the daily traffic jam, or a body that is giving you trouble due to not being in the best of shape – those types of things are probably a good target for improvement.

In the case of my car situation, I had a Nissan Leaf which is wonderful to drive, but doesn’t have the range to travel anywhere outside of the Denver metro area. Then I had the van which is a clunky beast to drive, but is otherwise an amazing road tripper because I could bring along whatever and whoever I wanted. But the van was getting increasingly unreliable in several hard-to-fix ways which was making me nervous every time I thought about long distance travel. Which was causing me to avoid certain trips and miss positive lifetime experiences.

In other words, my lack of a reliable long-range car was a small but consistent source of negative stress.

Finally, Vanna gave me the gift of a final hot and smelly transmission failure on a mountain pass on the way home from my new project in Salida. It was just the nudge that I needed. And now I already feel excitement rather than dread at the prospect of all the road trips in the coming decades!

In that case, you might be interested in the Tesla Model 3 RWD, which uses only LFP – Lithium Iron Phosphate batteries (no cobalt and also no nickel). There are a few other advantages to this battery type as well, including even longer lifespan.

In the future, most cars will be using either LFP or Sodium-ion or other new chemistries based on even cheaper, more abundant minerals. But for now, even the cobalt content does not outweigh the benefits of avoiding oil consumption (which as you know also has a long history as a conflict mineral even before you consider the pollution)

I have a couple of points that come from what is glaringly obvious in your explanation of your purchases. The difference between someone who is a frugal saver and a spendthrift is that the frugal saver (I would put myself in this category) would not even consider the Dave’s bread at $7 and before buying the $4 bread would go look on the day old shelf for the same bread marked down to $2. The spendthrift ALWAYS buys this ONE treat, just this ONE time. The problem is, once the overpriced thing is bought, the thought of having overspent and treating ones self disappears from memory. Making this habit becomes the whole way of life for the spendthrift and come time to chuck the working life, the frugal guy says “Ok, let me do the math. Here’s my annual retirement budget and lot at this….I have 56 times this amount in liquid assets on my spread sheet inside my paid off house driven in by my paid off cars”. The spendthrift (who is actually a friend of Car Jack) looks and says “I have $100k in my 401k, rent and make payments on my car. How does anyone retire?”. So my advice is to check yourself each and every time you think about treating yourself. If you have the money and those treats keep you in the % spending, fine. If at the end of the year, you look at all that you spend and scream “Holy Shit….I spent what on this crap?”, you’ve failed to keep track of what you spend.

Ok, onto the Tesla. We all know you and many others have been very taken by the oversized electric golf carts. I went and drove a bunch of them myself in an effort to first find something I liked and then do the due diligence to justify a purchase. Do I sound like an engineer? Understandable with all the money I spent becoming one. In the end, I drove just about every EV, so I know the plusses and minuses of many of them. I will say that completely outside of the type of car, Elon has the absolute best way to buy a car. Go online, pick what you want, put in your deposit and wait till it’s ready. No listening to “What can I do to get you in a car today?” from some punk kid at a dealership. But in the end, I had to rely on math. What would it cost for ME to drive an EV of my choice. Well, I’d have to modify that to say the most efficient EV because to me the Audi e Tron GT was levels above every other EV I drove in luxury, quality and feeling more like a car with an electric drive system than an electric motor in tupperware. So the catch for me is that I live in a high electric rate area with wonderful total cost per kWh of 45.5 cents. And I’m seeing gas at the cheapo, competing gas stations for $2.89 per gallon on my way to the used tool store. My daily driver is a 2019 Subaru Crosstrek manual that gets 35 mpg in the summer. Note that ICE cars do worse in the winter because we have “winter gas” but also EVs do even more worse in winter temperatures. So in the end, a Tesla Model 3 single motor (the most efficient EV on the planet) calculates out to cost about 2 cents a mile MORE than my pedestrian Subaru that I bought new for $22k. So unless I’m looking to look like Richie Rich with a new Audi Electromobile, I can’t justify the thought of going electric. I’ll back up a second and admit that you people in like Texas who get electricity for 4 cents a kWh should absolutely look at EVs. But I don’t have that luxury. And gas is cheap here. And I like my car quite a lot with it’s utility, all wheel drive so I don’t have to trump up my driveway in the snow (it’s a steep hill that no 2 wheel drive can get up in snow) and I get fun from rowing gears. So my recommendation for anyone considering an EV is to DO THE MATH. the end.

Haha, yes I remember doing the same math when I saw that article! Although it looks like the Guardian has corrected the numbers in their article so it’s at least a bit less misleading.

It used to say that tires could emit over 9 grams of rubber dust per km of driving, and I calculated at the time the real number is 0.033 grams (33 milligrams) – because a tire loses about 2kg of mass over its 60,000 km lifespan. So, they were off by a factor of almost 300.

Now, they have fixed that to use a figure of 50 milligrams, which is close enough.

I don’t know how to calculate the amount that ends up in the air versus on the road, but either way, you have the same problem with electric cars or gas cars, and nowadays the weight is pretty similar across vehicle classes.

The best we can do is to make rough estimates of the NUMBERS behind each of our options, and then do tests and collect data so we can refine these numbers over time.

In other words, think of everything as a science experiment, and accept that you will always be somewhat wrong, but with sufficient humbleness and study you can gradually reduce this wrongness over time.

“What is the fallacy of worse things? Fallacy of relative privation (also known as “appeal to worse problems” or “not as bad as”) – dismissing an argument or complaint due to what are perceived to be more important problems. First World problems are a subset of this fallacy.”

Space X created reusable rockets that can land vertically, greatly reducing the cost to NASA to resupply the International Space Station and freeing NASA from reliance on Russian rockets and transport. Based on what I’ve read about happiness, humans are generally terrible about figuring out what will make us happy. However, we’re actually very good at identifying things that are making us unhappy; also, unhappiness vs happiness is not a 1:1 comparison (more like 5:1, I believe).

Therefore, eliminating those things that make us unhappy is a logical, sensible and efficient strategy.

For many of us, jobs are the number one cause of dramatic unhappiness, because of the opportunity cost (i.e. time we could be spending on other things we value more), but also stress, commuting, and lack of freedom over our own destiny, etc. So FIRE is the first priority, because that has, by far, the most impact on happiness for most of us. (It’s not the only consideration though, because it takes years to achieve, so the journey matters a lot too).

Once that is achieved, the next steps are going to look very different for everyone, because everyone is different. Many for someone, that’s cutting their own lawn, so they hire someone. For someone else, they hate baking bread, so they buy it pre-made.

Around my house, we refer to it as, “throwing money at the problem”. I detest working on cars, so I always take them to our trusted mechanic. However, I like (or at least don’t mind) carpentry, plumbing, electrical, etc, so I do almost all of that work myself.

MMM identified something that was negatively impacting his level of happiness/life satisfaction, determined the cost to fix it (vs doing other things with that money, because everything is balancing cost/benefit), and decided that the tradeoffs were worth it. It was a decision he researched thoroughly, and although it might not be perfectly logical (although it’s entirely possible it is), he even understood the emotional factors contributing to the decision – we’re humans, not Vulcans! It didn’t impact his life in a negative way financially or otherwise, it doesn’t disproportionately hurt the earth (given the society he lives in), and most importantly, he didn’t make the consumerist mistake of believing that buying the Tesla would make him happy.

That’s the root of the problem for most people, I think – they are constantly fed advertising that convinces them that spending money on something will make them happy. It won’t EVER do that, but using it to remove frustration and pain from your life can definitely improve our level of happiness.

It’s tricky and complicated figuring out that balance at times for sure, but everything is always a balance. Almost nothing in life is binary.

There’s very little difference in charging versus gas stops in a new Tesla like this, versus a gas car. Especially given the fact that your body needs to get up and move every few hours anyway. More details in the dedicated Q&A page: https://www.mrmoneymustache.com/the-model-y-experiment/

Charging in our Y is definitely way less convenient in multi supercharger distance trips than in a gas car. 20K miles of road trips so far. The key is MULTI. A distance of just one supercharger is fine. The problem is you trickle charge when above 80% full.

How inconvenient will depend on what you need/like currently. On the pure finances side, the point of FIRE in your example is the RE part: Your strategy of going straight to the high-spending model means that you have to work considerably longer, even though you are able to have the luxury spending level for slightly longer. With more than 40,000 runners expected to descend in Philadelphia, each of the three Rocky Run categories have sold out.

The first official Rocky Run began in 2014 with heavyweight beginnings, attracting 7,000 runners, but it has gone from strength to strength since. And, while organizers had expected around 30,000 competitors to descend in Philly this year, the final number will clock in at an incredible 40,000.

Those who are ready and set for November 14, 2026, have a choice of three categories, catering to different abilities, so that anyone can “Go For it.”

And for those, who still can’t get enough of Sylvester Stallone’s creation, the story of how a struggling actor defied the odds to become the star of one of cinema’s most successful franchises is also set to hit theaters, with “I Play Rocky” starring Anthony Ippolito as the struggling boxer given a once in a lifetime shot, and Stephan James playing Apollo Creed.

#8628. Robert Strauss Has the Full-Body F45 Workout to Stay Fit over 40

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

As the General Manager of WWE’s NXT brand, a pro wrestling coach, and the owner of eight gyms across Florida, Robert Strauss understands the importance of rapid workouts to stay ripped. To that end, the man known to millions of WWE fans as “Robert Stone,” says that F45 workouts are perfect for staying fighting fit, and he proved it with a dedicated demonstration for M&F.

The F45 concept sees gym goers from all over the world following the same daily workout. “Everybody does the same workout every day, and you’re never going to do the same workout twice,” says Strauss. “It’s a 45-minute workout that includes your warmup, your workout, and your cooldown.”

Indeed, F45 workouts tackle fitness from all angles. There are focused cardio days, strength days, and hybrid days to keep each session stimulating. And, there’s often a choice of two different exercises as you move through the circuit. “So, you really can get a full body workout in, any day that you come into an F45, and you’re always going to leave drenched in sweat, I promise you that,” adds the NXT GM.

F45 sessions begin as soon as the clock activates and include short demonstrations followed by a guided warmup with dynamic stretching, to prepare yourself for the pump ahead. Then, after the main session is done, there’s a cooldown period before you tackle the rest of the day, feeling ready to bodyslam the world.

Greeting us at his Baldwin Park, FL, location, Strauss, who is the father of twin boys, explained that F45 has provided structure so that he can keep up with the next generation at both at home and in NXT. He completed the following session between duties, proving that he hasn’t missed a beat.

(In this class, there were 4 minutes for setup)

Execute each exercise for 45 seconds.Rest and transition to the next exercise for 15 seconds.

High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) sessions such as this one can easily burn more than 500 calories in 45 minutes, depending on the effort put in, and you’ll supercharge your fat burning power with Excess Post-Exercise Oxygen Consumption (EPOC) for the rest of the day.

You won’t need to walk around a vast gym space to hit all of the muscle groups either, because you’ll be completing each station while staying pretty much on the spot. This particular workout offered back and core strengthening exercises like crunches and rows, upper body testers like presses and extensions, and movements that also build the lower body with sumo stances and lying leg raises.

“One of the most inspiring things about NXT is that most of the trainees there are half my age,” says Strauss of his motivation to maintain muscle. “They are all phenomenal athletes that come from all over the world, and they are in the greatest shape. So, seeing them inspires me to continue my fitness journey. Also, I’m a twin dad to 10-year-olds, and I want to inspire them the way NXT Superstars inspire me. I want to inspire my kids so that they see their daddy is fit, and they want to be fit. It’s an important part of life for your mental and physical well-being,”

You can catch Strauss in his role as General Manager Robert Stone, stamping his authority on NXT, every Tuesday night on the CW Network in the U.S. and streaming internationally on Netflix.

#8624. At 43, Robert Strauss Continues Training to Be the ‘Dad Bod Destroyer’

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Whether you know Robert Strauss for his work as “Robbie E” in TNA or more recently, “Robert Stone” as WWE’s General Manager of NXT, there’s no questioning this exciting performer’s work ethic. Fortunately, as the father of twin boys, and owner of several gyms in Florida, Stone is showing no signs of slowing down. And, at age 43, the “Dad Bod Destroyer” tells M&F how he’s evolved in order to hang with the next generation, both on screen and at home.

Formerly a physical education teacher, Robert Strauss made his pro wrestling debut in the year 2000 and soon worked preliminary matches for WWE until he signed a major deal with Total Nonstop Action in 2010, gaining fame as the charismatic “Robbie E.”  It was during his time in TNA that Strauss won a multitude of titles, including the promotion’s TV and X Division gold.

He also lifted the tag team belts on two occasions alongside Jessie Godderz, and in that team, known as “The BroMans,” the duo even received support from seven-time Mr Olympia, Phil Heath. Of course, Strauss is no stranger to Muscle & Fitness. In 2017, he became a popular contributor with his “Dad Bod Destroyer” workouts, detailing how he stayed in fighting shape while balancing life with his twin sons Cash and Carter, who were just months old as that point. In 2026, Strauss is still making a name for himself in the pro wrestling business, by keeping a tight leash on the young superstars of NXT, but while his current role involves a desk rather than a squared circle, Strauss is always ready for action.

As Robert Stone, the world traveled grappler has maintained his fitness and physique by evolving, to stay consistent. For example, as a young lion, he was able to throw around weights with the same reckless abandon that he showed to many a hapless foe inside the ring. But at 43, and juggling his now 10-year-old twins with a hectic role as NXT GM, coach at WWE’s Performance Center, and broadcast commentator to boot, Strauss has a busier schedule than ever despite the fact that he does not currently compete. Fortunately, the performer has combined his passion with his profession and also owns eight gyms across Florida — that’s five F45 and three FS8 studios—so he’s never stuck for a timely way to stay toned.

Because F45 workouts last no more than 45 minutes, Strauss is able to get great value from his sweat equity. “You’re able to get it all in,” he tells M&F, noting that following an efficient plan has cut down his workout time without sacrificing quality. “Sometimes there are days where I don’t have an hour and a half. I don’t have two hours to get in everything, if I want to stretch out, if I want to warm my body up,” adds Strauss, appreciating the fact that F45 sessions are already planned out and ready to go. “At 43, I do need to regularly warm my body up. So, the 45 minutes is clutch, to be able to just come in and leave, and everything be done.”

For mobility, Strauss shares that FS8 workouts focus on a lighter style of resistance training for improving mobility and maintaining longevity, while still building strength. That’s because FS8 sessions combine Pilates and yoga, with a major emphasis on the core as well as controlled, meaningful movements.

Because of his commitment to crushing each workout, Strauss still looks like he could step between the ropes at any moment, and he maintains a low level of bodyfat to stay ripped, but as a mature athlete, he prefers a sustainable approach to nutrition rather than the latest fads, and this means embracing the balance. “The thing is, I really know my body,” he explains. “Mentally, I want to enjoy things sometimes. I’m not always eating a strict, clean diet. I want to have a good time with my wife or my twins. If they want to get ice cream on the weekend, I’m going to get it too, if I want it.”

The clever coach says that allowing himself to indulge also provides him with the motivation to eat cleaner for the rest of the week. “It adds fuel to the fire for my next workout,” says Strauss. Still, this athlete is keen to avoid eating too late in the evenings and particularly avoids starchy carbs and processed sugars before he hits the hay.

Strauss refuses to rule out the possibility that Robert Stone could one day return him to the ring. He certainly would not be the oldest grappler on the roster if he did. Randy Orton and The Miz are 46, CM Punk is 48, and Rey Mysterio is 51. WWE fans also know that Stauss’s colleague and SmackDown General Manager, Nick Aldis, who is 39, returned for a one-off match against Gunther at SummerSlam 2026.

“If someone pushed me past the point where I need to step in the ring again, I don’t need a week to get ready,” says the authority of NXT. “I don’t need three months to get ready… I can be ready in an hour.”

The highest-value hotel redemption for families using Chase Ultimate Rewards

Picture this: your kids are splashing in an infinity pool that overlooks the turquoise Caribbean, your partner is sipping a cocktail at the swim-up bar, and you're on your third gourmet meal of the day — all without opening your wallet once. No mental math at dinner. No "should we do the excursion?" budget anxiety. Just a genuinely luxurious family vacation where everything is already paid for. This is what the Hyatt All-Inclusive sweet spot feels like. And the ChooseFI community has quietly been using it to take family vacations that their neighbors are financing on credit card debt — except you're doing it nearly free. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop. A family of four at a Hyatt Ziva property — think Hyatt Ziva Cancun, Hyatt Ziva Los Cabos, or Hyatt Ziva Cap Cana — will typically run **$500 to $1,500 per night** in cash when you factor in the all-inclusive rate for two adults and two kids. Over a five-night stay, you're looking at a cash outlay of $2,500 to $7,500. That's a trip many families save years for. With World of Hyatt points, that same night costs **25,000 points**. At a cash rate of $1,000 per night (a very achievable number at peak Ziva properties), you're extracting **4 cents per point** in value — and at $1,500 per night, you're pushing **6 cents per point**. The industry benchmark for a "good" hotel redemption is 1-2 cents per point. You're doubling or tripling that benchmark on a family vacation. The pricing inefficiency here is structural and beautiful: Hyatt's award chart is **fixed**, meaning they set a category for each property based on its tier, not its cash price. All-inclusive resorts are priced in the award chart like any other Hyatt — but the cash rate includes *every meal, every drink, every activity*. The loyalty program hasn't fully "priced in" the all-inclusive premium. That gap is your opportunity. For families pursuing FI, this redemption is especially powerful because the value scales with family size. Four people eating and drinking all day at a resort adds up fast in cash — but costs exactly the same 25,000 points whether it's two people or a family of six. The bigger your family, the more you win.

The core insight here is understanding what the 25,000 points actually buys — and why Hyatt's award chart creates an accidental arbitrage for all-inclusive resorts.

World of Hyatt uses a fixed award chart, categorizing properties from Category 1 (3,500 points/night) to Category 8 (45,000 points/night). Hyatt Ziva and Hyatt Zilara properties typically fall in the Category 4–6 range (18,000–25,000 points/night depending on the specific property and season). The key word is fixed: your points cost doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash prices do. A sold-out week during spring break or Christmas holiday that drives cash rates to $1,500/night still costs the same 25,000 points as an off-peak Tuesday.

Now layer on the all-inclusive structure. When you book a Hyatt Ziva or Hyatt Zilara on points, all meals, drinks, and activities are included in the award rate. This isn't a separate fee. This isn't a resort charge tacked on. The award redemption covers the full all-inclusive experience — the same unlimited dining, premium open bar, water sports, and entertainment that cash guests pay for. Hyatt is one of the few hotel brands that doesn't strip out the all-inclusive component when you book with points.

The Transfer Path: Chase Ultimate Rewards to World of Hyatt

This is where the ChooseFI earning strategy snaps into place. Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, instantly. There's no waiting period, no processing delay — you initiate the transfer and the points appear in your Hyatt account within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, instantly, which matters if you're earning points on rent payments through the Bilt Mastercard.

The transfer ratio is significant because Chase UR points are among the easiest transferable points to earn in volume. The Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Chase Ink Business Preferred, and Chase Ink Business Cash/Unlimited (when paired with a Sapphire card) all feed into the same UR pool. A family spending across categories can accumulate 100,000+ UR points annually, which translates directly into four or more nights at a Ziva property.

World of Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges or carrier-imposed fees on award bookings. The only cost you'll pay out-of-pocket is the government taxes on your award night — typically $10–25 per night depending on the property location. Your 25,000 points buys you a clean, nearly free night without surprise fees draining the value.

Family vs. Adults-Only: Know Which Property to Book

Hyatt Ziva properties are family-friendly — kids are welcome, family suites are available, and there are dedicated kids' clubs and activities. Hyatt Zilara properties are adults-only. This distinction matters enormously when booking. Searching for availability and finding great dates at a Zilara won't help if you're bringing a 9-year-old. Always confirm the property type before transferring points.

Before searching for availability, confirm your points position. Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account at chase.com/ultimaterewards and check your combined UR balance across all eligible cards. Remember, points from Chase Ink cards can be pooled with your Sapphire Reserve or Preferred. You'll need at least 25,000 points per night you want to book — a five-night trip requires 125,000 points. If you're close but not there, set a target date 3–4 months out and focus earning in the meantime.

Go to hyatt.com and search for your target property directly. Use the "Use Points" toggle to see award availability. Key properties to search for families:

For adults-only trips, search Hyatt Zilara Cancun or Hyatt Zilara Cap Cana. The booking window opens 395 days in advance, so you can search nearly 13 months ahead — this is your best window for securing prime dates like school breaks, spring break, and holiday weeks.

Search flexible date ranges to find the best combination of availability and value. Hyatt's calendar view makes this efficient — you can see which nights have standard award availability vs. premium pricing. Note that some peak dates may show higher point requirements; always check if your target dates are at the standard 25,000-point rate or a peak rate.

Once you've confirmed award availability for your exact dates, navigate to Chase Ultimate Rewards and select "Transfer to Travel Partners." Choose World of Hyatt from the partner list. The transfer ratio is 1:1 and the transfer is instant — your Hyatt points will appear within minutes. Only transfer what you need for the specific booking; there's no reason to transfer excess points speculatively.

Return to hyatt.com, log into your World of Hyatt account, and complete the award booking for your confirmed dates. At checkout, select points as your payment method. You'll pay only minimal government taxes (typically $10–25/night). Keep your confirmation email — it will specify that the all-inclusive meals, beverages, and activities are included.

Award availability at popular Ziva/Zilara properties can be limited during peak school break windows. Your moves: (1) Search 395 days out as soon as your target dates open, (2) consider shoulder season dates that offer strong weather but lower demand, (3) call the World of Hyatt member line at 1-800-323-7249 — agents sometimes see availability the website doesn't display, (4) check alternate Ziva/Zilara properties in different destinations.

The math on Hyatt all-inclusive redemptions is what makes this a true sweet spot for the FI community. At a standard hotel, your points cover the room — but you still pay cash for meals, drinks, and activities. At an all-inclusive, the points rate covers everything: room, all meals, unlimited drinks, pool and beach access, kids clubs, entertainment, and most resort activities. A family of four at a Hyatt Ziva paying $700 per night in cash (a common rate) would spend $4,900 for a 7-night stay — plus tips. The same stay at 25,000 points per night costs 175,000 World of Hyatt points total, which equals approximately $3,500 in transferable points value at a conservative 2 cents per point. But the actual value received is closer to $5,000 to $7,000 when you factor in all the meals, drinks, and activities that would cost extra at a regular hotel. This is why Hyatt all-inclusives consistently deliver 3 to 4 cents per point — double the already-strong Hyatt average.

Let's walk through a real family booking so you can see exactly how the numbers work.

The Trip: 5 Nights at Hyatt Ziva Cancun for a Family of Four

You're planning a spring break trip — mid-April, when the weather in Cancun is spectacular and school is out. A family of four (two adults, two kids) wants five nights at Hyatt Ziva Cancun, one of the flagship all-inclusive properties in Hyatt's portfolio. This is a beachfront resort with multiple restaurants, a waterpark-style pool complex, and dedicated kids' programming.

The Cash Price: During spring break, Hyatt Ziva Cancun's all-inclusive rate for a family room runs approximately $900–$1,200 per night for a standard room, all meals and drinks included. At $1,000/night average, five nights costs $5,000 cash. At $1,200/night, you're at $6,000. That's real money for a family.

The Points Cost: At 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night, five nights costs 125,000 points. You'll pay approximately $75–100 total in government taxes across the stay. That's it.

The CPP Math: $5,000 value ÷ 125,000 points = 4 cents per point. At the higher cash rate of $6,000, you're at 4.8 cents per point. The World of Hyatt program's own editorial value benchmark is considered strong at 1.7 cents per point — you're earning nearly 3x that benchmark on this booking.

What Your Family Actually Gets: Every breakfast, lunch, and dinner at the resort's full-service restaurants. Unlimited alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages from morning coffee to late-night cocktails. The resort's pool complex with water slides the kids will talk about for years. Non-motorized water sports. Evening entertainment. This isn't a stripped-down experience — Hyatt Ziva is an upper-upscale brand, and the quality of food and service reflects it.

The Transfer: You move 125,000 Chase UR points to World of Hyatt at 1:1 — instantly — and book directly on hyatt.com. The entire booking process takes under 30 minutes once you have availability confirmed.

Families who wait until 6 months out regularly find those prime weeks already gone on points. This is the single biggest mistake families make with this redemption.

Search Multiple Properties to Triangulate Availability

Don't anchor on one property. Run searches simultaneously at Hyatt Ziva Cancun, Hyatt Ziva Cap Cana, Hyatt Ziva Los Cabos, and Hyatt Ziva Rose Hall. Different properties have different award release patterns, and finding five consecutive nights at one property is easier than it sounds if you're flexible about which destination.

Use 5th Night Free to Stretch Your Points Further

World of Hyatt has a 5th night free on award stays benefit for World of Hyatt credit card holders. Book five nights and pay points for only four. On a 5-night Ziva trip, that saves 25,000 points — enough for one additional night. If you have or are considering the World of Hyatt Credit Card, this benefit alone justifies it for this specific redemption.

The fastest path to 125,000 points for a 5-night family trip is the Chase trifecta: Sapphire Preferred or Reserve (dining and travel), Ink Business Preferred (business spending at 3x), and Ink Business Unlimited or Cash (flat-rate earning). A family running normal spending through these cards can realistically accumulate 100,000+ UR points annually.

This sounds obvious, but adults-only Zilara properties appear in the same search results as family-friendly Ziva properties. Always confirm the property type before transferring points. Once points are transferred into Hyatt, they don't transfer back to Chase.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with a small earning or redemption every two years. A single qualifying activity — even earning 1 point through a partner — resets the clock.

Avoid Booking Refundable Rates on Points Speculatively

Some members book award stays far out with the intent to cancel, just to "hold" dates. While Hyatt does allow cancellations, this practice can strain award availability for other members and creates unnecessary complexity. Book when you're confident.

This redemption was designed — structurally, if not intentionally — for families pursuing financial independence. Here's why it fits the ChooseFI worldview so perfectly.

The ideal user is a family of three to six people who want a high-quality, genuinely relaxing vacation without the mental overhead of per-meal, per-drink, per-activity budgeting. The all-inclusive format eliminates the "should we splurge on dinner?" anxiety that can undercut vacation enjoyment. You've already "paid" with points. Just enjoy.

You need a minimum of 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night. For a realistic 5-night family trip, plan for 125,000 points — or 100,000 if you hold the World of Hyatt card and qualify for the 5th night free benefit. This is very achievable if you've been accumulating Chase Ultimate Rewards through normal household spending on a Sapphire card.

This redemption is also excellent for couples celebrating anniversaries or honeymoons (use Zilara for the adults-only experience), parents of young children who want a vacation where the kids are engaged so the adults can actually relax, and travelers who want a warm-weather, beach vacation without the complexity of international award flight bookings.

This is NOT the right fit if you prefer boutique, off-the-beaten-path travel over resort-style vacations, you're a solo traveler (the per-person value scales poorly), or you're chasing ultra-premium redemptions like business class flights or city luxury hotels. The Hyatt portfolio has those too — but this specific sweet spot is about maximum family value, not maximum luxury status.

This redemption earns an **Easy** rating — and it genuinely deserves it. The ChooseFI community members who struggle with it usually hit one of two friction points, and both are easily solved. **The Earning Side: Very Easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers 1:1 to World of Hyatt instantly. If you have a Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve, you already have access to the best transfer path. Earning 125,000 Chase UR points for a 5-night trip is a reasonable 12–18 month project for a household running normal expenses through rewards cards. **The Booking Side: Easy, With One Catch.** The Hyatt website is clean and the points booking process is straightforward. The one challenge is **peak date availability** — spring break and holiday weeks book up fast at the most popular Ziva properties. The fix is simple: use the 395-day booking window. Set a phone reminder 13 months before your target trip and search the day availability opens. **The Transfer Confidence Hurdle.** Some beginners are nervous about transferring points to Hyatt before they have a confirmed booking. The practical risk is real — if you transfer and then can't find availability, those points are stranded in Hyatt (though they're still useful for future bookings). The solution: always **confirm availability before transferring**. Hyatt lets you select dates and see the points cost before you're asked to pay. Get to that confirmation screen first, then transfer. If you can navigate a hotel booking website and move money between financial accounts, you can execute this redemption. Start with a low-stakes search on hyatt.com today — just to get comfortable with how award availability looks.

Log into your World of Hyatt account and search for all-inclusive properties at your desired destination. Filter by the Hyatt Ziva (family-friendly) or Hyatt Zilara (adults-only) brands. Check the nightly points rate — it will show the standard award rate and whether peak or off-peak pricing applies.

Check the same dates at the cash rate to calculate your cents per point value. If the cash rate is $600 per night and the award rate is 25,000 points, you are getting 2.4 cents per point. For all-inclusives, values above 2 cents per point are common and 3 or more cents per point is typical during peak season.

Transfer the required points from your Chase account to World of Hyatt. Transfers are instant. If you have a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Sapphire Reserve, or Ink Business Preferred, you can transfer directly. Freedom and Ink Cash points can be pooled to a Sapphire card first.

Complete the booking using your World of Hyatt points. Select the standard room type on points — all-inclusive benefits apply to all room categories. Add any special requests for your family (crib, connecting rooms, dietary needs) in the booking notes.

If you have World of Hyatt Globalist status (earned at 60 nights or through the Globalist challenge), you unlock suite upgrades (subject to availability), late checkout, and other premium benefits. Even without elite status, the all-inclusive base experience is exceptional — every meal, drink, and activity is covered.

A 7-night stay at a Hyatt Ziva or Zilara typically costs 175,000 to 245,000 World of Hyatt points (25,000 to 35,000 per night depending on the property and season). This covers the room, all meals, unlimited drinks, activities, and entertainment for the duration of your stay.

At Hyatt Ziva (family-friendly) properties, children typically stay and eat free when sharing a room with parents. Policies vary by property and the child's age — generally children under 12 are included at no additional cost. Hyatt Zilara properties are adults-only (18+). Check the specific property's policy when booking.

You can, but you will get significantly less value. The Chase portal values points at 1.25 cents (CSP) or 1.5 cents (CSR) per point. Transferring to Hyatt for an all-inclusive typically delivers 2 to 4 cents per point — roughly double the portal value. For a $600-per-night all-inclusive, the portal would cost 40,000 to 48,000 Chase points per night, while a direct Hyatt transfer costs only 25,000 points.

Most Hyatt all-inclusive award stays include resort fees in the points rate, but you may owe taxes and some incidental charges. Expect to pay $30 to $80 per night in local taxes depending on the country. Some premium experiences (spa treatments, excursions, premium alcohol) may carry additional charges. Tips for staff are at your discretion and appreciated.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Hyatt all-inclusive resorts represent the single best hotel redemption for families in the travel rewards ecosystem. The combination of a premium resort experience, all meals and drinks included, and 2 to 4 cents per point value makes this a sweet spot that is hard to beat. A family of four can enjoy a week-long beach vacation at a Hyatt Ziva for 175,000 transferable Chase points — a stay that would cost $4,000 to $7,000 in cash. For the ChooseFI community, this is the redemption that makes points tangible: your kids are splashing in the pool, you are enjoying a beachfront dinner, and the entire experience was covered by your Chase credit card rewards. Transfer to Hyatt, book early for peak dates, and give your family the vacation you have been optimizing for.

#8619. The Peptide Door Is Cracking Open, Even If The Risks Aren’t Going Away

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Recently, an interesting thing happened. An athlete could read the World Anti-Doping Agency’s prohibited list and conclude that using certain peptides was a good way to lose a medal and win a ban. Then he could read a new federal announcement about those same compounds and conclude that Washington was opening the door to them. Same molecule. Two government-adjacent messages that seem to be saying two entirely different things. This could lead to quite a headache if you don’t bother reading the fine print.

On Oct. 30, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) published a draft interim policy involving six experimental peptides: BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, MOTS-c, epitalon, and Semax. The idea is to use enforcement discretion while regulators decide whether these substances belong on the list of ingredients that certain licensed pharmacies and physicians can use in compounding. In plain English, HHS says it does not intend to pursue enforcement against qualifying compounders who follow a set of conditions. That is not the same thing as approving six new drugs.

Compounding is when a licensed professional prepares a medication for an individual patient rather than dispensing a mass-produced, approved product. The proposed policy calls for patient-specific prescriptions, traceable ingredients, quality documentation, reporting of serious adverse events, and other safeguards. It’s a long way from some internet chemist shipping you a vial labeled “research use only” with a complimentary discount code from a guy who benches four plates on Instagram.

I can see the argument for this. People are buying these things anyway. If a person is determined to use an experimental peptide, there’s an obvious appeal to getting it through a licensed professional instead of trusting an anonymous supplier whose laboratory might be a shack in a Chinese suburb. HHS says the policy is intended to steer people away from risky, unregulated sources. Fair enough. But a cleaner supply chain is not the same as a molecule that has been proven to work.

That’s the part the peptide evangelists tend to skip. BPC-157 has a reputation for repairing practically everything except a a broken heart. TB-500 gets talked about like it comes with replacement tendons in the box. But the clinical evidence supporting these sweeping claims in humans is thin. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) scientists raised concerns about the lack of convincing clinical data and about product safety.

An advisory committee nevertheless supported broader compounding access for six substances. Disagreement among experts is not proof that either side has discovered a miracle. But, the empirical data is unavoidably overwhelming. It’s a clear case of not believing the dyno numbers – the car feels faster. Such reports have dialed up to the point where the usual culprits smell dollar signs. However thin the clinical data, its being drowned out by an ever growing cadre of gym bros who swear it works, the list is prestigious too. Now all of a sudden the government tosses a glimmer of light down the hallway?  Out of nowhere? Isn’t it usually the government that’s slamming the door shut?

Note that the draft doesn’t authorize supplement companies to dump these compounds into pre-workouts and doesn’t establish that a product is safe or effective. The federal notice is open for public comment, and the policy can be revisited if safety or quality problems emerge. There are also state-level rules to contend with. Anyone announcing that peptides have been “FDA approved” has either misunderstood the document or is counting on you not reading it.

Now comes the part where competitive athletes have to pay close attention: BPC-157 and TB-500 remain prohibited under the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) rules used by many tested sports. A change in how federal regulators view compounding peptides does not rewrite the WADA rulebook. A prescription is not automatically permission to compete with a substance in your system.

The U.S. Anti-Doping Agency (USADA) has already sanctioned athletes over these compounds. Proof that the obstacle is here to stay.  What the outlaws will have to contend with is that while there are banned peptides that can already be detected directly in an athlete’s urine or blood, others present a much tougher analytical problem. And a ban doesn’t require WADA to have a practical routine test for the substance before they ban it. So, that right there is the loophole. And trust me when I tell you, it’s going to be exploited. Why? Because peptides work.

I’m all for serious research. I’m also for admitting when thousands of testimonials cannot all be wrong. If the new policy leads to better manufacturing controls and useful clinical data, good. If it merely replaces the sketchy online vial with a more expensive sketchy vial wearing a white coat, we haven’t accomplished much. There’s an important difference between making something easier to obtain and proving it’s worth obtaining. And if you compete in a tested sport, there’s a third question: whether using it costs you your career. Don’t confuse the three. And remember, if an athlete is prone to cheating, chances are he will cheat. And with what will he use to cheat? The stuff that works. Peptides are just now showing up in force and its a force to be reconned with.

On Episode 310 of The Menace Podcast, host Dennis James was joined by Milos Sarcev, Chris Cormier, and special guest Terrence Ruffin, and the conversation moved towards the 2027 Mr. Olympia final. The man they call “Ruff Diesel” talked to the panel about the progress he needs to make, to finally win a title at the Olympia.

Ruffin, an iconic Men’s Physique competitor has appeared in nine Olympia finals, and qualified for his tenth by securing victories at the Mexico and Slovakia Pro events in October. Ruffin was at ninth place at the ‘O’ in 2016 and 2018 but found a career high placing of second in 2020 and 2021. He came fifth in 2026, so what does he need to work on, in order to progress in 2027?

“Do you believe in your heart that you can still win the Olympia,” asked host Dennis James. “100%” came the quick response from Ruffin, who explained that despite his vast experience, he is still very excited about that prospect. Ruff Diesel then provided a glimpse into the adjustments he may need to make, if he is to dominate bodybuilding’s biggest stage.

“My biggest issue is, I always end up doing too much,” he explained. “I told myself, this year, I’m going to say no to a lot more stuff.” Ruffin shared that his constant travel and business interests could be spreading him too thin. “But I’m trying to not do so much,” he relented.

“But you’ve started a new business too,” challenged The Menace. “You’re prepping for the Olympia and you’re opening up a gym. I mean, come on.”

Ruffin agreed that he takes on a lot. “I’m even (going to) have a meeting with the gym tomorrow, about handing off a couple of things,” he said. “Just to make sure I can focus like I need to.”

Ruffin says that he has learned to appreciate that getting to the pinnacle of bodybuilding requires his complete attention. “I’m giving up a part of the business at the gym, so I don’t have to do, like, the day to day,” he explained. The competitor now intends to keep his diary clearer by turning down events and reducing his travel. “I’m just all in, on just the gym training, and all of that.”

With a renewed focus on the prize, Milos Sarcev pushed further on what progress Ruffin will need to make with his physique, in order to win. “Conditioning, or size?” asked The Mind. “Both,” answered Ruffin, with a smile.

To see this conversation in full on The Menace Podcast, where the panel also discussed the latest bodybuilding gossip, news, and results, check it out on the Muscle & Fitness YouTube channel.

#8612. Joe Baena Gave Fans a Glimpse of His Bodybuilding Debut

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Joe Baena may be the son of Arnold Schwarzenegger, but he is certainly forging his own path in the competitive bodybuilding business. The 29-year-old recently made his debut at the INBA PNBA World Cup in El Segundo, CA, reaching an impressive fifth place on the natural stage. And, for anyone who is aspiring to compete in the future, Baena chronicled his first pro outing for an insightful glimpse.

“Each photo has a great story of what it is like to be a competitor at a bodybuilding show,” posted Baena for his 895,000 Instagram followers, providing all the backstage goings on during the World Cup on November 7.

Earlier this year, the young upstart dominated in the Men’s Physique category of the NPC Classic Physique and Open, during his amateur debut, and then went to earn his pro card at the INBA Iron Gladiator event a week later on April 4.

Sharing his feelings as he arrived for the World Cup, Baena said, “Tan on, nerves high, and just trying to mentally prepare for the day ahead. Excited to see the carbs doing their work and that the abs are still there after two meals.”

Sharing an image of the changing room, Baena explained that before each competitor gets under the spotlight, they like to watch the other athletes first. “Seeing the guys in the other classes is always very exciting,” he wrote. “As you can see new things in their posing routines and styles. Everyone brings their individual personalities to the stage.”

Half an hour before his own routine, Baena began to carb up. “About 20 to 30 minutes before stepping on the stage, I’m getting my last light carbs in to fill up the muscles and look as pumped as possible,” he shared. “A couple rice cakes and a little honey drizzle does just the trick.”

Then comes “The Pump Up” to get the blood flowing into the muscles. “There’s no gym or equipment provided for most bodybuilding competitions, so you have to bring your own resistance bands or get some help from another competitor backstage,” explained Baena. “The camaraderie was amazing and everyone was just so excited to be there.”

For this detailed prepper, being specific about which muscles to pump is highly important. “You gotta make sure you pump up the right muscles, especially the ones that are lacking or need the most volume to present,” he shared. “For me, I know my arms aren’t the biggest, so I always put a little extra effort into pumping up the biceps and triceps.”

“The first thing when you step out on stage is you all lineup and basically square up next to each other,” said the competitor. “Presenting yourself in the best way possible is important along with standing out from the other competitors. After you’ve all lined up and done the mandatory poses it’s time for the pose down! You all get as close to the judges as possible and flex off together. Standing next to each other, hitting all your favorite poses and trying to present yourself as the largest, most ripped and best-looking competitor out there. Occasionally going pose for pose or just doing your own thing, you want to attract the judge’s attention as much as possible.”

The posing routine is the “last but definitely not least” aspect of the competition, wrote Baena. “The posing routine is my favorite part of the whole process. The artistry aspect of bodybuilding is what I think makes the sport so great. Building your body up to be statue-like and choreographing a routine that emulates and shows the aesthetic and beauty of the body.”

Having flexed for all that he was worth at the World Cup, Baena explained that with 11 competitors in his category, “It was extremely nerve-racking, standing there waiting for my name to get called out. My goal going into the show was to get into the top five so when I heard my name get called at fifth place it was a huge relief. I achieved what I signed out for and could finally think forward about getting a burger. Of course, the dream is to win the show and be the number one overall, but it all comes in due time and with the right amount of work. This was only my first pro show, and I couldn’t be more proud of myself. This is my first year competing with my first show being the end of March, the second show been the week after, and this being only my third show. A lot of the guys I competed with have been competing for many years now, so it is great motivation to be able to stand up and stack up next to them.”

Finally, Baena indulges in a well-earned meal. But what did he eat? “The Apple Pan,” he revealed. “Definitely one of the best burgers in LA. Had to celebrate at the Apple Pan for my first meal post competition. I ordered two burgers and two slices of pie. Somehow, even after eating all that I still had room for more.”

Glowing after “The Champion’s Pie,” Baena said, “I’m a huge pie lover and having been on prep during many weddings, my birthday, and other celebrations (where) I had to skip on many desserts, this pie tasted incredible, but I will say achieving a goal you set out for is a lot sweeter than any cheat meal.”

And that’s just as well, because soon begins the prep for Baena’s next competition.
