#8611. The Comfort Crisis

As with many things in life these days, it all started with an episode of the Peter Attia podcast.

In this edition, our nation’s most Badass Doctor was interviewing a guest I initially dismissed as not overly applicable to my own lifestyle. A young,excessively handsome dude who happened to be a writer with a new book out. But the headline of the episode was just intriguing enough to get me to click.

Wow, what an amazing turn of phrase, and what a concise summary of the core of this whole Mustachianism thing I’ve been trying to express for the past dozen years.

While the news headlines cry constantly about our nationwide personal debt crisis or health crisis or any other number of things that suggest that life is so hard these days, I have always seen the opposite: on average, we Americans seem to have a problem of ridiculous overindulgence and easiness in our lives, and our main problem is not recognizing it, and the damage it does to us.

So of course I had to click, and then listen to the whole two hour episode, and then buy the book, and then spend the past month reading and digesting it in small, meaningful chunks like the modern-day chunk of scripture-like wisdom that it is. And wow, am I glad I did so.

The author is Michael Easter, a former writer for Men’s Health magazine was also once catastrophically addicted to alcohol – and descended from a long family line of ancestors with the same affliction.

He was lucky to catch himself from that fall in time to save his own life, and that story alone makes the book worth reading as someone who has stood by helplessly as loved ones battled with addiction. But I think his history with overindulgence in the hollow comforts of alcohol also gives him an edge on writing about the battle between comfort and hardship on the bigger stage of life in general.

So what is The Comfort Crisis about, and how can it make all of our lives better?

The best part about this book is just what a damned good writer this Easter guy is. Like many of the most fun popular science books*, it follows a split narrative which jumps back and forth to interweave the story of an insanely difficult caribou hunting trip he joined in a remote pocket of Alaska, with the appropriate bits of science, psychology and cultural commentary that help us explain and learn from each chapter of the epic shit he had just endured. This allows us to process and apply the lessons in our own lives.

For example, have you ever wondered why the type of bored, rich suburbanites who populate the board of your local Homeowner Association and whine about unacceptably tall weeds or unauthorized skateboarding on Nextdoor are so insufferable?

Why can’t they do something better with their time?

It turns out that there’s a scientific explanation for these unfortunate people, along with most of our other problems:

The tendency of humans to always scan our environment for problems, regardless of how safe and perfect that environment is.

The book cited a study in which researchers told people to look for danger, in an environment which gradually became safer and safer:

“When they ran out of stuff to find they would start looking for a wider range of stuff, even if this was not conscious or intentional, because their job was to look for threats.”

“With that in mind, Levari recently conducted a series of studies to find out if the human brain searches for problems even when problems become infrequent or don’t exist.“

“As we experience fewer problems, we don’t become more satisfied. We just lower our threshold for what we consider a problem.“

In other words, even when our lives are virtually problem free, instead of appreciating our good fortune we just start making up shit that we can complain about instead.

And then our politicians cock their greasy, finely-tuned ears in our direction and make up policies to appease our mostly-insubstantial concerns. And they invent their own trivial “wedge” issues to get us to all bicker about our different cultures and religions, suddenly caring about things that would not have even been problems if nobody told us they were.

And there’s America’s weakness in a nutshell, and meanwhile our strength comes entirely from the times we choose not to waste our time stooping to this level.

Meanwhile, the opposite effect holds true: people who survive in rougher environments than us end up more resilient and less prone to complaining.

In a series of recent interviews, Ukrainian people living in the war zones of their occupied country were asked “is it safe to live where you live?” and a strangely high percentage still said “Yes” – not all that different from the responses of US residents when asked the same question about their own cities.

This adaptation principle also explains why some first generation immigrants tend to build businesses and wealth while their own offspring in second and third generations are more likely to become complacent and spend it down. As an immigrant myself, I can see why this is: conditions were just slightly more harsh and less comfortable and wealthy where I grew up, so I adapted to those conditions as “normal” which made the United States seem posh and easy by comparison. Which made it easier to spend less money and accumulate more.

The trap of pointless worry is just one of the many revelations of The Comfort Crisis. It also gives insightful explanations for why spending time in Nature boosts our mental and physical health, while cubicles and car driving grind us down.

There’s something in our biological wiring that responds instantly and powerfully to everything natural, in ways that you can’t get anywhere else.

Even placing a single plant into a hospital room will measurably improve the recovery of almost all patients from almost all ailments. So can you imagine the power of the medicine you are inhaling if you step into a real, living forest? And what if you spent several hours there, or even several days?

Later, we get lessons on our human adaptation towards the ratio of effort to reward:

And our bizarre natural aversion to physical exertion:

Which is remarkable, given the absolutely insane cost this tendency imposes upon us.

Moving your body, even a bit, has enormous benefits – again to almost all people towards reducing the probability and severity of almost all diseases. So can you imagine the benefit of moving your body for several hours per day in a natural environment, and including heavy load bearing and bits of extreme exertion?

These things are not speculative pieces of alternative medicine. They are known, easily and reproducibly tested, and proven to be the most effective things we can possibly do with our time.

So why, the actual fuck, are people still sitting inside, watching Netflix, driving to work, and then driving to the doctor’s office to get deeper and deeper analysis of a neverending series of exotic and mysterious and unsolvable problems with their physical and mental health?

We should at least start with the stuff we know is essential – maximum outdoor time every day, heavy exertion including with weights, minimal time spent sitting and driving, and minimum junk food, sugar, and alcohol. You definitely don’t have to be perfect, but just understand that these are the big levers for physical and mental health.

Only then, once you reach these minimum basic things for human survival, should you expect that more exotic and niche medicines and treatments are the only course of action.

By all means, follow your doctor’s orders and don’t just dump all of your medications down the sink because of this MMM rant. But at the same time, realize that the stuff that is hard and uncomfortable is very likely to be the stuff that improves your life the most.

It’s all the stuff that Mr. Money Mustache has been telling you since 2012, but with more detail and less distraction. This book is a concentrated packet of advice for solid living.

In a happy coincidence, I happened to be in the middle of some hard stuff** of my own as I worked my way through The Comfort Crisis and I found the perspective quite useful and transformative to apply hot off the press.

Normally somewhat of a homebody, I had embarked on a solo journey for some Carpentourism deep in the mountains of Southwestern Colorado. I had my whole life shrunk down into the new Model Y including food, bed, and the necessary tools and materials to tackle a pretty long laundry list of tasks on two different construction projects (fixing up a mini-resort property in Salida, and starting construction on a small cabin in Durango)

The trip immediately took a turn towards the dramatic as I climbed into the mountains and drove straight into the most torrential rainstorm I have ever seen, then accidentally broke a traffic law in a remote mountain town right in front of both of the local police officers ($115 fine and two points off my license), then five minutes after that had a small pebble hit my brand-new windshield which instantly spread into a crack that spans the whole thing, all before finally limping into Salida to unpack and get started on the work.

“Big deal”, I can already hear you saying, “Retired man experiences two minor incidents while taking a vacation in his luxury car.”

And you’re right, and that is exactly my point.

My life is so stable and comfortable that even these two miniature challenges threw me off balance, and I arrived in a slightly bummed and stressed-out state. But I still knew that in the bigger picture, they are good for me if I accept them as the lessons they are rather than choosing to continue to worry about them.

As the trip went on, more things happened, almost as if The Comfort Crisis book were trying to prove a point. I drove three hours deeper into the mountains and up the steep dirt road to arrive at my second friend’s piece of land – a plot of forest in the mountains just outside of Durango.

My work days in that high desert environment in the peak of summer were hot and physically demanding. It was hard to keep my tools, and my food supply in the cooler, and myself protected from the scorching sun (and a strange neverending blizzard of tree pollen) while still getting the job done. There was no indoor plumbing and we had to be very careful with our limited water supply. And then at the end of each day I had to reshuffle everything and set my car back up as a bedroom and crawl in for the night. Alone and far from home.

But instead of feeling depressed as I experienced this constant hardship, the opposite thing was happening: I felt more alive and more badass with each passing day. I got better at being a feral forest man.

One day, my co-builder and I decided to take the afternoon off and head to the wild, remote Lemon Reservoir for some paddleboarding. We didn’t bring our phones or any other conveniences or amenities – just two boards and the minimal clothing required for swimming. And we headed out into a stiff headwind and little whitecap waves, laughing at the freedom of the experience.

It was hard, and slightly scary, as we got further and further from the shore. Progress was slow even with serious paddling, and we didn’t have any particular plan beyond the spirit of “let’s GO!”

But again Michael Easter was there whispering in my ear, saying,

“Is this difficult, Mustache? GOOOOoood! Then you’d better keep going!”

So we did. And we got way out into that lake, to a point where the water was shielded from the wind by the mountains on the other side. And it was awesome.

We cruised over to the shore to explore a particularly scenic meadow, coated with the softest green mossy grass and exuberantly colored wildflowers, and set at an impossibly steep angle. And damn I wished that I could have taken pictures, but in a strange way this forced me to burn that spot more thoroughly into my memories using my own senses instead.

Then we headed back out into the center of the lake, set down the paddles, and just laid down on our boards to let the wind and the waves take us back towards the far end of the lake where we had started. And what a strange, serene feeling it was, floating on just a tube of air over two hundred feet of cold blue water, feeling like a jungle man with no cares and no plans and no material possessions. It could have been scary, but instead it was one of the best and most relaxed moments of my life.

Eventually, this week of forest living and exertion had to come to an end so I could get back to my own town to be a Dad again. But it ended with a final reminder of the principles of the Comfort Crisis – after so many days relatively extreme work and a relatively sparse food supply, I had grown used to a healthy background hunger. Which is yet another thing that we are meant to experience as humans – being satisfied and free from hunger all the time is neither normal nor healthy.

But when my hosts took me out on the town for a final night thank you dinner at the Mexican restaurant, the immense Burrito platter I consumed turned out to be the most delicious meal of my life.

Purposeful Hardship vs. Purposeful Spending

There has been a lot of talk directed at the FIRE community recently about how bad we are at spending our money, and how we all need to loosen up. And there’s a small amount of truth to it, as my local friends Carl and Mindy recently admitted during a grilling on the Ramit Sethi podcast.

But we also need to keep this whole idea of excessive comfort in mind, and the damage it does to the natural human condition.

It’s great to spend money on adventures and improving yourself, being generous to others, and making the world a better place.

But it’s also way too easy to fool yourself into thinking you “want” things that just make your life easier and easier.

So your job is to catch yourself before this happens, and learn to keep things challenging, even as you upgrade the rest of your life experience.

In other words: buy yourself better tools, not softer chairs.

For me, the questions that help me decide which “jobs” are worth doing for life include these ones: – Would I still keep doing this job for life, even if I didn’t get paid for it? – Does this job contribute to my physical and emotional health? (positive contact with other humans, plus physical exertion outdoors) – Does the job allow enough time flexibility or time off that I can also take care of myself and those around me? (8 hours of sleep with no alarm clock, time to spend with your kids or travel to take care of your aging family members, etc)

If all these things apply, it may well be a good job regardless of how hard it is.

If few or none of them apply, there is still good news: there are lots of jobs that DO offer these things. Especially thanks to the power of self employment.

One thing my family did that most people find crazy is to get rid of most of our seating furniture. We ditched one couch, two armchairs, one chair-and-a-half, one upholstered ottoman, and six dining room tables. We also lowered our table and replaced our conventional beds with wool pads on the floor.

Now we sit and sleep on the floor for the most part. It’s encouraged us to move our bodies more (lots of floor space means room for stretching and exercising) and getting down to the floor to sit or sleep (and then getting back up again) means lots of movement that strengthens our legs. My sister in particular thinks this is verging on child abuse and most of my friends just think we’re nuts. But this is a normal way to live in much of the world; we just find it odd because our culture says it’s not how it should be done.

It was difficult at first, and sure, a nice cushy couch still feels good to me (for about five minutes), but it’s amazing how quickly you start to crave things that require more effort once you change your mindset about it.

One thing I didn’t see anyone mention is the fact that humans, like virtually all other mammals, are hard-wired to do as little as possible outside of the necessities (finding food, shelter, fornicating, fighting enemies) because energy expended on activities not related to those necessary for survival may just cost one their survival, at least in the “old days” of the jungle. The same evolutionary factors that make our bodies not want to shed fat or what to eat (sweet, not bitter) are in play when deciding whether to take the stairs or the escalator. It’s highly likely that without the default of lazy that most of what makes up civilization wouldn’t exist, since virtually everything we’ve ever invented beyond ensuring basic survival has been to reduce energy expenditure. Why walk when you can drive? Why forage when you can farm? ETC.

So the human animal has to consciously make the decision to do that which goes against his/her basic instincts.

#8607. Why the Jefferson Curl Can Be Valuable for Some Lifters

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Repeated or prolonged spinal flexion can increase stress on the tissues around the spine. The Jefferson curl targets spinal flexion by improving spinal control and strengthening positions you might find yourself in and out of the gym.

It’s considered an obscure exercise. If you’ve never heard of or seen it, you might think it’s the latest move for giving your biceps a pump. But the Jefferson curl is far from an arm-day exercise.

The Jefferson curl ia actually lower-back move—one that contradicts almost everything known about lower-back health. To perform it, you hold a weight in front of you and slowly lower it toward the floor while flexing your spine. In other words, you round your back under load and keep bending.

End-range spinal flexion is a key reason many trainers hesitate to add the Jefferson curl to their clients’ workouts. But for the right lifter, it can mean better control, greater flexion tolerance, and improved mobility. However, if it isn’t a good fit, it can increase your injury risk.

So, should you include it in your program?

According to two strength experts, the answer is, it depends.

The Jefferson curl is a controlled exercise where you deliberately flex the spine one segment at a time while holding a light weight. From the neck down, slowly round your back through the upper, middle, and lower back as you reach toward the floor.

The goal is not to see how far you can flex, but to control spinal flexion through a range you can own while placing the entire posterior-chain tissues under tension.

Sets and reps: According to Physical Therapist Bo Babenko, start with 3 to 5 repetitions at a time, using only 15 to 20 pounds as a stretch. Emphasize taking 2 to 3 deep breaths at the bottom, with an elongated exhale to stretch the tissues involved.

Placement: After your main strength work or during a mobility session.

The Jefferson curl challenges (arguably) one of strength training’s biggest blind spots: the idea that the spine should always stay rigid. Outside of a neutral spine while lifting, your spine is designed to move. You flex to tie your shoes, pick things up, sit, reach, climb, and perform plenty of athletic movements. Avoiding spinal flexion doesn’t prepare you for those demands.

That is where the Jefferson Curl can help. When performed well, it lets you train spinal flexion rather than encountering it when fatigued or in a variable environment. The point is not to teach you to round your back during a max deadlift. The point is to recognize that spinal stiffness and spinal movement are both movement skills.

But spinal flexion is dose-dependent. Too much of anything, even water, will hurt you.

That is why this lift deserves neither a blanket ban nor a free pass.

There are some rewards with the risk, and here they are.

One of its biggest benefits is that it asks you to move the spine one segment at a time, rather than treating your entire spine as a single rigid block. That controlled flexion and extension can improve body awareness and give you more options for how you move.

The Jefferson curl also places the hamstrings, spinal erectors, and other posterior tissues under tension through a longer ROM than many strength exercises. “I believe the Jefferson curl certainly has a place,” explains Babenko. “To decompress the spine and stretch out the posterior chain.”

Most flexibility work is passive, but the Jefferson curl takes a different approach by loading the range you are trying to improve. That means the hamstrings and trunk are not just becoming more flexible; they are learning to produce and control force in that range.

If your hamstrings are tight, your spinal control disappears, or you start chasing depth without control, you’ll find out quickly. That makes the exercise useful for both mobility assessment and training.

Repeated or prolonged spinal flexion can increase creep in passive tissues such as ligaments and discs, raising the risk of lower back injury. Critics view it as an unnecessary risk. Their argument is simple: if you can improve mobility without loading end-range spinal flexion, why take the chance?

Any lifter worth their salt knows to keep their back neutral during deadlifts, squats, and rows. “Most lifters need to generate, transfer, and resist substantial forces while maintaining core stiffness and controlling spinal motion,” explains strength coach Matt Wenning. “These exercises can develop these qualities without requiring loaded end-range spinal flexion.”

Loading flexion can blur the line between a controlled mobility drill and poor technique during heavy lifting.

It’s not meant as a strength test, but some people will always try to see how much weight they can do. “I had a patient show up with back pain,” says Babenko. “She was trying to build up well over 150 pounds on the Jefferson curl, and, well, she hurt her lower back.”

Too much load increases the risk. Instead of slow, controlled segmental flexion, you get a loaded collapse with little benefit.

Hamstring stretching, hip-hinge drills, and RDLs can all enhance hamstring mobility without taking the spine through deliberate loaded flexion. That makes the Jefferson Curl optional.

There is no direct research on the Jefferson curl itself—a point backed up by Wenning.

“Direct evidence that Jefferson curls improve athletic performance, prevent low-back injuries, or outperform established strength and mobility interventions is insufficient.”

But most research focuses on spinal flexion, segmental spinal movement, flexibility training, and how spinal tissues behave under repeated or prolonged flexion.

A 2023 study comparing spinal flexion and extension exercises with more trunk movement found improvements in spinal flexibility, including finger-to-floor distance. This supports one of the Jefferson curl’s main purposes: learning to move through spinal flexion gradually rather than treating the spine as a single rigid unit.

One study found that 20 minutes of full lumbar flexion altered passive tissue contributions and increased demand on the spinal extensors afterward, meaning the extensors had to work harder after sustained flexion.

That study focused on sustained or repeated flexion exposures, not a few slow Jefferson curls. A set of five deliberate reps is not the same dose as sitting or hanging in deep flexion for 20 minutes.

No current research says spinal flexion is dangerous. “The spine can certainly flex, and spinal flexion itself is not inherently dangerous,” says Wenning

You know the pros and cons, but that doesn’t determine whether the Jefferson curl is a good fit. But this does.

The Jefferson curl sits in the moderate- high risk, moderate-reward category. The risk comes from loaded spinal flexion. That does not mean flexion is dangerous, but it does mean the dose matters. Too much load, range, fatigue, or volume can turn this mobility drill into unnecessary stress on the spine’s passive tissues.

“Jefferson curls offer limited advantages for most lifters,” says Wenning. “Particularly when more established exercises can address the same training goals with greater specificity and more controllable loading.”

The reward is that the Jefferson curl can train something most strength programs avoid: controlled spinal flexion. It can improve segmental spinal control, reveal mobility restrictions, and load the posterior chain through a long range of motion. For healthy lifters who tolerate flexion well, it can be useful.

The biggest factor in the risk-to-reward equation is intent. If you treat the Jefferson curl like a max-strength lift, the risk climbs fast. If you treat it like a light, slow, carefully progressed mobility-strength drill, the equation changes.

The reward isn’t massive, and the risk isn’t trivial, which is why this exercise belongs in the “use with a reason” category rather than the “everyone should do it” one.

The Jefferson curl isn’t one-size-fits-all, and people have opinions on both sides of the spectrum. Critics see a rounded spine and assume danger. Supporters sometimes swing too far the other way and act like controlled flexion makes the spine bulletproof.

Many exercises have a larger margin for error, like biceps curls, while others have a smaller margin, like the Jefferson curl. That means you should approach this exercise with caution.

But for the right lifter, used with light loads and a slow progression, it can be one way to train a position most strength programs avoid altogether. Spinal flexion sometimes happens, so it helps to be prepared.

The problem isn’t always spinal flexion; it’s treating flexion without respect.

#8602. Scott Eastwood Is Still Seeking a Rush, Just at a Slower Pace

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

He still surfs. He still trains jiujitsu and Muay Thai. And the actor still lifts and still enjoys putting himself in situations that demand something from him physically.

What has changed at 40 is the way he prepares for all of it.

There was a time when Eastwood could train hard, wake up sore, and trust that his body would bounce back. Now, he is far more interested in staying mobile, pain-free, and ready for whatever he wants to do outside the gym.

Over the last five years, Eastwood says that shift has become increasingly intentional.

“Recovery is probably the biggest difference,” Eastwood told M&F. “I think I’d probably put it number one. I listen to my body more and take more care in my recovery than I ever did in my 20s or 30s.”

This doesn’t mean that he’s less serious about training, it just means Eastwood’s objective has evolved. Looking like a capable athlete has given way to a much more important goal: staying physically capable.

“Obviously I want to be strong, but I also want to be really flexible and limber and be able to react to whatever the world throws at you, where you’re not going to pull something or you’re not going to hurt yourself.”

Eastwood ,who’s latest film, Lucky Strike, is now streaming on Hulu, used to organize his gym work around the familiar bodybuilding split—chest, back, and different muscle groups on different days.

Now he prefers training that puts his entire body to work.

“I think [now I’m] just a little bit more focused on holistic workouts,” Eastwood said. “I’m far more focused now on my core, just because of body pain and how your body feels, and all the things that feel better, which kind of stem out from your core.”

When he isn’t working on a film, Eastwood says he typically lifts three or four times per week, splitting those sessions between gym and home workouts. He also tries to fit in Muay Thai or jiujitsu. Yoga has become a constant.

Eastwood says there isn’t a day that passes where he doesn’t do some version of it, often half an hour in the morning and another later in the day.

When he is filming, the expectations change.

A 6 a.m. call time might require a 5 a.m. gym session. Long production days can already be physically taxing, so those workouts become less about progress. It’s an evolution in the thinking that every training session needs to prove something. Eastwood still trains hard, but there isn’t much value now in forcing his body through movements that no longer feel worth the risk.

“You’re spending a lot of time on your feet, and it’s typically physical,” Eastwood said. “So you’re kind of just doing a little more maintenance when you’re working. You’re not getting the gains that you might get if you’re not working.”

The gym has never been the only testing grounds for Eastwood.

Surfing, martial arts, and hiking are still a part of his life, and each demands something slightly different from his body.

It’s a large part why strength alone no longer satisfies him.

“If I want to continue to do jiujitsu, and I want to do Muay Thai, and I want to continue to surf, I’ve got to take care of my body,” Eastwood says. “Which means strength, flexibility, and mobility. I’ve got to kind of do all these things, or my body is going to get trashed doing these sports.”

Those activities also provide him with feedback that a mirror will miss. A stiff body doesn’t perform well on a surfboard. Poor mobility isn’t less obvious when someone is trying to control you on a mat. Carrying unnecessary soreness into either activity can turn something meant to be enjoyable into a problem quickly.

Eastwood hasn’t lost his appetite for these passions that come with risk. However, age has made him more selective about which risks within those passions are worth taking.

That means foregoing chasing a massive surf or testing himself on the mat against whoever wants to go the hardest. When he was younger, these thoughts might have not even entered into his thinking.

Now, it’s more thoughtful. He still wants the challenge, to compete with himself, and to feel capable. These activities are just no longer a barometer for his toughness.

Ask him what physical quality matters more now than it did at 25, and the answer is an understandable one.

“Flexibility,” Eastwood says. “Flexibility and just not being in pain. If you can take care of your body where you’re not in pain all the time, that’s really valuable.”

One of the biggest shifts for Eastwood is the attention to recovery.

Yoga, sauna sessions, and Epsom salt baths have all been part of his routine for years, but sleep has become especially important as both his training and work demands have changed.

“Just getting a good night’s sleep, I value it so much more now,” Eastwood says.

10 to 15-hour set days require focus, energy, and often physical effort. Arriving not fully rested often produces immediate consequences.

“I can’t do the job that I do well and focus if I haven’t had a great night’s sleep,” he said.

His approach to nutrition is also uncomplicated. Eastwood says he follows a Mediterranean-style diet built around whole foods, including fish, red meat, grains, and plenty of vegetables. He also refuses to turn an occasional bag of chips or dessert into a moral crisis.

“I don’t make it some hard and fast rule that you have to do,” he says. “I just think those just get a little too rigid.”

His preference for simplicity also played a role in why Eastwood became a co-owner of North Performance.

Eastwood says longtime friend Mike Lucas shared the frustration of trying to travel while managing individual supplements. Both men wanted something easier to maintain without pretending a supplement could replace the fundamentals.

“You still have to work out. You have to get good sleep and have good recovery,” he says. “Having good supplements is just going to help those things. The basics are the basics. They don’t change regardless.”

When he is filming, Eastwood says North is part of his morning routine, but the rest of his priorities remain the same.

He still has to eat well. He still has to move. If the day is packed and there are only 25 minutes for himself, he’ll find somewhere to fit in exercise, yoga, or mobility work. Everything beyond that is what he calls “extra credit.”

It’s a simplicity that defines fitness at 40 for him.

Looking strong doesn’t mean anything if his back is aching or his body is too tight to do the things all of his training was meant to prepare him for.

The goal going into the next decade is simple: keep enough strength to be useful, maintain mobility to move well, and have enough durability to keep saying yes to the things he enjoys.

“I think fit is more how you feel and less aesthetic,” Eastwood said. “[Looking good] is great, but if you’re in pain because you’re not doing it correctly, then who gives a shit about what you look like?”

The ultimate domestic travel rewards benefit for families and couples

Imagine this: you book a flight for yourself, and your spouse — or your best friend, or your mom — flies with you for the cost of taxes alone. Not a discount. Not a sale. Completely. Free. For up to two full calendar years. That's the Southwest Companion Pass, and it is, without question, the single most powerful perk in all of domestic travel rewards. The ChooseFI community has a saying: if you only ever pursue one travel rewards strategy in your life, make it this one. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop. A round-trip Southwest flight from Denver to Cancún might run $400 per person. A family of four flying during spring break? You're looking at $1,600 cash. But with the Companion Pass, you pay for two tickets and the other two fly nearly free (taxes and fees only) — cutting your out-of-pocket cost in half, every single flight, for nearly two years. Run the numbers over a year of typical family travel and you're looking at **$2,000 to $8,000 in total value** from a single benefit. The CPP (cents per point) range here — **1.5 to 5.9 cents per point** — is what makes this genuinely remarkable. Southwest's Rapid Rewards program values points at roughly 1.4 cents toward any flight. But the Companion Pass doesn't just redeem points efficiently; it *doubles the value of every redemption you make while it's active*. That's the pricing inefficiency the loyalty system has quietly built in, and the FI community is uniquely positioned to exploit it. Think about what 135,000 points normally buys: roughly $1,890 worth of Southwest flights. Solid, but not earth-shattering. Now attach the Companion Pass, and those same points — redeemed strategically over two years — effectively unlock $3,780 or more in flight value for your household. No blackout dates. No seat restrictions. No change fees. Just book, fly, repeat. This isn't a first-class lounge or a lie-flat bed over the Pacific. It's something arguably more valuable for the FI-minded family: **sustainable, repeatable, nearly free domestic travel** that works with your actual life.

The Companion Pass isn't a points redemption — it's a status benefit. That distinction is everything, and it's the insight that separates people who get this from people who miss it entirely.

Here's how it works: Southwest grants the Companion Pass when you earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. Once you hit that threshold, you designate one person as your companion, and that person flies with you on every flight — paid or points — for the remainder of that calendar year plus the entire following calendar year.

The key word is "earn." Points transferred in from partners count. Credit card signup bonuses count. Shopping portal purchases count. Almost every way you accumulate points counts toward the 135,000 threshold — except points purchased directly from Southwest.

The pricing inefficiency here is a calendar arbitrage opportunity. If you earn the Companion Pass on January 2nd, you get it for the rest of that year and all of the next year — nearly two full calendar years of 2-for-1 flights. If you earn it on November 15th, you get roughly 13 months. The strategy is to time your credit card signup bonuses to post in January, maximizing your benefit window.

Most ChooseFI members build their 135,000 points through a combination of strategies:

Chase Ultimate Rewards → Southwest Rapid Rewards (1:1, Instant) Chase transfers to Southwest at a 1:1 ratio and the transfer is instant — points appear in your Rapid Rewards account within minutes. This makes Chase points (earned on cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Ink Business cards) the most efficient fuel for this strategy.

Marriott Bonvoy → Southwest Rapid Rewards (3:1, 1-5 days) Marriott transfers at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Southwest point), and transfers take 1-5 days. This is a less efficient path — use it only if you have a surplus of Marriott points and no better option.

The most reliable path to 135,000 points is stacking Southwest credit card signup bonuses. Southwest's consumer and business cards frequently offer bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points each. A couple who each opens one card, or one person who opens both a personal and business card, can often hit the threshold with signup bonuses alone — before spending a dollar on the portal.

Since Southwest charges no fuel surcharges on award flights and points never expire, there's no penalty for building this balance over several months. The Rapid Rewards program is revenue-based with dynamic pricing, meaning points cover the full fare including taxes — no hidden redemption fees to erode your value.

Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards account and your Southwest Rapid Rewards account and tally your existing points. You need 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points earned in a single calendar year to trigger the Companion Pass. Note: points already sitting in your Rapid Rewards account from prior years don't count — you need to earn 135,000 in the target calendar year.

The optimal window is October through December of the prior year. Apply for Southwest credit cards (personal and/or business) so that your signup bonuses post to your Rapid Rewards account in January. Verify with Southwest's current card offers — signup bonuses of 50,000-75,000 points are common. A couple can each apply for a card; a solo pursuer can apply for both a personal and a business card if they have qualifying self-employment income.

Call Chase or Southwest after your first statement closes to confirm when points will post. Timing is everything.

Once your signup bonuses post, calculate how many points you still need. If you're short:

Southwest will notify you by email once you've crossed 135,000 qualifying points. Log into your Rapid Rewards account at southwest.com and navigate to "My Account" → "Companion Pass" to confirm the benefit is active.

You can designate — and change — your companion up to three times per calendar year. Name your most frequent travel partner first. Go to southwest.com, log in, and find the Companion Pass section to add their name and contact information.

Searching is simple: go to southwest.com and search any route. Toggle between "$ Dollars" and "Rapid Rewards Points" to see your cost. When you book with points and your companion is designated, Southwest will automatically prompt you to add your companion to the same flight. Your companion pays taxes only — typically $5.60 each way for domestic flights.

Pro tip: Southwest opens its booking window 330 days in advance. For peak travel like spring break or holiday weeks, set a calendar reminder and book the day the window opens.

The Companion Pass works because Southwest treats it as a status benefit rather than a points redemption. Most airline companion programs require you to burn miles for the second ticket or limit usage to specific fare classes. Southwest flips this model: once you earn the pass, your companion flies on every single flight you take — paid or award — for the remainder of the qualifying year plus the entire following calendar year. The only cost is taxes. Because Southwest has no blackout dates, no fuel surcharges, and no change fees, the pass amplifies in value with every trip you take. The January-earning calendar arbitrage is the key optimization that turns a good benefit into an extraordinary one.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's make this real. It's March, and your family of four wants to spend a week in Orlando this July — theme parks, pool time, the works.

A quick search on southwest.com shows round-trip flights from Chicago Midway to Orlando for $320 per person. For four tickets, that's $1,280 cash. Standard family travel math: painful but doable.

You have the Companion Pass active, earned back in January. You book two tickets: yours at 22,000 Rapid Rewards points (worth ~$308 at 1.4 cents per point), and your spouse's ticket at $5.60 in taxes as your designated companion. Your two kids? You use 44,000 more points for their tickets. Total out-of-pocket: 66,000 points + $11.20 in taxes.

Let's value those 66,000 points at their Chase transfer cost — you transferred them 1:1 from Chase Ultimate Rewards, where they were worth roughly $825 in travel via the portal. But by pairing them with the Companion Pass, your spouse flies nearly free, effectively doubling your points' purchasing power on this trip.

Cash price: $1,280. Your cost: 66,000 points + $11.20. That's a CPP of roughly 1.9 cents per point on the base redemption — but accounting for your companion flying nearly free, the effective CPP on the entire trip rockets to 3.8 cents per point. Well within the 1.5–5.9 cent range where this sweet spot lives.

And here's what makes Southwest specifically wonderful for families: no change fees. Book in March, change in June when your kid's baseball tournament schedule shifts, rebook without penalty. No one in the FI community is paying $200-per-person change fees.

The experience itself? Economy class on Southwest, open seating, snacks, and friendly crew. It's not lie-flat business class to Tokyo — but that's not the point. The point is your family of four flies to Florida for a week, and the flights barely register on your annual budget. That's FI-level travel.

Time your credit card applications so signup bonuses post in January of your target year. A bonus that posts January 5th gives you until December 31st of the following year to use the Companion Pass — nearly 24 months of 2-for-1 flights. This single timing decision can mean the difference between 13 months and 23 months of value.

The Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal (rapidrewardsshopping.com) awards points on purchases at hundreds of retailers. Even after you've earned the Companion Pass, continuing to earn Rapid Rewards points means more flights at lower point costs. Treat it like a cashback portal and check it before any online purchase.

Southwest opens availability 330 days in advance. For Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and summer weekends in popular markets, set a calendar reminder and book the exact morning the window opens. Southwest doesn't have blackout dates, but high-demand flights sell out in Wanna Get Away fare class — the cheapest points tier — quickly.

You can change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. If your life situation changes — a different travel partner, a new relationship, a child aging into a separate ticket — use this flexibility. Just don't burn all three changes frivolously.

Purchased points do not count toward the 135,000 qualifying threshold for the Companion Pass. Don't make this mistake when you're close to the threshold — transfer from Chase instead.

Some people try to earn the Companion Pass in November or December. You'll get it for only a few weeks before the calendar resets. The math simply doesn't work. January earning is the only strategy worth pursuing.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards Performance Business Credit Card (or similar business cards) have separate signup bonuses that stack with personal card bonuses. If you have any self-employment income — freelancing, a side hustle, a rental property — you likely qualify. This is often the fastest path to 135,000 points for a single applicant.

The Southwest Companion Pass was practically invented for the FI-minded family. If you have a consistent travel partner — a spouse, a partner, a parent you visit annually — and you fly domestically more than two or three times a year, this benefit will transform your travel budget.

Minimum points to get started: You need to earn 135,000 qualifying Rapid Rewards points in a single calendar year. In practice, this means you either need access to Southwest credit card signup bonuses (which requires good to excellent credit, typically 700+) or a substantial existing balance of Chase Ultimate Rewards points to transfer at 1:1.

How it fits the FI strategy: The Companion Pass is a force multiplier. Every dollar you would have spent on a second ticket stays in your investment accounts instead. Over a two-year Companion Pass window, a couple who takes six domestic trips per year could easily bank $2,000-$4,000 in travel savings — real money that compounds.

Who this is NOT for: Solo travelers get zero benefit from the Companion Pass. International travelers who primarily fly non-Southwest routes won't find much use here. And if you're averse to economy class or require a specific airline's premium cabin, this redemption isn't your path.

The Southwest Companion Pass earns a **moderate difficulty rating** — and that rating is almost entirely about the *earning*, not the booking. Once you have the Companion Pass, booking is literally the simplest award experience in travel rewards: search southwest.com, find your flight, click "Add Companion." There are no partner airlines to navigate, no availability calendars to decode, no call centers to endure. It's a 5/5 on ease of booking for a reason. The moderate rating comes from **three earning challenges**: **1. The credit requirement.** Southwest credit cards require good to excellent credit. If you're early in your credit-building journey, this strategy may need to wait 12-18 months while you strengthen your profile. **2. The timing discipline.** Earning the pass is straightforward, but earning it in January takes planning. You need to apply for cards 2-3 months in advance and coordinate signup bonus posting dates — something most people have never had to think about. **3. The 135,000-point threshold.** This is a real number. It requires intentional credit card strategy, not casual spending. For a single applicant without a business card, it may require supplementing with Chase transfers or portal activity. **How to overcome these challenges:** - Start planning in **October or November** for a January earn target - Check whether you qualify for a Southwest business card — it dramatically simplifies reaching the threshold - Use the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal year-round to passively accumulate qualifying points If you've successfully applied for a travel rewards credit card before and you have a consistent travel partner, you can absolutely do this. The ChooseFI community has helped hundreds of families earn the Companion Pass — and not one of them regretted the effort.

Open a personal and/or business Southwest credit card so that signup bonuses of 50,000 to 75,000 points each will post to your Rapid Rewards account in January. Call to confirm when points will post after your first statement closes.

Once signup bonuses post, calculate your gap. Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards at 1:1 (instant) to fill any shortfall. Use the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal for additional earning on everyday purchases.

After Southwest confirms your Companion Pass, log in to southwest.com and designate your travel partner. Book flights as normal — Southwest will prompt you to add your companion for taxes only ($5.60 each way domestic).

Set calendar reminders for Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and summer travel. Southwest opens its booking window 330 days in advance. Book the morning the window opens to lock in Wanna Get Away fares at the lowest point costs.

The Companion Pass is valid for the remainder of the calendar year in which you earn it plus the entire following calendar year. If you earn it on January 2nd, you get nearly 24 months of 2-for-1 flights. If you earn it in November, you get roughly 14 months. This is why timing your earning to January is the critical optimization.

Yes. Signup bonuses, spending on Southwest cards, points transferred from Chase Ultimate Rewards, and points earned through the Rapid Rewards Shopping Portal all count as qualifying points. The only points that do not count are those purchased directly from Southwest.

Southwest allows you to change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. Log into your Rapid Rewards account on southwest.com and update the companion information in the Companion Pass section. Plan strategically since you only get three changes per year.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Southwest Companion Pass is the single most powerful domestic travel rewards benefit available to FI-minded families and couples. At a cost of 135,000 qualifying points — achievable through credit card signup bonuses and Chase transfers — you unlock nearly two full years of 2-for-1 flights on every Southwest route with no blackout dates and no change fees. A family of four taking six domestic trips per year can realistically save $2,000 to $4,000 annually, money that goes straight back into your investment accounts. Time your earning to January, stack your signup bonuses, and designate your most frequent travel partner. This is the redemption that makes domestic travel a rounding error in your FI budget.

#8595. Science Finds that Dairy May Not Lead to Excess Fat as First Thought

For a long time, the public were cautioned against regular dairy food consumption, but a recent study from the University of Toronto, published by the Journal of Nutrition, appears to show that frequently delving into eggs, milk, and cheeses, could actually benefit your health and won’t make you fat. Here’s why.

In the ‘70s, a war on saturated fat consumption encouraged us to avoid products like whole milk, butter, and cheese because of the high levels that they contain. Then wellness culture in the new millennium further derailed the case for diary, citing inflammation, acne, and disrupted hormones on this food stuff. Of course, some people are lactose intolerant, and have problems processing dairy food, but the Toronto study has challenged the campaign against dairy, with some surprisingly edible results.

74 overweight adults undertook a 12-week study and were randomly assigned to one of three groups:

All the groups were counseled on healthy eating, so that they could manage their food intake. At the completion of the trial, the team took measurements including body weight, composition, cholesterol, blood markers, and metabolic health.

In both of the regular high fat dairy eating groups, the participants experienced improvements in their blood pressure while consuming a greater amount of protein, calcium, and vitamin D than the first group. Importantly, neither their waistlines nor BMI suffered. “Those that had three servings of dairy didn’t have adverse levels of blood cholesterol or lipids or evidence of insulin resistance,” explained Gerald Harvey Anderson, who was the lead author and works in the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Toronto.”

With full-fat dairy containing more saturated fat than reduced fat products, how could this be? The experts believe that dairy’s combination of fats and protein is what makes it a positive food. “With dairy products, it’s got two proteins, casein and whey, that are bound together with fat and with nutrients mixed in,” said Anderson. The “Dairy Matrix Hypothesis” suggests that the physical structure of dairy determines how the body processes its nutrient profile.

Of course, ice cream, milkshakes, and other treats that contain a ton saturated fat as well as massive amounts of sugar is a different story, but the Toronto study said its results with natural dairy products showed that  “Neither treatment nor time affected waist circumference, fat and fat-free mass, resting metabolic rate, fasting blood cholesterol, and urine creatinine.” The team concluded that “Frequent and daily consumption of full-fat dairy as part of a healthy diet is consistent with CFG (Canada’s Food Guide).”

This news also adds to another promising benefit of dairy, that was reported earlier this year. The American Academy of Neurology showed that those who regularly ate high fat cheese presented a 13% lower risk of dementia overall, and a 29% risk of vascular dementia. Cream was also associated with a 16% lower risk of all-type dementias.

The Toronto study found dairy to be a significant source of magnesium and potassium to boot. “The results align with the conclusion of an expert group that there is no evidence to support the avoidance of high-fat dairy in diets,” it said.

#8592. How to Correctly Add Forward and Reverse Lunges into Your Legday Workouts

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

When it comes to strengthening your legs, building muscles in your lower body, and improving all-round balance, lunges are a great move to lean into, but what is the difference between the forward and backward lunge? In a recent Instagram post, IFBB Pro, endurance athlete, and transformation coach Petar Klancir demonstrated the details.

Take a step in the right direction with these unique lunges.

“What is the difference?” asked The Croatian Colossus, who has built an Instagram base of more than one million followers thanks to his informative training videos. In essence, both of these variations are compound movements, so they tax multiple muscle groups at the same time. Whether you lunge forward or backward, you’ll be working the quads, hamstrings, calves and core. You will also flex the hips either way. But what does change is the emphasis placed on each muscle, and how they build your legs in different ways, as Klancir showed.

“Front step lunges target the quads more, due to the mechanics of the exercise,” explained Klancir. “The emphasis is on stepping forward, which requires the quads to control the impact of the foot’s landing. And there is a high degree of flexion.”

The quads take the majority of the load with forward lunges, because the mechanics that Klancir mentioned, require the quads to negotiate the lowering, and then lift your center of mass and return you to the starting position.

Tip: To avoid knee stress, be sure not to step out too far forward on the lunge. At the bottom of the lunge, your knee should only just be ahead of your chin.

“Back step lunges target the glutes and hamstrings,” said Klancir. “Due to emphasized hip-hinge movement.”

Reverse lunges are often considered easier to execute, because the front foot remains flat on the floor, providing a greater foundation and less requirement for core balance. They are also less stressful on the knee, because the load is shifted by the hamstrings and glutes to a greater extent than the quads.

Tip: Keep the front foot stable by keeping knee over ankle at all times.

For a complete leg blaster, your can try both movements by focusing on form. Then, once you are comfortable with your foot placings, you can build in some additional hypertrophy by adding a pair of dumbbells to the overall load.

#8590. What to Do About These High Interest Rates

Whoa, have you seen what just happened to interest rates!?

Suddenly, after at least fourteen years of our financial world being mostly the same, somebody flipped over the table and now things are quite different.

Interest rates, which have been gliding along at close to zero since before the Dawn of Mustachianism in 2011, have suddenly shot back up to 20-year highs.

Which brings up a few questions about whether we need to worry, or do anything about this new development.

These questions are on everybody’s mind these days, and I’ve been ruminating on them myself. But while I’ve seen a lot of play-by-play stories about each little interest rate increase in the financial newspapers, none of them seem to get into the important part, which is,

“Yeah, interest rates are way up, but what should I do about it?”

Why Is This Happening, and What Got Us Here?

Interest rates are like a giant gas pedal that revs the engine of our economy, with the polished black dress shoe of Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell pressed upon it.

For most of the past two decades, Jerome’s team and their predecessors have kept the pedal to the metal, firing a highly combustible stream of easy money into the system in the form of near-zero rates. This made mortgages more affordable, so everyone stretched to buy houses, which drove demand for existing homes and new construction alike.

It also had a similar effect on business investment: borrowed money and venture capital was cheap, so lots of entrepreneurs borrowed lots of money and started new companies. These companies then rented offices and built factories and hired employees – who circled back to buy more houses, cars, fridges, iPhones, and all the other luxurious amenities of modern life.

This was a great party and it led to lots of good things, because we had two decades of prosperity, growth, raising our children, inventing new things and all the other good stuff that happens in a successful rich country economy.

Until it went too far and we ended up with too much money chasing too few goods – especially houses. That led to a trend of unacceptably fast Inflation, which we already covered in a recent article.

So eventually, Jay-P noticed this and eased his foot back off of the Easy Money Gas Pedal. And of course when interest rates get jacked up, almost everything else in the economy slows down.

And that’s what is happening right now: mortgages are suddenly way more expensive, so people are putting off their plans to buy houses. Companies find that borrowing money is costly, so they are scaling back their plans to build new factories, and cutting back on their hiring. Facebook laid off 10,000 people and Amazon shed 27,000.

We even had a miniature banking crisis where some significant mid-sized banks folded and gave the financial world fears that a much bigger set of dominoes would fall.

All of these things sound kinda bad, and if you make the mistake of checking the news, you’ll see there is a big dumb battle raging as usual on every media outlet. Leftists, Right-wingers, and anarchists all have a different take on it:

The one thing all sides seem to agree on is that we are “experiencing hard economic times” and that “the country is headed in the wrong way”.

Which, ironically, is completely wrong as well – our unemployment rate has dropped to 50-year lows and the economy is at the absolute best it has ever been, a surprise to even the most grounded economists.

The reality? We’re just putting the lid back onto the ice cream carton until the economy can digest all the sugar it just wolfed down. This is normal, it happens every decade or two and it’s no big deal.

Okay, but should I take my money out of the stock market because it’s going to crash?

This answer never changes, so you’ll see it every time we talk about stock investing: Holy Shit NO!!!

The stock market always goes up in the long run, although with plenty of unpredictable bumps along the way. Since you can’t predict those bumps until after they happen, there is no point in trying to dance in and out of it.

But since we do have the benefit of hindsight, there are a few things that have changed slightly: From its peak at the beginning of 2022 until right now (August 2023 as I write this), the overall US market is down about 10%. Or to view it another way, it is roughly flat since June 2021, so we’ve seen two years with no gains aside from total dividends of about 3%.

Since the future is always the same, unknowable thing, this means I am about 10% more excited about buying my monthly slice of index funds today than I was at those peak prices.

Should I start putting money into savings accounts instead because they are paying 4.5%?

This is a slightly trickier question, because in theory we should invest in a logical, unbiased way into the thing with the highest expected return over time.

When interest rates were under 1%, this was an easy decision: stocks will always return far more than 1% over time – consider the fact that the annual dividend payments alone are 1.5%!

But there has to be some interest rate at which you’d be willing to stop buying stocks and prefer to just stash it into the stable, rewarding environment of a money market fund or long-term bonds or something else similar. Right now, if a reputable bank offered me, say, 12% I would probably just start loading up.

But remember that the stock market is also currently running a 10% off sale. When the market eventually reawakens and starts setting new highs (which it will someday), any shares I buy right now will be worth 10% more. And then will continue going up from there. Which quickly becomes an even bigger number than 12%.

In other words, the cheaper the stocks get, the more excited we should be about buying them rather than chasing high interest rates.

As you can see, there is no easy answer here, but I have taken a middle ground:

For most of us, the biggest thing that interest rates affect is our decisions around buying and selling houses. Financing a home with a mortgage is suddenly way more expensive, any potential rental house investments are suddenly far less profitable, and keeping our old house with a locked-in 3% mortgage is suddenly far more tempting.

Consider these shocking changes just over the past two years as typical rates have gone from about 3% to 7.5%.

Assuming a buyer comes up with the average 10% down payment:

This all sounds kind of bleak, but unfortunately it’s the way things are supposed to work – the tough medicine of higher interest rates is supposed to make the following things happen:

The net effect of all this is that prices should stop going up, and ideally fall back down in many areas.

This is a tricky one because the real “value” of a house depends entirely on supply and demand. The right price is whatever somebody is willing to pay for it. However, there are a few fundamentals which influence this price over the long run because they determine the supply of housing.

The first item (construction cost) is pretty interesting because it is subject to the magic of technological progress. Just as TVs and computers get cheaper over time, house components get cheaper too as things like computerized manufacturing and global trade make us more efficient.

I remember paying $600 for a fancy-at-the-time undermount sink and $400 for a faucet for my first kitchen remodel in the year 2001. Today, you can get a nicer sink on Amazon for about $250 and the faucet is a flat hundred. Similarly, nailguns and cordless tools and easy-to-install PEX plumbing make the process of building faster and easier than ever.

On the other hand, the last item (bullshit restrictions) has been very inflationary in recent times. I’ve noticed that every year another layer of red tape and complicated codes and onerous zoning and approval processes gets layered into the local book of rules, and as a result I just gave up on building new houses because it wasn’t worth the hassle. Other builders with more patience will continue to plow through the murk, but they will have less competition, fewer permits will be granted, and thus the shortage of housing will continue to grow, which raises prices on average.

Thankfully, every city is different and some have chosen to make it easier to build new houses rather than more difficult. Even better, places like Tempe Arizona are allowing good housing to be built around people rather than cars, which is even more affordable to construct.

But overall, since overall US house prices adjusted for inflation are just about at an all-time high, I think there’s a chance that they might ease back down another 25% (to 2020 levels). But who knows: my guess could prove totally wrong, or the “fall” could just come in the form of flat prices for a decade that don’t keep up with inflation, meaning that they just feel 25% cheaper relative to our higher future salaries.

The funny part about our current “high” interest rates is that they are not actually high at all. They’re right around average.So they might not go down at all for a long time.

Remember that graph at the beginning of this article? I deliberately cropped it to show only the years since 2009 – the long recent period of low interest rates. But if you zoom out to cover the last seventy years instead, you can see that we’re still in a very normal range.

But a better answer is this one: Interest rates will go down whenever Jerome Powell or one of his successors determines that our economy is slowing down too much and needs another hit from the gas pedal. In other words, whenever we start to slip into a genuine recession.

In order to do that however, we need to see low inflation, growing unemployment, and other signs of an economy that is finally cooling down. And right now, those things keep not showing up in the weekly economic data.

You can get one reasonable prediction of the future of interest rates by looking at something called the US Treasury Yield Curve. It typically looks like this:

What the graph is telling you is that as a lender you get a bigger reward in exchange for locking up your money for a longer time period. And way back in 2018, the people who make these loans expected that interest rates would average about 3.0 percent over the next 30 years.

Today, we have a very strange opposite yield curve:

If you want to lend money for a year or less, you’ll be rewarded with a juicy 5.4 percent interest rate. But for two years, the rate drops to 4.92%. And then ten-year bond pays only 4.05 percent.

This situation is weird, and it’s called an inverted yield curve. And what it means is that the buyers of bonds currently believe that interest rates will almost certainly drop in the future – starting a little over a year from now.

And if you recall our earlier discussion about why interest rates drop, this means that investors are forecasting an economic slowdown in the fairly near future. And their intuition in this department has been pretty good: an inverted yield curve like this has only happened 11 times in the past 75 years, and in ten of those cases it accurately predicted a recession.

So the short answer is: nobody really knows, but just for fun I’ll make a guess. Then if I’m wrong in public, you can come back and make fun of this in the comments.

I think we’ll probably see interest rates start to drop within 18-24 months, and the event may be accompanied by some sort of recession as well.

I like to read and write about all this stuff because I’m still a finance nerd at heart. But when it comes down to it, interest rates don’t really affect long-retired people like many of us MMM readers, because we are mostly done with borrowing. I like the simplicity of owning just one house and one car, mortgage-free.

With the current overheated housing market here in Colorado, I’m not tempted to even look at other properties, but someday that may change. And the great thing about having actual savings rather than just a high income that lets you qualify for a loan, is that you can be ready to pounce on a good deal on short notice.

Maybe the entire housing market will go on sale as we saw in the early 2010s, or perhaps just one perfect property in the mountains will come up at the right time. The point is that when you have enough cash to buy the thing you want, the interest rates that other people are charging don’t matter. It’s a nice position of strength instead of stress. And you can still decide to take out a mortgage if you do find the rates are worthwhile for your own goals.

So to tie a bow on this whole lesson: keep your lifestyle lean and happy and don’t lose too much sweat over today’s interest rates or house prices. They will probably both come down over time, but those things aren’t in your control. Much more important are your own choices about earning, saving, healthy living and where you choose to live.

With these big sails of your life properly in place and pulling you ahead, the smaller issues of interest rates and whatever else they write about in the financial news will gradually shrink down to become just ripples on the surface of the lake.

In the comments: what have you been thinking about interest rates recently? Have they changed your decisions, increased, or perhaps even decreased your stress levels around money and housing?

Well the first reason is that I’m not totally rational :-)

So like most of us, my decisions around money are made around what “feels” good, especially now that extra money doesn’t serve much purpose. It feels good pay off a margin loan that is at over 6%, and feels less good to see big interest bills coming in every month.

But if we’re talking about actually *selling* shares to move to another form of investment, the bar is much higher because you would owe full income tax (probably long-term capital gains tax) on the withdrawal.

Another reason is that 6% returns on a bank account are taxed as income while paying off 6% debt is after-tax. For a high earner, it’s closer to 9%.

Mr. Money Mustache September 5, 2023, 2:56 pm

I’m usually in favor of at least 20%, because when you work out the effective interest rate increase that PMI is hitting you with, it usually works out to a very good return on that extra 10%.

For example, imagine a 500k house, and you are debating between a 50k or 100k downpayment (10 or 20%). And let’s say the interest rate is down at 5%.

If the PMI premium is a typical 0.8% of the loan value $450k, you’d be paying an extra $3600 per year in PMI premiums. Just for the privilege of not putting down the extra $50k.

That’s 7% of the potential extra downpayment that gets eaten up every year!

Or to put it another way, if you put in the second $50k, you are earning 5% in foregone loan interest PLUS 7% in saved PMI premiums. 12% in total, which is the best return around.

It’s a similar return when deciding between a 15 vs 30 year mortgage (the 15 year mortgage provides the extra risk free return). The return decreases the longer one keeps the mortgage, but for most people who move / re-finance within 7 years or so, it’s well worth it.

My brother got a mortgage from Navy Federal Credit Union with no PMI. So those deals are out there. This is not a VA loan, just standard mortgage. I’m thinking other credit unions might offer the same.

This is why timing and luck is so important in life.

A good option at the moment for military people looking to purchase homes is a VA assumption loan. Essentially you “assume” the VA loan of another person instead of getting a new loan at today’s rates. The downside is that the purchase takes much longer, and since interest rates have been going down for decades, it hasn’t made sense to do an assumption loan for decades, so most people aren’t familiar with the process. We’re about 3 months into the process, and it’s looking like end-to-end it is going to take 5-6 months, but we’re assuming a 2.25% interest rate instead of today’s ~7%. You also can’t choose how much your down payment is. You have to have enough cash on hand to pay off whatever the difference is between the purchase price and what the seller has left on the mortgage.

My mortgage is 2.5% – P&I is $886/mo. Last year, we had about 28 years left and the interest was slightly higher than the principal payment each month – about $450/mo. or so in interest. Did a lump sum payment and cut off about 15 years of payments – now almost all my payment goes to the principal. The interest each month is now only about $230/mo.

In this sense, the savings in interest each month is about equal to what I’d be earning if I’d kept the lump sum in a money market. I’ve also got peace of mind because A. if I didn’t make another extra payment, I’ll still have a paid-for house in about 13 years, and B. since the money is already spent on the mortgage, it removes the temptation to find something else to use it on.

So the short answer to your comment is: yes, the front-loaded nature of the mortgage does factor into the equation. From an interest savings perspective, it’s definitely more profitable to pay the mortgage down during the first half of the amortization versus the last half.

As I understand it, the front-loaded nature of interest on a mortgage is just a reflection (the mirror image, maybe) of compound interest. So an extra principal payment in year 1 of a 30 year fixed-rate mortgage has a greater impact than one in year 25 because it has longer to compound, not because it gives a greater rate of return.

If you make an extra payment of $100 this year, next year your balance will be lower by $102.85. And in 27 years your balance will be lower by $100*1.0285^27=$213.56.

But if instead you put $100 in your high-yield savings account, next year you will have $105. So you really will approach the payoff amount faster that way (as long as the interest rate you’re earning remains higher).

You understand it correctly! You don’t pay more or less interest as a percentage of your loan by paying it off early or by paying it for 30 years – when you make extra payments early, you simply borrowed the total amount of money for less time. Naturally you pay less aggregate interest if you pay the loan off early, because you borrowed the total sum for less time. If your mortgage is 5%, for example, the total interest you pay as a percentage of what you borrowed will be 5% regardless of whether you pay off the loan in year 1 or year 30. Amortized payments confuse people into thinking that they’re paying more interest in the beginning than the end – no, you’re paying the percentage of whatever is outstanding. The amortization just allows one to have the same payment over the life of the loan, rather than a huge payment now and a itty bitty payment later. So it appears that you are paying more in interest, but it’s just that the interest that is owed is a greater percentage of the payment amount in the beginning because you owe more money.

In any case, you are totally correct that in a static situation paying yourself $100 into a 5% bank account instead of paying $100 extra to a 2.75% mortgage will earn you the delta (5-2.75 =2.25%) real annual return, compounded. Of course there’s no guarantee the savings return remains at 5%, whereas the interest rate on the fixed mortgage is guaranteed to be 2.75%.

But I think that cities SHOULD open up the floodgates for infill redevelopment – stuff like the old parking lots and abandoned shopping malls that currently take up most of the space in central cities including mine.

But to stop the self-perpetuating problem of crowding and car traffic, make sure you have modern, people-friendly rules in place (which are also builder friendly because we’d rather build more houses rather than wasting land on car parking).

– eliminate “minimum parking” requirements – shrink roads and eliminate free taxpayer-paid car parking and make all the asphalt self-funding – add super safe and pleasant bike and pedestrian accomm0dation instead, which is more than 90% cheaper to build.

“Infill redevelopment” – I didn’t know there was a proper term for this but YES, that’s exactly what I’ve been saying for years. So much moaning & groaning over the “lack of affordable housing” – and yet, on the flip side, equal moaning & groaning over “strip mall ghost towns” and blighted areas of empty commercial properties. Instead of hacking up and parceling off more farmland and prairie to build overpriced McMansions with postage stamp-sized yards, why not develop what’s already there into housing? There are already all the roads, highways, byways, and parking lots you could ever need. Most also have some sort of parks or green space nearby, unkempt tho they may be, plus schools and access to public transportation. It seems like a no-brainer to me: instead of destroying more of what’s green and unsullied, why not rehab the bounty of concrete & steel & asphalt just sitting empty & unused?

I don’t pretend to understand all the reasons behind it, but I suspect it has more to do with a very few making a very large amount of money, than it does with anything truly prohibitive or “bad for humans” in trying to re-develop urban wastelands into habitable neighborhoods.

From what I’ve heard, commercial-to-residential conversions can be pretty complex, which is why you don’t see that many. The biggest challenges from what I hear are plumbing (offices/storefronts aren’t designed to have bathrooms/kitchens everywhere) and lack of windows (only on the outside, so interior spaces can’t be used as separate apartments). Not impossible, but often the retrofitting can wind up running more than just bulldozing the whole thing and starting from scratch. Starting with a parking lot might be easier.

Some developers are figuring out this puzzle, so hopefully the situation improves. There’s certainly plenty of unused commercial property to repurpose.

Bottom line is that it’s cheaper (for the developer) to build on fresh land in 95% of the cases. Redevelopment is far more expensive than new development. The costs for new development are often outsourced (new roads, new schools, new utilities, etc) whereas the developer is going to foot the bill on redevelopment (with some exceptions where a state/fed offers incentives for blighted areas, industrial waste sites, etc).

Attempting to control overpopulation is an unequivocally bad idea. A horrible scenario is going to play out in China in about a decade due to their one child policy. Most of the first world is heading for a situation of very problematic demographics (too many old people, not enough young). There is plenty of water even in a place like phoenix if it was priced and regulated appropriately, and we would have more than enough space in existing city boundaries if we didn’t subsidize parking and transportation in the worst ways possible. Changing those pricing and regulation schemes are the angles we need to look at, but we definitely need more units of housing.
