#8565. How To Afford a House These Days

The other day, an MMM reader stopped by and left the following comment on one of my older posts about the principles of FIRE:

“While I still find some of MMM’s advice relevant, it seems like every FI blogger out there worked in tech 20 years ago, pulled down a 6 figure salary and bought a house for a bag of potatoes before 2019.

I wasn’t smart enough to find FI when I was young so I sometimes feel like a lot of their advice is not going to help me or others who don’t already own a home and don’t have six- figure salaries in this post-pandemic world.

A lot of the ideas given to young folks are “house hack” “buy a fixer upper” but that is still out of reach and/or complex to navigate with current prices and interest rates. Most townships around me do not want you to chop a house up into ADU’s or multiple units. My cousin owns 60 acres of land but he is not allowed to live on a trailer on that land.

I don’t know what the next generation of FI bloggers will offer, perhaps they are already out there and I just don’t know who they are, but I’d like to hear from them.”–

As with every critique of our ideas, I thought about this comment for a while. Tried to determine if there were any Principles of Mustachianism that were genuinely going obsolete, versus the more common side effects of Complainypants and/or Excuse-itis, two afflictions which have been weighing down our critics since the beginning.

After all, this isn’t the first time FIRE has gone obsolete. Over my retirement I’ve seen it:

Our commenter focuses on two things: the solid salaries of tech workers, and the major increases in house prices (and interest rates) in the most recent four years.

The first one — high salaries in general – is still a factor and I don’t expect that to change. Some jobs just pay more than others, and there’s a lot you can do to increase your income and switch jobs, and I’m all for it. However, ever-increasing income is not my usual focus here on MMM, because I have seen first hand that most people can waste almost any amount of income and still have very little to show for it.

In fact, the very existence of software engineers and doctors and other high earners who are my age and still feeling financial stress is proof of this: it’s mathematically impossible to earn so much for almost 30 years and not have an absolute shit-ton saved, unless you are also spending an absolute shit-ton of money the whole time.

So instead, we focus on how to streamline your spending and live joyfully and efficiently without compromise. We focus on reducing waste, while maintaining or even increasing all of the other benefits that come from spending money more purposefully. These skills are essential even for the highest earners, but they become even more valuable as you move down the income ladder.

So now for the second issue: housing. Does the state of housing here in 2024 screw up the whole FIRE plan?

As with any question, let’s start by looking at the data: how much have US house prices actually risen – adjusted for inflation – since 2019?

It turns out that our own St. Louis Fed makes this extremely useful  information available here.

So there’s our answer: houses “feel” about 25% more expensive right now than they did at the start of 2019 relative to the average salary and the price of everything else. Although interestingly enough,  they are only up about 10% since the last peak in early 2006, a full eighteen years ago! So housing is a blow, but not a FIRE-extinguishing one.

However, this nationwide data masks some much bigger increases in certain popular cities, including my own: Plain old Longmont Colorado now sports a hilariously high $540,000 median home price. So houses are about triple the price they were when I started writing in 2011, which means they’ve risen much faster than the average salary. Which means houses are much further out of reach for the average person in my area.

The solution to this is the same as most other problems: to stop thinking in the way our culture likes to train us (as a victim of outside forces beyond our control) and go back to thinking like a Mustachian.

Houses are just like any other manufactured product, and as such they come at a wide variety of prices, subject to supply and demand.

And just because you happen to live in a certain place (even if you were born and raised there), doesn’t mean you’ll automatically be able to afford to buy a house there. Just as a baby born upon the Apple campus in Cupertino today doesn’t automatically get a new iPhone Pro Max every year.

With every purchasing decision, you need to go through the same series of choices:

So when it comes to houses, you run the numbers, then decide between renting or buying or house hacking. You might start by doing the analysis right in your own city, but also keep in mind that there are lots of other cities and even countries in the world, and there are happy people living in all of them.

But Wait: I don’t want to move to a whole new place!

At this point, people get defensive. We all have ties to our current location, and the stronger the ties the more difficult it becomes to consider moving.

But there’s a difference between genuine, positive bonds to a place and just plain old fear of change. So it’s my job to at least make you question your assumptions, because not doing so is what got you where you are, and it’s also what got our country where it is.

And on a country-wide basis,  I notice that our general fear of relocating creates a very irrational pattern of house prices. They are ridiculously high in some places and ridiculously cheap in others. There does seem to be a general correlation between niceness and cost, but not a perfect one (especially since everyone has their own definition of “nice”)

I moved to Longmont in 2005 because it met our young family’s needs at the time, at the right price with homes about $200,000. Today, at the $540,000 price level (houses average about $450 per interior square foot) it has to compete with a much broader range of cities which offer nicer amenities at equal or lower prices.

Let’s do a hypothetical search using another amazing tool: FRED’s list of the top 1000 metro areas with price per square foot, and plot some of them based on my own judgment of their desirability:

I’m biased towards Colorado because I have so many ties there, and I also highly prioritize sunny climates. My chart suggests that if I wanted to save money, I might start looking around in Albuquerque, whereas Denver would give me a nicer life in the same price range as my current city of Longmont. And if I were willing to spend even more on housing to live somewhere even nicer, I should suck it up and move to Boulder.

Just for fun, I pulled the data from that same FRED website into a separate google spreadsheet (which I’ll share here) and sorted it by cost per square foot. Then, I highlighted a band of affordable cities with housing centered on the $100 per square foot range, which would mean a 2,000 square foot house is about $200k.

As an added bonus, I added a column to calculate the change in house prices over the past year, just in case it helps us see if a city is on the way up or getting cheaper at the moment.

A chart like this is just a starting point – you’d need to read more about any place and then go visit in person before considering a move. But the idea is to start with data, and then do some fun research based on what you learn.

The Earth Awaits: Casting a Worldwide Net

House prices are a valuable metric, because they influence the cost of living more than almost anything else for the typical Mustachian. After all, biking and nature are always close to free, Costcos are available nationwide, and we probably care less than average about the costs of other services like valets and salons.

But there’s still plenty of value in looking at the bigger picture, considering more data points, and also being open to renting versus buying your housing. For this, I’m a big fan of a FIRE blogger-created site called The Earth Awaits, and we can take it for a test drive right now with the following search criteria:

Apartment type: Two bedroom (outside city center)

Temperature range: January lows not colder than 10F

The exact parameters don’t matter too much, as long as you don’t make them too narrow. The important thing is the resulting list, which is meant to give you ideas to research further. For example, that first simple search gave me this list:

Hey, that’s interesting. I like how the site shows the population right on the main list, because that provides a big clue to the “feel” of a city. I personally like the feel of a 50k-200k person town, so I might look into Fayetteville, Columbia or Athens. I’ve also been to Chattanooga and really like that place – who knew it was only about as expensive as Columbus Ohio?

In the end, your physical environment – the people, access to nature, urban features and the weather patterns – is probably the most important factor to get right in creating a happy life. The cost of living there is only one of the factors, and definitely not the most important one.

But if you choose carefully, you can probably slide yourself in the right direction along that “Nice for the Price” scale in order to get more from your life. Even if it just means making a move within your own city to live along a walking path, a little closer to work or to the people or places you care about most.

The key is just to remember that housing is like almost everything in life: It’s a choice that you get to make, and there are great rewards for putting some solid thought and effort into that choice.

Another Fun Example: Doing the Analysis on Tempe/Phoenix Arizona vs Denver

This is a fun exercise, because I’m currently living in the Phoenix area (more on that here)  that is way different than the Denver metro area where I normally live. We can start with the rough measure of housing cost per square foot across each region:

In other words, pretty close. Denver metro* is about 10% higher on average, but the variations from one neighborhood to another within any major city are much larger than that anyway.

So the other factors are more important. Both are surrounded by beautiful mountain recreation and get lots of sunshine, but the climates are famously quite different. Denver is more compact but Phoenix has nicer towns in the foothills around the outskirts.  In the end it’s just personal preference in weighting these various factors, and right now I kind of like the idea of both (Phoenix in winter but Colorado for the other three seasons)

More Adventurous: Let’s Try This in South America!

Going back to The Earth Awaits, if we repeat our earlier search but in South America, we get results like these:

Many of these spots have nice writeups if you click the “Details” button, and if anything sounds right for you, you can go on to learn much more.

It’s true that moving to a new country comes with all sorts of new learning experiences: citizenship and passports, laws and traditions and driver licenses, and of course having to cross an international border every time you want to return to your home country to visit family.

But guess what? If this stuff sounds daunting to you, it’s probably a sign that you need to do it more.

At its core, moving to a new place – even internationally – is just a series of relatively easy Adulting Puzzles. You type stuff into your computer, read the resulting stuff that pops up on your screen, and make the occasional phone call and visit to an official office. I had to do all the same stuff when moving from Canada to the US, alone and just six years out of high school myself.

Sure, it can feel like a “hassle” if you think of it the wrong way, but you know what’s a way, way bigger hassle? Living in a not-very-good place for life, or working an extra 15 years just to afford the higher cost of living in your current city, because you’re too scared to do a few weeks of work to make a big move to a better place.

If a rules-and-paperwork-hater like me can do it, almost anyone can.

While we covered a few examples of actual places in this article, the real purpose was to explain the thought process behind deciding when and where to move. And there are many of you out there besides me who can do the same thing, but better. And we’d love to hear from you!

If you have some favorite cities and countries for good living, or useful techniques for scoping them out, please share them in the comments. I strongly believe that the more we help each other find the right place and enjoy the planet more thoroughly and more efficiently, the better off we’ll all be. So let’s get moving.

* Denver metro on the Fed site includes all the suburbs rather than just the core city which is much smaller and more expensive, but the same is true for the nicer parts of Phoenix so I figure it’s a fair comparison)

I’ve felt similar to the OP about this for a while and I appreciate MMM’s thoughtful analysis and response.

His acknowledgement of the fact that the overall inflation-adjusted US Home Price index masks much much greater increases in many other parts of the country is salient, but I found his follow-on analysis frustrating.

Yes – absolutely – you are *not* entitled to buy a home in whatever location you want just because you live there and believe that you are is not going to get you to FIRE very quickly if at all. He gives his own experience of geographic arbitrage as a good example of how he was able to move somewhere much less expensive than the big city to achieve his goals faster. Plenty of other FIRE types from the MMM age group did the same thing – they moved to Vermont, Bend, Bozeman etc. because those places were affordable and beautiful. The entire point of FIRE is to have the time to enjoy doing what you love and the most FIRE way to do this is by taking on hobbies in the great outdoors.

But here’s the thing: over the last ten years – and especially the last five – beautiful places with access to great low-cost outdoor recreation activities almost all fall into the data that the “US Home Price” graph hides.

Sure you can purchase a home in a climate-ravaged hell-scape or among the rows and rows of flat corn fields this country has to offer for a very reasonable price. Someplace that will make it extremely difficult to do all the many Mustachian things MMM has lauded through the years (biking, parks, outdoors, car-free life, etc.). Food deserts. Bankrupt suburbs or rural towns etc.

I don’t know that I’ve got better advice for these trying times however. I think if it were me, I would probably find a high-paying job in a city with reasonable rents and ease of a non-car lifestyle (funnily enough, in many cities, rents have actually grown at a fraction the rate of real estate). Seattle, Denver, Chicago, Portland, Philadelphia, DC are decent examples of this. NY, Boston, SF, LA, are not. Spend a decade or so (or however long it’ll take you) putting away as much money as you can and then reassess.

Maybe home prices will adjust way down everywhere? Maybe rent forever? Americans hate this idea, but the math makes more and more sense IMO in many parts of the country. Or maybe see if you can find a part of the country that will enable you to live a somewhat Mustachian life with low real estate costs. If it were me, I would be looking at the good parts of the Midwest – Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota. Places resilient to climate change with low housing costs and ample outdoor activities that maybe aren’t as high-brow as those of the wealthy class but still plenty enjoyable.

Sorry this was a bit of a rant, but while I think MMM is doing a lot to brush off the vast difference between the geographic arbitrage available to him and that available today, but I do still thing FIRE is possible for those of us in our 20s!

This reminded me of a guy whose story I saw on TikTok. He moved from uber-expensive Washington, DC to southeast Pennsylvania, where he bought a beautiful, historic 8,000-square-foot mansion for the same price as his old DC apartment:

https://www.msn.com/en-us/money/realestate/man-showcases-his-300000-coal-baron-mansion-in-pennsylvania/ar-AA1knJsl

It seems like most of the price appreciation is happening in rich, trendy cities. There are still a lot of bargains to be had if you’re willing to move to less-cool areas. Of course, jobs are also easier to find in big cities, but there are so many jobs that can be done over the internet now, that should be less of an obstacle than it used to be.

The one cautionary note I’d add is to also consider the politics of the place. If I was LGBTQ+, a person of color, or a woman of child-bearing age, there are some states I wouldn’t consider moving to any time in the near future, even if they’re affordable. It’s scary how aggressive some places are getting about denying people’s access to health care and taking away their rights, even the right to travel somewhere else. As Mustachians, we have extra power to vote with our dollars, so we should choose places that care about making people’s lives better.

Agree that geographic arbitrage is the answer, but I do think that the objective quality of the places available for geographic arbitrage 20 years ago is vastly different than today.

One of the big consequences of the internet has been that all the beautiful places of the world (and this country) are simply far better known to everybody. In the 1990s it would have been seen as a very strange decision for somebody from San Francisco to move to (or to even have heard of) Bend Oregon. But now, you wouldn’t blink twice and the real estate market and prices has reflected this “globalization” of local real estate markets.

Still plenty of great places out there though!

I would also propose that folks consider renting indefinitely more seriously. While the cost of purchasing a home has risen quickly in the last decade, rent has (generally) not risen nearly as quickly and renting will give you a lot more flexibility if you decide you don’t love where you’re living! It’s also a nice fixed cost relatively to the risks inherent in home ownership. I’ll caveat that this works a lot better in cities than it does in smaller towns (like Bend) where bad zoning / housing policy has led to restrictions on rental housing propping up prices quite a bit.

Good point about the bad policy – this seems to be the root cause of almost all the expensive housing in US cities. Whenever you have NIMBYs being allowed to complain to their city councils and get them to block the rezoning and building of new housing on land that THEY DO NOT OWN THEMSELVES, you end up with less new housing and potentially higher housing and rent prices due to the artificially restricted supply.

It is just him and his cat when he is home. The house could easily fit 2 full families with the proper setup. However, getting the approval from the city would likely be impossible.

The larger issue with a redistribution of square footage or other zoning issues would be most people don’t want to buy a multi-family unit. The “American Dream” is not to own a rental unit (for the majority of people), and especially not to rent. Society looks down upon people who don’t own their own homes as failures. It takes a strong independent thinker to not cave to the group think.

The point about internet-generated movement is spot on and really significant. I’ve seen this firsthand in my hometown, which has changed dramatically in the past ten or fifteen years.

As recently as the early 2000s, my hometown was a sleepy seaside town off the beaten path, beautiful but known only by locals and a few others. This was before MapQuest, Google Maps, Zillow, online news, satellite car navigation, etc. If you didn’t already know what it was like there or have a personal connection to tell you, you’d never think to visit or buy property there.

There had always been a community of wealthy seasonal residents with vacation houses on the water, but the rest of the town was solidly middle class or even high blue collar. The local auto mechanics and construction workers lived in town and socialized with the white-collar locals.

But that all changed when the town was “discovered” and people from out of town began outbidding everyone else for the houses. The multigenerational continuity that made the community so strong has been broken by my millennial generation, since most of us couldn’t afford to buy the houses in town that our parents bought. It’s gotten so bad that the school is now at risk of closing for lack of kids, since no young families can afford to live there anymore.

I think that a similar phenomenon is happening at the global level. Housing costs are affected by the (lack of) supply, i.e. NIMBYism, but they’re also affected by demand generated by large-scale immigration. Other things being equal, an influx of new people makes housing more expensive. We see this in some parts of the US, but the effect is stronger in other places like Canada and Australia, where recent unprecedented amounts of immigration have coincided with huge increases in the cost of housing. The internet facilitates immigration by making it much easier for prospective immigrants to see what other places are like and what opportunities are available.

I often say that Philly is an aggressively underrated city if the northeast Megalopolis appeals to you. High speed rail gets you to DC, NY, and Boston. You can live in a giant skyscraper condo directly downtown or in a single-family rowhome on the outskirts. You can get a 1200 square foot house for $300-400k in a great neighborhood. Buses and bike lanes abound. Everything is flat and walkable. Good jobs in meds and eds.

His double wide is way bigger than my 900 sq foot bungalow in SF. He bought a nice home for what people pay for annual property taxes here. This isn’t a one-off deal. There are a lot of places in his community like this. No, it’s not a beautiful Victorian, but for someone with limited income, he lives a good life. Now he works part time for the local golf course and get to play golf for free.

Another thing to watch out for is something we might call Irrational Local Driverphobia Syndrome (ILDS):

– it has always worked out just fine. I got where I needed to go. – the residents of EVERY. SINGLE. CITY. have said the same thing: “Oh, it’s not safe to ride bikes HERE.. the drivers here are all crazy, and drinking and driving, and texting on their phone, and they hate cyclists.”

Yes, human-driven cars generally pretty dangerous. But you can mitigate most of that danger by choosing your route carefully, learning bicycle safety and getting lots of practice with bike control through trail and off-road-riding, and very importantly adding super bright flashing lights, front and rear, which you use at all times, sun, rain or shine.

I think anecdotes are best discarded in favor of data. And I tried to do this once a while ago, although this article could use an updating with more recent statistics: https://www.mrmoneymustache.com/2012/06/07/safety-is-an-expensive-illusion/

The summary is that biking is SO GOOD for you, and not really all that dangerous in the big picture, that it has an effectively negative level of danger. i.e. your lifespan and healthspan increase when you do it.

But, if you’re in a rough urban area you gotta treat it like a hockey game where YOU are the puck and every moving thing is trying to hit you. So have the literal flashing lights installed on your bike in all directions, and have your figurative radar running on high as well, especially at every curb cut and intersection.

With proper awareness, you should be able to make it almost impossible for a car to hit you even if they are trying to do so (which of course they aren’t), because you’re riding so defensively.

It sounds harsh, but this is also the same thing it takes to be a good CAR driver and avoid accidents over a lifetime of driving.

I just tallied up our non-house net worth yesterday and we’re at $1.1M. Hopefully I can early retire very soon (age 48 with a rather high paying job, but one that varies throughout any particular day from “great” to “rage quit”).

But also what strikes me is the persistent assumption that everyone needs to own a house. I’ve never owned a house and never even lived in one as an adult. I do own a boat however, which is like a tiny house, that we’ve lived on for 7 years. Renting a small apartment is perfectly valid.

I would suggest to your commenter that he explore the “tiny house/dwelling” movement. Changing the size of your home is often an even easier way to save than location arbitrage. Humans don’t need really need as much space as they think (many average suburban homes feel “mansion-sized” to me).

I recently bought my first home using the little known hack called “marry an electrician and then get a house with all knob and tube wiring, because no one else will want it due to the wires being old, even though if they were going to burn the house down they likely would have by now.”

Yup. Homes that need remodeling and new plumbing or electrical can be had for hundreds of thousands less in hotter markets. Having the trade or skills to do the work will save so much money.

I’ve added probably between $20k and $75k in value to each of my homes in these ways–always spending way less than the value returned by either doing most of the work myself or contracting out after many bids and significant time considering the design. I’ve never had a house sit on the market. All have gone under contract at about ask or over in a few days or less.

What I’ve appreciated about the Moustachian philosophy (at least from what I can tell) is that it doesn’t assume that we humans deserve to get everything we want and right now!

I’m actually a compulsive debtor in recovery, and reading blogs like this one and books like “Your Money or Your Life,” are very helpful tools for me. My past ridiculous and childish thoughts about money included:

~I deserve this ~Everyone else is doing it, I should be able to as well ~It’s my right ~I shouldn’t have to work and save. I shouldn’t have to sacrifice or make difficult choices.

These thoughts and the silly and financially damaging actions they lead to are not just the affliction of those who are compulsive, but are the foundational philosophy for our consumerist culture.

Just because I live in the U.S., doesn’t mean I deserve to be able to buy a house; especially when I did NOTHING during my pre-recovery days to save for one.

The amazing news is, however, that even though I got into recovery and began to practice sound financial principles only 10 years ago, my hubs and I own a great home in a dream location. We went from overspending each month by about $1,500 (today we’d be almost $250,000 in debt – and that doesn’t include interest payments!) to being worth over $1.5 million (this does include the estimated value of our home).

I work in my dream career and make 2/3 as much money as my hubby, but work 1/4 the time he does (this is the way we both like it).

All this to say that once you turn the ship around, once you begin to change even the smallest behaviors with money to align with Moustachian ideas, it doesn’t take long at all to see HUGE results.

Thanks, Mr. Moustache and all who embrace FIRE and principles of financial sanity! Natalie :^)

I had been ‘living’ in San Francisco as a flight attendant in a 3 bedroom with 18 roommates for $375/mo. I had begun making an excel of places I thought I would like to live and move to then the pandemic hit and it forced me to move as I was laid off. I made a list of requirements including drivable in 2 hours to a major airport/hub or closer if I commuted (I don’t have to go to work every day). It needed to be affordable housing, community-based, good internet (my parents live in Alabama and it’s not available where they live), things for me to do (entertainment), and in a climate with 4 seasons (Alabama has hot or wet, SFO has damp and less damp). I used best places which has a quiz that also asked some other good questions and I decided I probably wanted some kind of university town so there was 24 hour services (because sometimes I work nights) as that would be good for me. I then converted my Honda crv to a van and road tripped and stayed a few days to a week in each area I was considering. When I got to my current town of Harrisonburg Va I fell in love with it. As others have said, the first half of this article (the FRED graph of average sales prices across the US) is statistically questionable and has the feel of “see? housing is actually affordable, you’re just wrong to be looking at actual sales prices in your area”. As you mention, it’s a national average, when all RE markets are local, so it’s unclear what it means at all. Another distortion is that the FRED data comes from FHA, which means that it excludes cash sales and sales with jumbo loans. This distortion tends to result in lower home prices than you see when looking at, say, the Case-Schiller data. Even if you average over the whole country.

But I’m glad I ground through that part because the rest of this has some really practical advice for how to find somewhere to live. There is a classic old Raptitude post “Most Lives are Lived by Default” which suggests that probably your current location is a side-effect of your job, or school, or relationship, and that you could do better if you actively tried to find the “right” location for you. Unfortunately the article provides no advice for _how_ to do this; it mostly suggests moving to a different neighborhood in your current town, with the assumption that you have a good idea of whether you want to be closer/further to nightlife or grocery stores or bike paths or whatever, and you just need to pull the trigger.

But for somebody who is near-FIRE, or “FIRE except for housing”, it’s hard to figure out where to even start. These resources are a great way to filter for locations that are financially reasonable and also in the right part of the country. Another thing I did was keep an eye on r/financialindependence and r/fatfire to see if anybody posted cool understated places to live. Chattanouga popped up, as did Kansas City MO, and Asheville NC.

In 2020 I visited a pile of such cities, as well as big ones like Philly and Portland and NYC, by going on AirBNB and finding a spare room that I could rent for a month or more. In the Portland area I wound up doing this for several months in a row, since it’s a huge place and you can change locations dramatically without leaving the metro area.

When I first started doing this I would always look to stay in whole houses, but this is the wrong approach! Aside from not distorting housing markets by using SFHs as hotels, you actually want to find a place with a host who you can talk to about the city and who can tell you about different neighborhoods. And if you rent spare rooms for long periods, it’s a surprisingly affordable thing to do. Especially as you can often meet people who are willing to let you stay with them without going through a fee-skimming platform like AirBNB.

This strategy might only be practical for single light-travelling digital nomad types but I encourage anybody to seriously consider it.

Thanks for the Albuquerque shoutout! It’s not a perfect place to live, but if you like being outside, it’s hard to do better for what it costs to live here.

FIRE is often about making different choices than everyone else to emphasize the things that really matter to you. You rent a small apartment close to work instead of buying a McMansion in the exurbs. You bike or walk instead of driving a 3-row SUV. You cook at home instead of eating out. You go to the library instead of the movie theater…

…and you move to New Mexico instead of Colorado.

If you’re still working, the national labs are solidly above-average employers that emphasize work-life balance. The outdoor recreation is almost as good as Colorado, and Durango is only a few hours away if you want bigger mountains. There’s a nice airport, a zoo, great museums, and 3 Costcos. The weather is great: cooler than Phoenix in the summer, warmer than Denver in the winter, and sunny almost all the time. Plus, the state is doing lots to support working families, with subsidized daycare and free college tuition.

So if you’re discouraged about how much it costs to live in Bend or Boulder, make less popular choice and check out New Mexico.

As a former Coloradoan, newly adopted New Mexican I can reiterate Joel’s statements. NM isn’t perfect but I feel like I have greater access to outdoor recreation here in NM than I did in the Front Range of Colorado, plus much less people to compete with. There are slightly more sunny days, so I can’t complain about that either.

I’m in Santa Fe, which is pretty comparable to many parts of Colorado regarding cost of living and the weather feels nearly identical to Colorado with our almost 7000′ elevation. Santa Fe punches above it’s weight as a city in regards to culture, restaurants, and museums. There is a good bit of tourism that feeds into that, but the restaurant scene is pretty great. The history of the region keeps me engaged as I continue to learn more about the area.

I keep eyeballing the affordability of Albuquerque and the offerings of a city that is 5x the size of Santa Fe, but Santa Fe fits the bill for now

The key thing, as this article exemplifies, is to EXAMINE both reality, and your own assumptions. So much “can’t afford a house” mania is based on vague unexamined feelings, and vague media-based proclamations. When you cut through that with a bunch of facts and self-examination . . . the world opens up. As this piece shows. In our case, a limiting factor (we thought) was the “must be close to family” idea. Then we realized that 1. family members keep making plans and moving without consulting us, so why base our whole lives on their (temporary) locations? 2. once we did the math and realized how often we “see family” it became clear that 3 visits a year with a couple of family events each time would cover all the hanging-out time we do, anyway. YMMV.

We love to see these people! But in reality, they’re all busy, they move around, and there’s a limit to everyone’s time. So now we are free to live mostly in Europe, where we prefer to be (and where it’s cheap to live a great, low-footprint life), and not feel disloyal because of some presumed idea of “being too far away from family.” We see them as much as ever did! Now it’s just during our annual out-and-back migration. So yeah: really, truly examine everything that seems to be liming your choices.

I think the one thing you missed calling out is how this is especially relevant to FIRE folks who are no longer working. Many of these lower cost cities don’t have the high paying jobs that really helps us along the way.

Personally I went the route of moving to a small apartment and renting in a HCOL city to maximize my income in my younger years. Now that I’m coming up on 40, I’ve moved to a small town in MN and enjoying the much lower cost of living.

The other cool aspect of this idea is that you can live in a very neat neighborhood within these type of towns. For example, I’m living in the heart of the historic neighborhood within walking distance of two lakes and downtown for super cheap. If I had done that in any moderate cost of living city, I’d pay 5-10x as much for housing. So while it’s a small town, it’s still very walkable & bikeable because I’m not stuck out in some suburban wasteland.

As a hospice physician, Jordan Gurmet discusses a familiar tragedy beyond the emotional weight of medical illness: the sudden, overwhelming chaos that unfolds when aging intersects with a lack of intergenerational financial planning.

Aren’t inheritances supposed to be a big deal? All dollars should be treated equally regardless of their source or use, but human brains aren’t wholly rational, and inherited money feels like it should be different from rents, dividends, gains, or earned income. It should be special.

Should we consider claiming Social Security earlier to squeeze more life out of it? Or, put another way, is there a subjective reason why $2000 per month at age 62 is more valuable than $3500 per month at age 70? And is that subjective reason so powerful that it’s worth locking in those lower payments for life?

Stop deluding yourself with the notion that only money will protect and guarantee a great retirement. Building muscle is the cheapest insurance you will ever purchase. It lowers your risk of falls and injuries. Sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass, is a leading cause of frailty in older people.

#8561. Year-End Tax Planning for Physicians. What To Do Before 2026 Is Over

Taxes may be the last thing on your mind right now. The kids are studying for mid-terms and the holidays are almost upon us. But with less than 3 months left in 2026, you have a small window to implement strategies to minimize your tax bill for 2027.

According to Medscape’s 2026 compensation report, physicians earn, on average, $386,000 a year. Primary care physicians earn $298,000 and specialists make, on average, $417,000.

In 2026, a single filer’s taxable income of $256,225 puts them in the 35% bracket. Same for an income of $512,450 MFJ (married filing jointly). The 37% bracket starts above $640,600 for singles and $768,700 for couples.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) made permanent many provisions that had been scheduled to expire after 2025. It also added limits and phaseouts that affect higher earners specifically. In this guide, I’ll cover the changes that matter to physicians and what you can do before the year is up.

You can’t always choose when you receive income but some form of income like bonuses, self-employment income, Treasury bill income, and voluntary retirement distributions can be timed to reduce your tax bill for 2026.

Deferring income means you receive it in 2027 instead of 2026, and thus pay the tax a year later. Accelerating work in the opposite way. You can also defer or accelerate deductions to either lower this year’s bill or leave it on the table for next year.

If your employer pays a $20,000 bonus on Dec. 20, it counts as 2026 income. If your employer pays it on Jan. 5, it counts as 2027 income. At a 35% rate, that single date change delays $7,000 of federal tax by a full year.

If you expect to be in the same bracket with lower rates next year, you can defer the bonus. If you think you’ll be in a higher bracket next year, go ahead and take it in 2026.

According to this comprehensive guide by Plante Moran, pushing income into 2027 and pulling deductible expenses into 2026 delays tax, which usually helps. A higher bracket next year means you should take the opposite approach because you pay tax on 2026 income at your lower current rate.

If you’re starting as an attending in 2027, you fit the second group. Taking taxable gains or converting pre-tax IRA money to Roth this year will cost you less than doing it after your pay jumps.

Learn more: The Best Time for Roth Conversions May Be Now

Discover legitimate, IRS-recognized tax strategies physicians can use to potentially reduce their tax bills, which options high earners qualify for, and which aggressive approaches could attract IRS scrutiny.

Ideal for: Physicians and high-income professionals looking to understand their tax-saving options before speaking with their CPA.

Sat, Nov 14  ·  1:00 pm ET  ·  10:00 am PT

Employed physicians don’t have much control but ask your group whether it can pay a year-end bonus in January. Locums and 1099 physicians can, however, control invoicing and equipment purchases.

Check your Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) exposure before you defer anything. AMT works like a second tax calculation.

First, you calculate your regular tax, then, you recalculate with certain deductions added back, including your SALT deduction. Then you subtract an AMT exemption, which in 2026, is $90,100 for single filers and $140,200 for joint filers. You then must pay whichever tax is higher.

The OBBBA shrank that exemption for high earners in 2026. It starts the reduction at $500,000 of AMTI for singles and $1,000,000 for couples. It then cuts the exemption by 50 cents for every dollar above those thresholds.

The exemption disappears at $680,200 for singles and $1,280,400 for couples.

All that is to say that each extra $1,000 of income inside the phaseout range costs you $500 of exemption, so $1,500 becomes taxable at 28%. That equals a 42% marginal rate, which beats the 37% top regular rate.

Once the exemption disappears, your marginal AMT rate drops to 28%. Estimate your marginal rate for 2026 and 2027, then move income toward the lower-rate year.

Your employer withholds the additional 0.9% Medicare tax only on wages above $200,000, regardless of your filing status or your spouse’s pay. The tax itself applies above $250,000 for joint filers.

Two married physicians who each earn $300,000 have an employer who starts withholding the extra 0.9% Medicare tax once that physician’s pay passes $200,000. Each physician has $100,000 above that line, so each employer withholds $900. Together, the couple has $1,800 withheld.

With a combined wages of $600,000 the joint cutoff is $250,000, so the couple owes 0.9% of the rest of the $350,000. That’s $3,150. After subtracting the $1,800 withheld by the employers, the  couple owes $1,350 more when they file.

You can raise your W-4 withholding before Dec. 31 to cover it. This will require you to submit a new W-4 to your employer and enter the extra amount per paycheck in Step 4(c).

Withholding counts as paid evenly across the year so it beats a late estimated payment. Penalty protection requires payments of at least 90% of your 2026 tax or 110% of your 2025 tax. The 100% safe harbor covers only taxpayers with 2025 AGI of $150,000 or less, which rules out most attendings.

The annualized income installment method helps when income skews toward year-end, as locums and bonus income often do.

The 3.8% net investment income tax (NIIT) starts at $200,000 of MAGI for single filers and $250,000 for joint filers.

Those thresholds have stayed the same since 2013, so every raise adds more of your investment income into the tax. Anything that lowers MAGI, including retirement contributions and HSA deposits, lowers your NIIT too.

The IRS raised the 2026 employee limit for 401(k), 403(b) and governmental 457 plans to $24,500. Catch-up contributions add $8,000 at age 50 or older, for a total of $32,500.

There’s also a bonus catch-up of $11,250 for ages 60 to 63, which brings the total to $35,750. If your hospital also offers a governmental 457(b), that plan carries its own limit of $24,500.

SECURE 2.0 now requires employees who earned more than $150,000 in 2025 wages to direct catch-up contributions to Roth accounts. That’s all attendings. If your plan offers no Roth option, you can’t make 2026 catch-up contributions at all.

Direct Roth IRA contributions phase out between $153,000 and $168,000 for single filers and between $242,000 and $252,000 for joint filers.

Employed physicians can contribute $7,500 to a nondeductible traditional IRA and convert it. This works best when neither spouse has funds in a traditional IRA, and you owe tax only on growth between the contribution and the conversion.

A pre-tax IRA balance makes part of the conversion taxable, so roll it into your 401(k) before Dec. 31 if your plan accepts rollovers.

Practice owners have bigger options. A profit-sharing plan allows total contributions of $72,000, or $80,000 with catch-up, or $83,250 at ages 60 to 63.

A SEP allows $72,000 and requires at least $360,000 of self-employment income before the deduction.

A defined benefit plan can allow larger deductible contributions than either, depending on your age and target benefit. The 2026 maximum is $290,000 or 100% of your highest 3-year average earned income, whichever is lower.

Self-employed physicians can set up a plan and make 2026 contributions as late as the tax return due date, including extensions. If you have employees, you likely must let them participate.

Also read: Backdoor Roth IRA 2026: A Step by Step Guide with Vanguard

For 2026, the HSA limits are $4,400 for self-only coverage and $8,750 for family coverage, plus $1,000 at age 55 or older. Contributions reduce AGI and qualified withdrawals come out tax-free. A family contribution of $8,750 can save you about $3,063 in federal tax at a 35% rate.

A health FSA is limited to $3,400 and you can carry over up to $680 of unused funds to 2027. The dependent care FSA limit rose to $7,500 from $5,000, which saves you $2,625 at a 35% rate. Those contributions reduce the expenses you can claim for the child and dependent care credit.

Today’s relatively low rates raise the odds that your retirement rate will be higher.

Permanent rates have no expiration date but Congress can still raise them. Converting in chunks over several years keeps each year’s income from jumping into a higher bracket. But a Roth conversion adds to your taxable income in the year you convert so confirm you can pay the tax from outside the IRA.

Early-retired and part-time physicians must now deal with expiration of the enhanced premium tax credit. This means that the ACA cliff now applies to them.

If you earn $1 above 400% of the poverty line, you lose all marketplace subsidies. The threshold is $62,600 for a single person and $129,000 for a family of 4 in 2026.

Tommy Lucas, a CFP at Moisand Fitzgerald Tamayo recommends pairing a high-deductible plan with HSA contributions, which lower your AGI.

Two new rules have reduced the value of itemized gifts.

A 0.5% of AGI floor is now in effect which means a physician with $500,000 of AGI can’t deduct the first $2,500 of donations.

The OBBBA also caps the tax benefit at 35 cents per dollar for filers in the 37% bracket.

Bunching charitable giving can fix most of the floor issue. The floor applies once per year, so 5 years of $10,000 gifts at $500,000 of AGI forfeit $2,500 each year and leave $37,500 deductible.

One $50,000 gift forfeits $2,500 once and leaves $47,500 deductible. The extra $10,000 saves $3,500 at a 35% rate.

Charissa Anderson, a CFP at Ferguson Wellman Capital Management, says that bunching works best when you pair a donor-advised fund with appreciated stock. A donor-advised fund lets you make 1 large gift now and send grants to charities over time.

Plante Moran warns that you should get written acknowledgment that the sponsoring organization holds exclusive legal control of the assets.

If you itemize, shares held for more than 1 year before donating let you deduct full market value and skip the capital gains tax you’d pay otherwise. Most physicians pay 15% on long-term gains plus the 3.8% NIIT, which totals 18.8%.

Physicians with taxable income above $545,500 (single) or $613,700 (joint) pay 20% plus the NIIT, which totals 23.8%. If you donate $50,000 of shares with a $20,000 basis, you can avoid up to $5,640 at 18.8% or $7,140 at 23.8% of the $30,000 gain.

The deduction is capped at 30% of AGI for public charities and you can carry the excess forward 5 years.

Donors can use tax lot selection, as in choosing which specific shares to give. Lots with the largest gains usually make the best candidates. Never donate shares that trade below your basis. Sell them, claim the loss and donate the cash.

Physicians who take the standard deduction ($16,100 single, $32,200 joint) can now deduct up to $1,000 of cash gifts or $2,000 for couples. A couple in the 35% bracket can save $700.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

Physicians aged 70 1⁄2 or older can send up to $111,000 from an IRA directly to charity in 2026. That transfer counts toward required minimum distributions and steers clear of taxable income.

For 2026, the SALT cap is $40,400. As your MAGI exceeds $505,000, the cap drops by 30 cents for every extra dollar.

A couple with $550,000 of MAGI have an excess of $45,000. The cap drops by 30% of $45,000, which is $13,500. Their cap falls from $40,400 to $26,900. As your MAGI approaches $606,333, the cap reaches its $10,000 minimum. Above that, it stays at $10,000.

If your 2026 state and local taxes will fall short of the cap, prepay your 2027 property tax bill by Dec. 31. Your county needs to have assessed the bill already.

Plante Moran estimates a single filer in the 35% bracket saves $14,140 by deducting the full $40,400. Check your AMT first, though. A large SALT deduction can trigger it. You also need enough total itemized deductions to beat your standard deduction.

The Section 199A deduction is permanent and equals up to 20% of qualified business income.

Medicine counts as a specified service business, so as your income increases, the deduction gets smaller before eventually disappearing.

The 2026 phase ranges from $201,750 to $276,750 for single filers, with double those amounts for joint filers. Part-time physicians, lower-earning specialties and couples with taxable income below $553,500 can still claim some deduction. Retirement contributions that lower your taxable income can pull you back into the range.

S corporation owners can take part of their income as distributions instead of salary, which avoids payroll taxes and the 0.9% Medicare tax. The IRS scrutinizes this closely, so make sure your salary is reasonable.

The OBBBA also lowered the cap on business losses that offset other income to $256,000 for single filers and $512,000 for joint filers in 2026. Rental income and losses count as passive unless you qualify as a real estate professional.

That status requires more than half of your personal services and more than 750 hours in property businesses. Special rules can help spouses meet material participation.

Equipment buyers can deduct 100% of the cost of qualifying property in the first year through bonus depreciation. This applies to property you acquire after Jan. 19, 2025. Section 179 expensing reached $2.56 million in 2026 and phases out above $4.09 million of purchases.

The equipment must be placed in service by Dec. 31.

Dec. 31 for most moves, including charitable gifts, payroll retirement deferrals and property tax prepayments. Self-employed physicians can set up and fund a retirement plan until the 2026 return due date, including extensions.

Add up your deductions and pick the larger amount. The standard deduction is $16,100 for single filers and $32,200 for joint filers. Itemize when your SALT, mortgage interest and charitable gifts exceed it.

Defer if you expect the same or a lower tax rate next year. Accelerate if you expect a higher one. A fellow who starts as an attending in 2027 fits the second group.

It is 0.9% of wages above $200,000 for single filers and above $250,000 for joint filers. Employers start withholding at $200,000 regardless of your filing status, so couples often owe extra when they file.

Pay at least 90% of your 2026 tax or 110% of your 2025 tax. Raise your W-4 withholding before Dec. 31 to cover any shortfall.

You can contribute $24,500 to a 401(k), 403(b) or governmental 457 plan. Add $8,000 at age 50 or older. Ages 60 to 63 can add $11,250 instead.

Employees who earned more than $150,000 in 2025 wages must make catch-up contributions to Roth accounts. If your plan has no Roth option, you can’t make 2026 catch-up contributions.

Direct contributions phase out between $153,000 and $168,000 for single filers and between $242,000 and $252,000 for joint filers. Most physicians use a backdoor Roth, which converts a nondeductible traditional IRA contribution of up to $7,500.

It affects early-retired and part-time physicians who buy marketplace coverage. Earn $1 above 400% of the poverty line and you lose all subsidies. CNBC reports the 2026 threshold at about $63,000 for a single person.

The cap is $40,400. It drops by 30 cents for every dollar of MAGI above $505,000 and bottoms out at $10,000 at about $606,333.

Often only in part. Medicine counts as a specified service business, so the deduction phases out between $201,750 and $276,750 of taxable income for single filers and disappears above that. Joint filers get double those amounts.

The 0.5% of AGI floor applies once per year, so one large gift loses less than several small ones. At $500,000 of AGI, a $50,000 gift saves $3,500 more than 5 yearly gifts of $10,000 at a 35% rate.

Yes. If you itemize and held the shares for more than 1 year, you deduct full market value and avoid the capital gains tax you’d owe on a sale. Donate publicly traded shares directly to the charity or donor-advised fund.

Yes. A CPA who knows your state and practice structure can model your return for you before you act.

The bonus-timing example is concrete: a $20,000 bonus paid Dec. 20 lands in 2026 wages, while a Jan. 5 pay date pushes the same dollars into 2027 and, at a 35% marginal rate, delays about $7,000 of federal tax for a year. Pairing that with the 2026 HSA ceilings ($4,400 self-only / $8,750 family, plus $1,000 catch-up at 55+) and the checklist on accelerating or deferring deductions gives employed physicians a short year-end punch list even when W-2 wages themselves are inflexible.

#8558. You’re Not Rich — And Neither Am I

Warren Buffett has spent decades telling anyone who’ll listen that he lives simply. Same house in Omaha he bought in 1958 for $31,500. No mansion, no car collection, nothing flashy.

He eats at McDonald’s, drinks Coke by the case and has said more than once that a person could live like him on a fraction of his fortune and lose nothing that actually matters.

A physician two decades into a cardiology career already has a six-bedroom house on two acres with a three-car garage. Something that would put Buffett’s Omaha home to shame.

But Buffett flies private. On his personal jet. Which he owns. (He also owns the company that made his plane just FYI).

That cardiologist couldn’t touch a private jet with a ten-foot pole. Not on a $600,000 salary carrying a jumbo mortgage, two kids in private school and a home equity line he opened for the kitchen renovation.

Buffett could write a check for that physician’s entire house and still have money left for the furniture.

My point is, quantifying wealth is not a black and white endeavor. McMansions don’t lead to private jets. And “modest” lifestyles don’t rule them out.

It’s a strange world we live in. One where most people are blindly chasing perception rather than what actually matters.

Ideal for: Physicians and high-income professionals looking to understand their tax-saving options before speaking with their CPA.

Sat, Nov 14  ·  1:00 pm ET  ·  10:00 am PT

Also read: Why Most Doctors Retire With Too Much Money (And What to Do About It)

The Federal Reserve’s Survey of Consumer Finances states that the median American household net worth is $192,084. The average is more than 5x that at $1.06 million due to a relatively small number of extremely wealthy households that pull the average up.

Physicians, as a group, are ahead of that median and the gap keeps widening.

Medscape’s 2026 Physician Wealth & Debt Report found that 24% of physicians now report a family net worth of $5 million or more — largely thanks to stock market gains and rising home values.

However, the same report makes it clear this wealth isn’t evenly spread. The physicians in the $5 million group are mostly in procedure-based specialties which have the highest earning ceilings to begin with.

Plenty of physicians in lower-paying specialties spend most of a career well short of that mark despite carrying the same title, the same debt load at the start, and the same years of deferred income during training.

All physicians start with some sort of student debt — small or big — regardless of specialty. The median medical school debt for the class of 2025 is $215,000, not counting undergraduate loans.

Or any non-education debt, credit cards and car loans that tend to accumulate during residency for that matter.

A newly minted attending earning six figures can still have a negative net worth. It takes years to pay down debt and bring it up to zero.

Years more to enter the black. Those early years are the reason for the gap between a $5-million-net-worth radiologist and a physician twenty years into practice who still hasn’t crossed seven figures.

Let’s talk about two doctors who have the same degree and the same starting debt but two very different philosophies on spending money.

For this example we’ll play into the most common stereotypes doctors have faced — and fought hard to shed — for years.

Dr. Flashy “invests” in a new Range Rover every three years. He’s got a lake house two hours outside the city, a boat he uses maybe four weekends a summer — if the weather cooperates.

And surprisingly to some, he’s not broke. He makes real money and a part of his lifestyle is funded from that same income.

Almost every single one of these major purchases generates its own follow-on bill which continues to recur exponentially.

The Range Rover’s routine maintenance costs more than a lot of people’s monthly car payment. The lake house needs a new roof eventually, landscaping every season, comes with a property tax bill that rises every time the county reassesses and someone to physically check on it every time a storm rolls through three states away.

The boat comes with marina fees, winterizing and a marine mechanic who bills by the hour. Buying something nice is the equivalent of signing up for a subscription with an indefinite term and a rising rate.

This is called the hedonic treadmill. Once someone upgrades something in their life, the old version stops being satisfying, permanently. And the new version only delivers that same satisfaction for as long as the novelty lasts.

Eventually the purchase itself becomes pointless. It was the feeling of upgrading that felt good but that feeling fades fast enough that the next upgrade becomes necessary just to get back to the baseline.

Luxury goods are sneakily good at triggering this because so much of what they deliver is the status attached to the price tag. Any functional improvement or value they bring is usually beside the point.

Dr. Flashy’s income may be large. He might even be a neurosurgeon earning $829,161. But at some point his lifestyle needs additional funding to keep up. That’s when he turns to financing.

Eventually, the bank becomes something he is increasingly dependent on.

To be clear, I’m not speculating on his character. Forbes reports that the highest-income American households, those above the 90th percentile, carry the largest average credit card balances of any income group (over $11,000 on average) despite being the group least likely to carry a balance at all.

So data shows us that the people who look the most financially comfortable are disproportionately dependent on revolving debt to stay there. Not all high earners are predisposed to open lines of credit, but when they do, they tend to rack up more of it because the lifestyle they’re financing costs more to maintain than anyone else’s.

The thing is, money is finite even with a large income. Spending more of it means you need more just to sustain the spending at its current level. And that treadmill doesn’t slow down as the years go by.

Dr. Net-Worth has the same income as Dr. Flashy. Same specialty, even, same call schedule, same patient panel.

But Dr. Net-Worth drives a Honda he’s had since fellowship. It’s got a cracked bumper he keeps meaning to fix. He lives in a house that’s nice but completely unremarkable from the street — not something you’ll see featured in Architectural Digest.

Still, his investment accounts feature a sum that would make your eyes water. No one except him and his accountant know what it is.

We have come to perceive net worth as some concrete evaluation of a person’s wealth. But it really isn’t. In fact, the more zeroes it has, the less real it is.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

I mean, this year we saw Elon Musk become (briefly) the first ever trillionaire. But does that mean he’s got a Scrooge McDuck vault full of gold coins stacked to the ceiling?  Well, he might — but he won’t have an actual trillion in there to dive into and swim around in.

That number is mostly the market’s opinion of his equity stakes on a given day. An opinion that can — and does — swing by tens of billions of dollars before lunch and back again by dinner. All without a single dollar changing hands or a single decision on his part.

Dr. Net-Worth’s number works the same way just on a smaller scale. Most of it lives in a house he’s still making payments on every month, a retirement account he can’t touch before a certain age lest he trigger a penalty, and an ever-growing brokerage account he could never imagine drawing from.

All of it is his. Yet, he doesn’t use a dollar of it beyond the mortgage payment and the grocery bill. He’s rich! Technically. Psychologically, it might as well be someone else’s money.

You can’t fault him for being this way. Sometimes it’s just temperament. Plenty of high earners are simply frugal by nature, genuinely uninterested in the lake house and actually happier to keep the Honda running for another hundred thousand miles. Nothing wrong with that. At least Dr. Net-Worth doesn’t need rescuing from the life he has chosen.

But sometimes the hesitation to spend stems from fear. Constant worry that the money could vanish overnight, that one bad market year or one malpractice suit could erase everything you’ve built.

That spending on anything beyond the bare essentials is an invitation for disaster to strike. Dr. Net-Worth worked his butt off to build a financial fortress that classifies him as financially free. Yet the day may never come when he actually gets to taste that freedom.

Dr. Flashy is one bad year/one slow season at the practice/one unexpected repair bill on the boat away from a very uncomfortable conversation with a lender.

Dr. Net-Worth has already won the game by any objective measure but refuses to enjoy it.

Financial planner Derek Hagen says that money that isn’t pointed at anything in particular just accumulates, and accumulation without a purpose behind it isn’t freedom. Dr. Net-Worth has plenty of money with no real purpose for it.

Dr.  Flashy has an answer: status and visible proof that he has “made it”. But his answer costs more to maintain with every passing year, never quite delivering the sense of arrival he’s chasing.

There’s no handbook that outlines exactly where the divide between enjoying the money and hoarding it is. And anyone who claims there is one wants to sell you something.

You, the physician reading this, are probably nothing like Dr. Flashy or Dr. Net-Worth. And asking which one is better or worse isn’t the point either.

Your money, no matter how it is accumulated or spent on, deserves to be used to fund a life you chose on purpose. Not one assembled by accident out of habit, fear or…what the neighbors might notice.

Buffett kept the house and bought the plane because both of those choices added up to a life he actually wanted. That is rich (of course being worth $144.6 billion doesn’t hurt).

Everything else is just perception in a strange world that will never stop raising the bar.

Good, thoughtful article, Thanks! I have to agree about the ongoing obligations that the treadmill gets us into. I have to identify with Dr Net-Worth, but rather than having no purpose, I would say that one real, tangible benefit he has is security. Knowing he or his spouse can incur some life altering accident or illness and not affect the well being of the rest of the family. As an example my mother in law has dementia and has been in memory care for a decade. Her current bill is 200k per year. She and her husband planned very well and regardless of how long she lives she will be taken care of. The kids have not needed to contribute at all. My household has planned in a similar way. I know I will never need to be supported by my kids.

Thank you for separating a headline net worth figure from a life actually funded by it. The contrast between Dr Flashy and Dr Net-Worth is useful precisely because neither extreme answers the question of what the money is for. I found the follow-on costs point especially practical: a purchase is rarely a one-off price, and marina fees, maintenance and rising property taxes can quietly turn a status purchase into a continuing obligation. On the other side, treating a net worth statement as a market snapshot, rather than spendable security, helps explain why accumulating without a purpose can still feel anxious. A more useful middle path might be to define, in advance, what ‘enough’ looks like in cash-flow terms — housing, time, work flexibility and family priorities — and then judge each upgrade against that, rather than against another physician’s lifestyle or another year’s market valuation.

Of course, $5 million in a West or East Coast city means something entirely different than $5 million in a medium sized town in the Midwest or South. By way of information, if anyone is interested in how their assets compare relative to the U.S. net worth figures (by age, education or region).

Also, in another 6-8 weeks, the Federal Reserve Bank will issue the results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finance (SCF), which presents its own set of (updated) net worth and income figures.

The lingering question is – how do you determine the net present value of future social security payments or a pension, if eligible for one? Do you include that in a net worth statement or not?

The takeaway I have this article is to be neither a hoarder nor a ‘flashy’. Be comfortable in your spending style. And, in spite of the stress of the medical profession, it is good to practice gratitude for the opportunities to serve and have a roof over our heads.

Btw, I think the US government is going to face financial headwinds over the next 10 years. Social security and Medicare are going to run out of money (2032, 2033). In 2027, a large number of long-term bonds are going to mature and need re-financing. The real details can be found on the web, but you have to go digging for them. Carpe Diem.

Thanks for reading, and for adding so much to the discussion.

You’re right about geography. Five million in Manhattan or the Bay Area buys a smaller house and a longer commute than the same number buys in Omaha, which might explain why Buffett never bothered leaving. (Your link to the net worth comparison looks like it got eaten by the comment system, by the way. Feel free to repost it.)

On Social Security and pensions: I leave them off the net worth statement. You can’t sell them or borrow against them, and most of their value dies with you, so folding them in puffs up a number that’s already mostly opinion. Where they earn their keep is the retirement income plan. A pension paying $40,000 a year does roughly the work of a $1 million portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate, which means the nest egg you need to build shrinks accordingly. I’d count them in that spreadsheet and keep them out of the other one.

On the trust funds, one detail tends to get lost in the headlines. When the reserves run dry in the early 2030s, benefits don’t drop to zero. Under current projections, incoming payroll taxes would still cover something like three quarters to four fifths of scheduled payments. Painful, sure, but a haircut is a very different problem than a guillotine. For younger docs, penciling in about 75% of your statement estimate seems like reasonable caution without veering into doom.

And I’m with you on gratitude. Most of this job’s stress comes with a roof, meaningful work and the chance to retire on our own terms, which is more than a lot of people ever get to complain about.

Carpe diem right back at you. -Jorge Sanchez, MD

#8557. Air France-KLM Flying Blue → Tahiti Business Class

Savings rate, FI number, and the path to freedom.
