The only points path to nonstop business class service to French Polynesia

Picture this: you're reclining in a fully flat bed somewhere over the Pacific, a glass of Champagne in hand, watching the sun melt into the ocean from 35,000 feet. In eight hours, you'll land in Papeete — French Polynesia's gateway to overwater bungalows, turquoise lagoons, and the kind of trip people save their whole lives for. And you got here on points. This is the Air France business class seat to Tahiti, and it represents one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. Not just because of where you're going — though Tahiti is bucket-list by definition — but because of the staggering gap between what you'd pay in cash and what you'll pay in miles. **The math will genuinely stop you in your tracks.** A business class ticket from Los Angeles (LAX) to Papeete (PPT) on Air France regularly retails between **$5,000 and $12,000 per person**. That's the cash reality. But with Flying Blue miles — Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program — you can book the same seat for as few as **88,000 miles**. At the high end of retail pricing, that's a value of **13.6 cents per point (CPP)**. Even at the low end, you're extracting **5.7 CPP** from miles that most programs value at 1–2 cents. In the ChooseFI community, we talk constantly about optimizing every dollar toward financial independence — and a redemption that turns 88,000 transferable points into a $5,000–$12,000 experience is about as powerful as it gets. Here's what makes this feel different from your average business class booking: Air France operates a **Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner** on this route, featuring a modern, premium business class cabin with direct aisle access for every seat, noise-reducing windows, better humidity levels, and that unmistakably French touch in service and catering. You're not just flying in a recliner — you're flying in a genuine lie-flat pod on one of aviation's most celebrated aircraft. And this is the only nonstop option. Air France is the **sole carrier operating nonstop LAX–PPT** service. That's not a coincidence — it's a pricing inefficiency baked into the route's geography, and it's exactly the kind of structural advantage the ChooseFI community knows how to exploit.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program is the only way to book the only nonstop flight between Los Angeles and Tahiti using points — and that program happens to offer some of the most generous award pricing in the world.

Flying Blue uses a dynamic award pricing model, meaning costs fluctuate based on demand and availability. That sounds like a disadvantage — and sometimes it is. But here's the inefficiency: Flying Blue releases Promo Rewards every single month. These are fixed-price award seats on select routes, discounted 25–50% off standard award pricing. When Tahiti appears as a Promo Reward destination (which it does periodically), the pricing drops dramatically — and crucially, Promo Reward tickets eliminate carrier-imposed fuel surcharges entirely.

Fuel surcharges on Air France-operated flights are normally moderate, but they're real — they can add $200–$500 to an award ticket. Promo Rewards wipe those out. This is the pricing inefficiency: Flying Blue is essentially subsidizing this cabin to drive demand, and you can capture the subsidy.

Here's the beautiful part for ChooseFI members: virtually every major transferable points currency sends to Flying Blue at a 1:1 ratio. That means:

The Chase, Amex, and Citi transfers are instant, which matters enormously when you're racing to lock down a business class award seat before someone else grabs it. You find the seat, you confirm it's available, then you transfer — because once points leave your bank, they don't come back.

This is the single most important rule in booking award travel, and it's especially critical here. Flying Blue's award availability on the LAX–PPT route is genuinely limited — this is a popular route to a popular destination on a single aircraft. You do not transfer points speculatively. You find confirmed availability on flyingblue.com, verify the seat count and pricing, then immediately transfer from your Chase, Amex, or Citi account (all instant) and book.

Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing, meaning you could potentially fly into Papeete and out of another South Pacific destination if Air France serves it — giving sophisticated travelers a way to build a multi-destination itinerary without paying for a separate return trip to your origin city. It's a small but meaningful piece of flexibility in a program that doesn't always offer it.

This is a moderate-difficulty booking. The steps themselves aren't complicated — but the sequencing matters enormously. Follow this in order.

Go to flyingblue.com and use the award search tool. You do NOT need a Flying Blue account to search — but you will need one to book, so create a free account if you haven't already. Search LAX → PPT in business class. Flying Blue's calendar view lets you scan across multiple departure dates, which is essential for spotting availability on a route with limited award seats.

Tip: Flying Blue's booking window opens 359 days in advance. For a route this popular and this capacity-constrained, searching at the 11-month mark is strongly advised. Set a calendar reminder for exactly 359 days before your target travel dates.

On the first of each month, Flying Blue releases its new Promo Rewards. These are fixed-price, reduced-cost awards with no fuel surcharges. Bookmark flyingblue.com/en/earn-spend/flying-blue-promo-rewards and check it monthly. If Tahiti appears, act immediately — Promo Reward availability disappears fast.

Once you find available dates and seats, note the exact miles price shown at checkout. Flying Blue's dynamic pricing means the cost you see on Monday might differ from Thursday. Screenshot the search result with the price clearly visible. This is your confirmation that the award is priceable before you transfer points.

Now — and only now — transfer your points:

Transfer the exact amount you need — no more, no less.

Return to flyingblue.com, complete the search again with your now-funded account, and book. Have your passport and traveler details ready. Pay any taxes/fees (usually $50–$150 on non-Promo awards; near-zero on Promo Rewards) with a travel rewards credit card to earn additional points.

Award availability on this route moves quickly. If your target dates are sold out:

Flying Blue uses dynamic award pricing, which usually makes award charts unpredictable. But the monthly Promo Rewards program creates a fixed-price overlay that dramatically undercuts the dynamic rates. When Tahiti appears on the Promo Rewards list, business class pricing drops 25 to 50 percent below standard and fuel surcharges are eliminated entirely. Air France is the sole operator of the LAX to PPT nonstop — no other airline flies it — which means Flying Blue is the only loyalty program with direct booking access to this route. This combination of route exclusivity and periodic promotional pricing is what makes this a genuine sweet spot rather than just a good redemption.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's make this concrete. Imagine a couple planning their 10th anniversary trip to Bora Bora in the spring of 2026. They want to start the trip right — meaning lie-flat seats over the Pacific, not a middle seat in economy for a nine-hour flight.

The cash price: Air France business class from LAX to PPT in spring typically runs $6,500–$9,000 per person round-trip. For two people, you're looking at $13,000–$18,000. That's a car payment for most families. Even if it's in the travel budget, it's a brutal number to justify when you're pursuing financial independence.

The points price: 88,000 Flying Blue miles per person, round-trip in business class. For two passengers: 176,000 Flying Blue miles total, plus approximately $200–$300 in taxes and carrier fees (less if you catch a Promo Rewards release, where surcharges are waived entirely).

The CPP math: At $8,000 in cash value against 88,000 miles, you're extracting 9.1 cents per point — nearly 5–9x the baseline value of transferable points currencies. That's the ChooseFI lens: every point you've earned on everyday spending just multiplied in purchasing power.

What you'll actually experience: You check in at LAX and are directed to the business class line — a detail that still feels quietly luxurious no matter how many times you've done it. Once onboard the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, your seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 6 feet in length. The cabin's reduced cabin pressure and higher humidity mean you arrive in Papeete meaningfully less fatigued than you would in economy — important when you have a connecting boat ride to Bora Bora ahead of you.

Air France's catering reflects its French heritage: expect a proper multi-course meal service, a curated wine selection, and warm bread — not a foil-wrapped tray. The flight is roughly 8–9 hours nonstop, so there's time to genuinely sleep, watch a film, and arrive rested.

For a couple using points they accumulated from normal household spending over 12–18 months, the $16,000 in combined cash value they didn't spend is the real number — and the one that matters most on the path to FI.

Flying Blue releases Promo Rewards on the first of every month. Set a phone reminder. These promotions offer 25–50% off standard award pricing AND eliminate fuel surcharges. On a Promo Rewards release, an 88,000-mile business class award could drop to as low as 44,000–66,000 miles with no surcharges. That's the difference between good and extraordinary. Don't miss a cycle.

Flying Blue's booking window opens 359 days in advance. The LAX–PPT route operates a single daily nonstop on a single aircraft — meaning business class inventory is finite and competitive. If you're targeting holidays, school break windows, or peak Tahiti season (July–August), mark your calendar to search at the 11-month mark.

Flying Blue permits open-jaw routing, meaning you could potentially fly into PPT and return from a different city — or fly from a different origin. This flexibility can reduce deadhead positioning flights and help families traveling from cities other than Los Angeles build more logical itineraries.

This is the cardinal sin of award booking. Transferred points cannot be reversed. Never move miles to Flying Blue until you have confirmed award availability on your exact dates with a price you've screenshotted. Chase, Amex, and Citi all transfer instantly — use that speed advantage after you've confirmed the seat exists.

Flying Blue's dynamic pricing means the same route can cost meaningfully different amounts day-to-day and even hour-to-hour. Don't assume the price from your earlier search is locked in. Always verify at checkout before transferring.

Because Flying Blue accepts transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, Capital One, and Bilt at 1:1, your earning strategy is flexible. Focus on a single flexible currency — the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve for Ultimate Rewards, or the Amex Gold/Platinum for Membership Rewards — and let everyday spending build toward the 88,000-mile target over 12–18 months.

Marriott transfers to Flying Blue at 3:1 — meaning 264,000 Marriott points become 88,000 Flying Blue miles. Unless you have a massive Marriott balance you can't use elsewhere, this is an inefficient path. Stick to the 1:1 partners.

This redemption is purpose-built for couples and families planning a landmark trip to French Polynesia — an anniversary, a honeymoon, a milestone birthday, or simply the trip you've been telling yourself you'd take "someday." If Tahiti or Bora Bora is on the life list, this is the redemption that makes it financially defensible from a FI perspective.

Minimum requirements: 88,000 Flying Blue miles per person for round-trip business class, plus approximately $100–$300 in taxes (less on Promo Rewards). For a couple, plan for 176,000 transferable points minimum.

For the ChooseFI community, this redemption represents the travel rewards philosophy at its best: redirecting the value of everyday spending into genuinely transformative experiences, without derailing the path to financial independence.

Use the Flying Blue award search calendar view to scan business class availability on the LAX to PPT route across multiple dates. Check both standard pricing and Promo Rewards pricing. Do not transfer any points until you confirm available seats.

Once you confirm award space, transfer the required miles from Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant), Amex Membership Rewards (1-2 days), Citi ThankYou (instant), Capital One (1-2 days), or Bilt (1-2 days). Only transfer after confirming availability.

Complete the booking on flyingblue.com as soon as your miles arrive. Select your preferred lie-flat seat through the seat map. For couples, choose adjacent seats in the business cabin. Promo Rewards availability is limited and can disappear within hours.

Standard dynamic pricing typically runs around 88,000 miles one-way in business class from LAX to Papeete. When Tahiti appears on the monthly Promo Rewards list, that price can drop to 44,000 to 66,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges — a savings of 25 to 50 percent.

Tahiti is not guaranteed every month. Flying Blue rotates destinations across its network. You may see Tahiti appear several times per year, especially during shoulder season. The key is having your points ready and checking on the 1st of every month so you can act immediately when it appears.

The nonstop Air France flight to Tahiti only departs from LAX. However, you can book a connecting itinerary through flyingblue.com that includes a domestic connection to LAX on the same award ticket. Alternatively, book a separate positioning flight to LAX using a different program.

This is a significant advantage over standard Flying Blue pricing, which can include carrier-imposed surcharges.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Flying Blue to Tahiti in business class is a genuinely unique sweet spot because no other loyalty program can book this route. The only nonstop from the US to French Polynesia operates exclusively on Air France out of LAX, and Flying Blue is the only way to book it with miles. #8556. 6 Best Subscription Management Apps (To Cancel Recurring Transactions)

By Deacon Hayes Updated November 15, 2026

Managing your money isn’t just about earning more. It’s also about stopping unnecessary losses. In today’s digital economy, recurring subscription charges (streaming services, premium apps, trials, memberships) quietly drain money each month. Most people spend hundreds, or even thousands, annually on services they don’t use. Subscription manager apps help you see recurring charges, track billing cycles, and cancel those you no longer want.

Before choosing an app, know what features matter most:

Rocket Money is one of the most well-known subscription managers. It scans your linked bank and credit accounts for recurring charges and displays them on a clear dashboard. People like it for its ability to detect subscriptions and assist with cancellations directly in the app, a major time-saver for busy people.

Why it stands out• Automatically detects recurring payments• Lets you cancel unwanted subscriptions directly from the app• Includes extra budgeting tools and spending alerts• Trusted security with read-only bank access

Who it’s for: People who want the fastest way to spot and stop unwanted recurring charges without manually entering every service.

Trim is another financial assistant that scans transactions and flags recurring charges. While subscription tracking is a smaller part of its feature set, it also provides bill negotiation support and money-saving alerts. Many users like Trim because it reaches out on your behalf about subscriptions via text or in-app messaging.

Why it stands out• Recurring transaction detection• Alerts about unusual subscriptions or trials converting to paid• Bill negotiation tools beyond basic subscription tracking

Who it’s for: Users who want automation plus help reducing bills and optimizing spending.

PocketGuard is primarily a budgeting app that includes subscription tracking as part of a broader financial overview. Instead of being solely a subscription manager, it integrates recurring expenses into your overall budget, helping you get a full picture of your finances.

Why it stands out• Syncs automatically with financial accounts• Highlights recurring expenses in the context of your whole budget• Helps track cash flow and affordability

Who it’s for: People who want subscriptions tracked inside a complete personal finance dashboard.

Monarch Money offers robust financial planning tools: budgets, goals, net worth tracking, and more, with subscription visibility included in the package. Users often choose it for its highly customizable interface and deep analytics. It’s not subscription-only, but it gives you full clarity on recurring expenses as part of larger planning.

Why it stands out• Powerful budgeting + subscription tracking.• Clean, customizable data visuals.• Goal-based money management.

Who it’s for: Users who want subscription insights in the context of total financial planning — and who are okay paying for premium features.

Why it stands out• No bank/credit card linking required.• Clean and minimal interface.• Calendar views and notification reminders.

Subby offers functionality similar to Bobby’s but is known for integrations and subscription reminders tailored for Android users. It lets you manually track expenses with flexible billing schedules and alerts. (While not all resources list Subby as a top pick, it’s frequently mentioned among good manual trackers.)

Why it stands out• Manual entry with customizable notifications.• Good choice for Android users.

Who it’s for: People who want a simple manual tracker without linking financial accounts.

If you’d rather not use a third-party app at all, both Apple and Google offer direct subscription management:

iPhone (Apple Subscriptions):Settings → Your Name → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel Subscription.

Android (Google Play):Open Google Play → Subscriptions → Select subscription → Cancel subscription.

These built-in tools won’t automatically find all recurring charges if some are billed outside the app stores, but they are a secure and effective way to manage many mobile subscriptions.

Here’s a quick guide based on what matters most to you:

You can also combine approaches — use a subscription app plus your budgeting system to spot recurring leaks and plan better for annual vs monthly charges.

Practical advice to help you make money, save money and pay off debt, from a family that paid off $52,000 in 18 months.

It’s almost Halloween, and much like everyone else, I have been sucked into the tradition of watching horror movies with my wife before we take our daughter trick-or-treating. One of the movies I’m still thinking about from last week is Backrooms. It is the highest-grossing film A24 has ever released, and most of it takes place in rooms that look like a hospital at 3 a.m.

Yellowed walls. Fluorescent tubes that buzz loud enough to notice. Carpet that has absorbed something you would rather not identify. Corridors that turn left, then left again, until you’re somehow back where you started. If you trained at a big academic center, you have walked these halls, and probably still dream about them.

The film grew out of Kane Parsons’s YouTube series about a dimension of endless, empty rooms. Instead of the creature feature I expected, I got a picture of the doctor who is close to financial independence and can’t bring themselves to leave.

Full disclaimer: only read ahead if you’ve watched the film because there will be spoilers!

Clark is a failed architect running a struggling furniture store in San Jose. He drinks too much, his marriage is over, and he has started sleeping at the store. One night he goes down to check the breaker box, notices a glowing slit in the wall, and falls through it.

On the other side is a copy of the world that is slightly wrong. Rooms that almost look like rooms. Furniture that seems to have melted at the edges. Hallways longer than the building could possibly hold. Later in the film it gets described as a faulty, misremembered version of reality.

That description fits medical training better than anything I’ve heard in a wellness lecture. Residency is a copy of adult life with the proportions off. You have a title and real responsibility for people’s lives, but you’re 31 with a negative net worth, and you haven’t made it to a friend’s wedding without checking your phone in years.

Real life is always one room ahead: after boards, after fellowship, after the loans, after partnership. So you keep walking.

After a few trips in and out, Clark leaves his therapist a message. He’s staying in the Backrooms, and he won’t be coming back. He has found a way out of the failing store, the drinking, the empty house. The place he picked is worse than the one he’s leaving, but it’s familiar, and it doesn’t ask him to deal with anything.

The FIRE crowd has a name for this: one more year. You hit your number, or get close enough to see it, and you sign another contract anyway. The reasons all sound sensible. The market is choppy. The kids start college in four years. The group is short two partners.

Besides, what else would you do on a Wednesday morning?

Plenty of physicians keep working after financial independence because they love the work, and that’s a good outcome. The question worth asking is whether you’re staying because you chose to, or because the hallway is the only place you know how to stand.

Early in the film, Clark shoots a cheap TV commercial for the store dressed as its pirate mascot. It’s a little embarrassing and a little sweet. It is the version of himself he has to perform to keep the business alive.

By the end of the film, the costume becomes a towering, distorted Clark in the pirate outfit, peg leg and all, is waiting for him in the Backrooms. Clark tries to calm it down the way you’d talk to a dog you raised from a puppy. It kills him.

The Backrooms in this film make monsters from what people carry in, their memories and their feelings, and build with it.

Doctors have a costume too. The white coat, the title, the steady voice you use to tell a family the scan came back bad. You need it, and your patients need you to have it. The trouble starts when it stops coming off after the shift. You introduce yourself as Dr. at your kid’s soccer game. The hobbies lapse one at a time. Every close friend works in your department. Your income, your marriage, and your sense of being a decent person all run through one job.

Then the job goes sideways. A lawsuit, a patient death you can’t stop replaying, an RVU target that climbs every year, a private equity buyout that changes everything except your title.

What turns on you in those moments is the professional self you spent fifteen years building, now bigger than the person wearing it.

The second half belongs to Clark’s therapist, Dr. Mary Kline (Renate Reinsve). Worried about her patient, she goes to the store and walks into the Backrooms after him.

She doesn’t walk in clean. Mary is still working through the demolition of her childhood home and her mother’s institutionalization. A professional helper carrying a stack of her own unprocessed losses into someone else’s crisis is a fair description of a lot of people in medicine.

Inside, Clark ties her to a chair in a fake dining room. Three human-shaped figures sit around the table with them. They don’t move or react to anything. Clark shows her they’re made of an edible white substance, and it becomes clear the Backrooms feed on them.

It might sound odd, but I couldn’t watch that scene without thinking about the Maslach Burnout Inventory. It measures three things: emotional exhaustion, a fading sense of accomplishment, and depersonalization.

Doctors are familiar with depersonalization. Patients start to feel like tasks, and after a while you feel like one too. You’re at the table every day, and you look fine from across the room, while the place slowly takes what it needs from you.

The pirate gets rid of Clark comes for Mary next. Her survival is noteworthy.

Cornered in a lopsided replica of the furniture store, she snaps the monster’s peg leg with a hat rack, then hits it in the face with a chunk of concrete from her childhood home. The thing she has been grieving the whole movie turns out to be the thing she fights with.

For a physician, that chunk of concrete is whoever you were before medicine. The kid who played bass in a garage band. The person who built bookshelves, or ran trails, or cooked for twelve friends on a Saturday. Those parts didn’t vanish when you matched. They got buried under a decade of training.

The doctors I’ve seen leave clinical work well, or drop to part-time without falling apart, usually started digging some of that back up long before they needed it. They had a corner of life the job wasn’t allowed into, and they’d been living in it for years by the time they gave notice.

This is where the analogy gets uncomfortable.

Mary’s fight with the pirate sets off a gas trap. Researchers in hazmat suits haul her out to a facility run by Async, a company that used to make MRI machines before it found the Backrooms and made them its main business.

Whether or not the filmmakers meant anything by it, a medical imaging company ending up in charge of the maze is a hard detail to ignore if you work in a hospital.

In the last scene, Mary sits in an interrogation room across from Phil, one of Async’s scientists. She asks whether they’re going to let her go. He tells her the decision isn’t his.

A lot of doctors make it through the burnout, the bad years, the cases that almost broke them, and end up in that room. They’re ready to leave, and they find out the exit belongs to someone else:

None of these are sinister on their own. Each one just moves the decision a little further from you and a little closer to a contract, a lender, or an employer.

For a physician, that’s what financial independence is really for. It’s less about retiring at 45 and more about who gets to answer the question Mary asks.

The film’s final shot is a copy of Mary, deformed and silent, sitting in a rough replica of that interrogation room somewhere deep in the Backrooms. The place has learned her. Whatever happens to the real Mary, a version of her stays behind.

Medicine leaves a copy of you behind too, and that isn’t all bad. The judgment, the pattern recognition, the calm you have in a code are yours for life. The goal isn’t to get out with nothing of the doctor left. It’s to make sure the doctor isn’t the only thing left.

A few things that help, roughly in order of effort:

Clark stayed because the maze was easier than his life. Most doctors who stay too long do it for a version of the same reason. Staying in medicine can be a great choice, as long as you’re the one making it.

The Pro Forma Never Paid Anyone’s Mortgage

If you bought into a multifamily syndication around 2021, you remember the deck. Glossy photos, a tidy IRR, a confident exit year. Then rates climbed, valuations slid, and plenty of investors watched distributions pause while their capital sat locked inside a deal that no longer penciled out.

Private real estate lending puts you in a different seat. The lender gets paid ahead of equity, holds a lien on the property, and collects interest from monthly loan payments rather than waiting on a sale that may never hit its number. You give up the home-run upside. In exchange, nobody calls you about a broken water heater at 2 a.m., a perk I’ve come to value after enough overnight shifts.

In a recent webinar, I joined Dr. Christy Burakovsky and Chris Lopez of Property Llama to discuss how private real estate loans are underwritten, where the actual risks lie, and what investors should ask any fund before wiring a dollar.

We also covered the importance of looking beyond projected returns and understanding the fundamentals behind a lending strategy.

The takeaway? Before investing, know how the loan is structured, what protects your capital, and what happens when a deal doesn’t go according to plan.

“I’m sick of the scaring, the terror, the fright. I’m tired of being something that goes bump in the night. I’m bored with leering my horrible glances, And my feet hurt from dancing those skeleton dances. I don’t like graveyards, and I need something new. There must be more to life than just yelling, ‘Boo!'”

—Tim Burton, The Nightmare Before Christmas

Dr. Wednesday Addams sat alone in her office at 11 PM, glaring at her retirement calculator the way you’d glare at a pathology report you already suspect is bad.

Twenty years of serious income, the kind that makes the neighbors assume you’re rich, and the screen looked like a crime scene.

Projected retirement age: 79. Probability of success: 23%. Her portfolio had roughly the life expectancy of a jack-o’-lantern left on the porch until Thanksgiving.

She was 58. She wanted out at 61, and blocking the exit stood a tangle of whole life policies her cousin had sold her, a 401(k) ignored for a decade, a pre-tax balance quietly wiring itself into a tax bomb, and a household burning $35,000 a month like a furnace nobody remembered to turn down.

Her story isn’t rare. It isn’t even interesting.

Physicians stumble into the same open graves with the reliability of a zombie shuffling toward the nearest brain, and the tax code waiting at the bottom helps itself to 37 cents of every married dollar above $768,700. Some of these graves are fresh. A few were dug by Congress.

The AMA’s latest national data has 41.9% of physicians reporting at least one symptom of burnout in 2025, down from 48.2% in 2023. Progress, technically. Emergency medicine and hematology-oncology still sit near 50%, coin-flip odds that the physician running tonight’s code is cooked.

Burnout steals your joy first and your retirement date second. You plan to work until 68, the call schedule wins at 61, and the seven years of full income your plan quietly assumed shrink to a few years of part-time pay, or nothing at all.

The itch is arriving earlier, too. In Doximity’s polling, the share of physicians aged 45 to 49 considering early retirement nearly doubled between 2023 and 2026, from 23% to 44%.

Dr. Smart and Dr. Addams both started at 35 earning $300,000. Smart saved 25%, or $75,000 a year. Addams saved 10%.

Run that $45,000 annual gap through 25 years at a 5% real return and it grows to about $2.15 million by age 60, a fortune separating two doctors with the same income at the same hospital, parked in the same doctors’ lot, one of them driving home to a plan and the other to a calculator that reads like a death certificate.

Discover legitimate, IRS-recognized tax strategies physicians can use to potentially reduce their tax bills, which options high earners qualify for, and which aggressive approaches could attract IRS scrutiny.

Ideal for: Physicians and high-income professionals looking to understand their tax-saving options before speaking with their CPA.

Sat, Nov 14  ·  1:00 pm ET  ·  10:00 am PT

Addams spent every productivity bonus. You’ve already met her at 11 PM.

You go from a resident making $65,000 to an attending earning $350,000, and the word “deserve” moves into your vocabulary. A bigger house. Then tens of thousands sunk into renovating it, followed by the new car, the au pair, private school, and first class to Maui.

Nobody warns you how hard it is to downshift once you’ve gotten used to the view. Your brain resets “normal” to match your paycheck and refuses to reset it back, so the spending tags along into retirement like a party guest who showed up uninvited and also brought luggage.

I watched an Arizona cardiologist discover at 66 that he needed $400,000 a year to keep living the way he lived. His portfolio could safely throw off maybe $180,000. He’s 71 now. Still full-time.

Simple, boring solution: live like a resident for two to five years after training, bank the gap, kill the student loans, and upgrade slowly enough that your brain never registers the drift.

Nearly every physician gets pitched whole life insurance, usually by a friend or relative whose licensing exam ink is still wet. The illustration promises cash value, tax-free growth, and a death benefit, all in one tidy package.

For most physicians who need life insurance, it’s mostly garbage. Premiums run many times higher than term. Commissions feed on the early years, and the cash value grows like it’s been bled.

Run an illustrative comparison: one physician pays $3,000 a month into whole life, while her colleague buys 20-year term for around $150 a month and invests the other $2,850, and at a 7% return that side account sits near $1.5 million after 20 years, with the policy’s cash value usually trailing by hundreds of thousands, still waiting for the illustration to come true.

Sold by family, illustrated in optimistic colors, and funded for 15 years by a doctor too busy to read past page two, Dr. Addams’s three policies carried combined premiums of $8,400 a month and a total cash value of $780,000.

Term plus investing would likely have left her near $1.9 million. She surrendered all three at 58. Ate the surrender charges. Started catching up.

In plenty of physician households, one person earns the money and the same person manages it.

Then the doctor dies, divorces, or has a stroke at 63, and the spouse inherits decades of decisions made behind a closed door, written in a language nobody bothered to teach them.

I’ve sat with widows who found out their physician husband had:

A spouse at the table pulls decisions toward the conservative side, a handy counterweight when the 2 AM version of you thinks genius has struck.

Build the plan simple enough that they could run it alone. Keep the account list and passwords somewhere they can actually find, which rules out your head.

Business school professors have a phrase for the bad investments that circulate in medical circles: deals that can only be sold to doctors.

Time poverty and overconfidence do the damage. Researching an investment takes hours you don’t have, so you trust people, and you assume that mastering the coagulation cascade somehow qualifies you to underwrite private equity. It doesn’t.

Physicians I know have poured money into restaurant groups that folded within 18 months, real estate “opportunities” that smelled faintly of Ponzi, and crypto tokens launched by a nephew’s roommate’s brother.

Index funds are boring. They work. Put $50,000 a year into low-cost index funds for 30 years at a 5% real return and you end up with about $3.32 million.

Lose 2% a year to fees and the same contributions grow to about $2.38 million, close to a million dollars handed to people in nicer suits than yours. If your portfolio needs a 40-page binder to explain, you’re the mark.

Most physicians blow past the taxable wage base ($184,500 in 2026) months before December, which puts you among the few groups who routinely qualify for the maximum benefit. Claiming age is a bigger lever for you than for almost anyone.

According to AARP, a worker at the 2026 maximum who files at 62 collects about $2,969 a month. Wait until full retirement age and that rises to $4,152. Hold out to 70 and it’s roughly $5,181.

Dr. Lucky filed at 62 because he “wanted the money while the government still had it.” Six months later he picked up locums at $200 an hour, and because Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480 before full retirement age, his own paycheck ate his benefit, which the SSA hands back after full retirement age in small monthly crumbs.

If you’re married, the higher earner’s claiming age also sets the survivor benefit, so delaying to 70 works like inflation-adjusted life insurance for your spouse at a premium no insurer will match. A serious diagnosis can justify claiming early.

For a healthy 62-year-old with a seven-figure portfolio, it’s usually the wrong call. You’ve delivered enough prognoses to know which patient you are.

Most physicians stuff nearly everything into pre-tax accounts during peak years, which makes sense at 37%. Trouble arrives when that’s the only move for 25 years, because a $4 million pre-tax portfolio is a smaller number dressed up for the party.

If you need $180,000 a year to live and pull it entirely from pre-tax accounts, you might withdraw $240,000 to get there. Your 4.5% withdrawal plan just became a 6% plan.

Required minimum distributions start at 73 (75 if you were born in 1960 or later) and stack on top of Social Security. Then Medicare notices.

IRMAA surcharges for 2026 begin at modified AGI of $218,000 for married couples, and at the top tier Part B jumps from $202.90 a month to $689.90, plus a $91 Part D surcharge, roughly $6,900 a year per person, a fine levied for the crime of saving diligently in the wrong bucket.

Medicare looks back two years, so the income you report at 63 sets your premiums at 65.

But if you retire at 58, delay Social Security, and you may get a decade of taxable income lower than anything since residency, a window for converting chunks of pre-tax money to Roth on purpose, in measured doses, the way you’d titrate a drip rather than push a bolus.

While you’re still working, fund a backdoor Roth IRA ($7,500 limit in 2026) and send part of your savings to the Roth side of your employer plan. If you’re 50 or older and earned more than $150,000 in FICA wages last year, the IRS already decided for you: your 2026 catch-up contributions go in as Roth.

Asset location matters too, and municipal bonds can help outside retirement accounts.

At 37% plus the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax, close to 41 cents of every taxable bond interest dollar goes to Washington. Keep bonds inside the 401(k) or 403(b). Hold broad stock index funds in taxable.

Two physicians can retire with identical portfolios and identical withdrawal rates and still get completely different endings. Timing decides which. Finance calls it sequence of returns risk, and you’ll call it something less printable.

Retire in February 2020 and you watched the Dow fall from about 29,550 to under 19,000 in roughly six weeks. Retire into 2022 and the S&P 500 dropped about 19% as inflation spiked.

Even 2025 had teeth: the S&P 500 fell almost 19% between its February high and early April as tariff headlines rattled markets.

Dr. Smart retires into three good years and coasts. Dr. Lucky (whose name keeps aging badly) retires into a bear market, sells near the bottom to fund two years of travel, and never gets those shares back.

William Bengen’s 4% rule, published in 1994, tries to account for that, and Bengen has since nudged his own number up to about 4.7%. The real mistake is treating any figure as carved on a tombstone.

Retirees who trim spending after bad years, or who keep two to five years of withdrawals in cash and short-term bonds, give their stocks room to recover instead of selling them on the way down.

Dr. Addams checked her allocation at 59 and found 95% stocks, 5% cash, and no plan for a crash. She moved to 60/30/10 stocks, bonds, and cash and started building a three-year buffer. Her mix won’t fit everyone, but “I’ll figure it out when it happens” fits nobody.

Don’t overcorrect into a bond basement either. Retire at 57 and your money may need to last 35 years, so stocks still have work to do.

CPI peaked at 9.1% in June 2022. Inflation cooled. Prices didn’t.

A $200,000 retirement budget becomes about $361,000 in 20 years at 3% inflation, and any income stream that doesn’t adjust, whether a fixed annuity, a pension without a cost-of-living rider, or a practice buyout paid in level installments, shrinks every year you hold it, rotting quietly from the inside the way pumpkins do.

You already know this feeling from the reimbursement side. The AMA estimates Medicare physician pay has fallen by roughly a third since 2001 after adjusting for practice-cost inflation.

Discover legitimate, IRS-recognized tax strategies physicians can use to potentially reduce their tax bills, which options high earners qualify for, and which aggressive approaches could attract IRS scrutiny.

Ideal for: Physicians and high-income professionals looking to understand their tax-saving options before speaking with their CPA.

Sat, Nov 14  ·  1:00 pm ET  ·  10:00 am PT

Give your retirement plan the same respect for erosion you’ve watched eat your fee schedule.

Your brother needs $50,000 for a business. Your sister needs $30,000 to stop a foreclosure.

A few years later your kid asks for $80,000 toward a house, because you’re the rich doctor, and the rich doctor is who people call, and nobody in the history of families has ever called the rich doctor to pay him back.

Treat money to family as a gift with no strings, sized to what you can afford to never see again. Dr. Addams lent her brother $120,000 for a restaurant. It failed. He filed for bankruptcy, and they haven’t spoken in six years.

Long-term rental losses usually land in the passive bucket, where they can’t touch clinical income. Short-term rentals play by different rules.

If the average guest stay runs seven days or less and you materially participate, most commonly by logging more than 100 hours a year and more than any other individual, the losses turn non-passive and can offset W-2 or 1099 income (a separate route from Real Estate Professional Status), the closest thing the tax code offers to a garlic necklace for your paycheck.

Pair that with a cost segregation study and 100% bonus depreciation, which the One Big Beautiful Bill Act permanently restored for property acquired after January 19, 2025.

A $500,000 short-term rental might produce $150,000 to $200,000 of year-one depreciation, worth roughly $55,000 to $74,000 in federal tax at 37%.

Locums, telehealth, medical director stipends, expert witness work: if any of it lands on a 1099, a Solo 401(k) usually beats the SEP-IRA most contractors open by default. For 2026 you can defer up to $24,500 as the “employee” (shared with any W-2 plan you also use), plus an employer contribution of roughly 20% of net self-employment earnings, up to $72,000 combined, with $8,000 in catch-up at 50 or $11,250 between 60 and 63. The SEP also poisons your backdoor Roth through the pro-rata rule.

Older 1099 physicians with steady income should price out a cash balance plan on top, where contributions often reach six figures for doctors in their 50s. Those deductions pull double duty because of the QBI cliff.

For 2026, married couples get the full 20% qualified business income deduction at or below $403,500 of taxable income, and it disappears at $553,500. A married 1099 doc with $500,000 of taxable income who funds both plans can slide below $403,500 and watch the deduction rise from the dead.

Medicine breeds a specific condition. You hit your number, decide you need a bigger one, and a market dip talks you into another year, then another, until you’re 68 with $9 million and a partner gently asking whether you’ve considered slowing down.

Every year worked past enough gets paid for with a year you’ll never get back at that age, a year of knees that still handle a trail and a back that still lifts a grandkid, traded for a margin of safety your spreadsheet stopped needing long ago, which makes one more year the only prescription in medicine with no ceiling dose.

Physicians who bolt without a plan for Monday get haunted by the opposite problem. You were Dr. Johnson, the cardiologist. Now you’re Bob, with 50 empty hours a week and no idea what to put in them.

Some Bobs end up unretiring just to have somewhere to be.

Easing out tends to go better than slamming the door. Dropping to 0.6 FTE, picking up locums, or teaching keeps income flowing and lets the portfolio grow untouched a few more years.

Watch for a malpractice tail bill on a claims-made policy, and remember that governmental 457(b) plans carry no 10% penalty once you separate from service, at any age.

In my experience, physicians who retire toward something stick the landing far more often than those simply running from the pager.

Dr. Addams caught her mistakes at 58 instead of 68, and that gave her room to work. She hired a fee-only fiduciary advisor, wrote a plan, surrendered the bad policies, sold the vacation home, and maxed every account she had.

She retired at 64 on about $18,000 a month instead of $35,000. Plenty, it turned out.

Several year-end moves for 2026 can’t wait for the week between Christmas and New Year’s:

For the rest of the year, check every beneficiary form, add up 12 months of actual spending, swap whole life for adequate term and disability coverage where it makes sense, and bring your spouse into the conversation. Then raise your savings rate 1 to 2 points every year until you hit 25% to 30% of gross.

You’ll make mistakes. Everyone does. What matters is catching them at 58, the way Dr. Addams did, while the options are still standing in the room, instead of at 70, when most of them have left the building and switched off the porch light behind them.

Pick one item from this list before the first trick-or-treater rings your doorbell. Make your CPA earn their fee in November instead of on a panicked phone call in March.

This article is for educational purposes and isn’t individualized tax, legal, or investment advice. Run any strategy past a CPA or fee-only advisor who knows your full situation.

Thanks for this informative and entertaining article. should be required reading for all docs. Made me realize that I am fortunate to have avoided the worst of bad decisions. I’m 78 now and comfortably retired with close family. Life is good.

I’ve made some of these mistakes in my 30s by falling into the luxury trap when decent salaries first hit the accounts. Living in Los Angeles it would be VERY easy to burn 35k per month without luxury cars or private schools. In fact we’re not too far off and we drive older EV cars that are paid off and the kids go to great public schools. The costs of living have increased to the point of needing to pay very close attention to all expenses and max out investment and retirement accounts even when it hurts. We’ve started catching rounding 40, traveling a bit less, no new cars, only making required fixes to the house. After reading this I’m more confident that we’ve made the right decisions to get smart and aggressive about this now.

Interesting article focused on finances with a smattering of other issues. Importantly, what are your support systems upon retirement, like spouse, friends, etc.? Sometimes friends are not there because they choose to move closer to their children or they are deceased. What are your interests in medicine and outside medicine? What are your hobbies? Do you want to volunteer? You have been going 90 miles mph and then slow down to 10 mph. Without some kind of plan to fill your time, with and without your spouse/significant other, this is a recipe for depression and disaster. Do you want to stay connected to medicine in some way? Maybe you can observe trainees doing an H&P and counseling. Maybe you can offer advice as to how to set up an office practice for senior residents. In another ote, how is your health and do you take care of yourself? Going into retirement with significant health issues can influence how your retirement goes and when you retire, perhaps restricting travel and other activities. We have written an article on retirement that might compliment the informative blog here. Whereas it is focused on academic physicians, there are many points applicable to those in practice (Greenberg L, Fischel JE, Siegel B. Academic clinician educators: Confronting the challenges to successful retirement. Educ Health (Abingdon). 2023 Jan-Apr;36(1):24-32. doi: 10.4103/efh.efh_192_22. PMID: 38047344.). Planning ahead is the key, applying principles mentioned in this blog and our paper. We all have worked so hard…..we deserve a great retirement.

great article…great advice. As the offspring of depression era parents, I was taught (by example) early to be thrifty and save. When burnout came at age 62, I was ready and haven’t looked back. My only regret is being too conservative with my investments, but then again being more aggressive would have forced me to hang on some extra years after the 2008 market crash.

I am so sorry, you lost me at the fact that you actually were burning 35k per month!!! how is that even possible!!! you are exactly where you chose to be, its consequences. Most of us, and I honestly believe I speak for the majority of physicians, do not even get remotely close to such an exaggerated figure. Most of us have limited our spending as our reimbursement has declined. Many of us have actually struggled even keeping a low profile and living with economic restraints. I stopped reading at that figure because it is just absurd.

I appreciate you taking the time to comment, even if you stopped reading at the $35K figure. Let me address your skepticism directly, because you’re right to be shocked—and that’s exactly the point. When I wrote this article, I had a word count limit on how much I could disclose on the background of Doctor Addams (who is really a he). What I did not go into detail about is how he arrived at where he is today. It’s not one absurd decision. It’s twenty years of reasonable-sounding decisions that compound like interest you can’t afford.

Dr. Addams didn’t wake up one day and decide to burn through $420K annually. He made decisions that seemed perfectly justified at each step. I would not have discovered what my friend was going through had I not asked him to invest in my startup back then. He then confided how illiquid he was and how much in a hole he was in.

The reality is that our monthly expenses are not the usual discussion physicians talk about in the physicians’ lounge. It’s really very personal, so I get it that this sounds absurd, but the reality is that there is a lot of shame ascribed to our salaries when we really aren’t visibly successful. So why would we share it? Which may explain why it sounds so absurd to you. Sadly, he is not the first person in such a financial hole since its more common than you think. So what happened?

His surgical group was thriving pre-COVID. She was making $400K+ and felt secure in budgeting for this lifestyle. Then the floor dropped:

Insurance reimbursements got slashed Hospital-based specialty groups ate their market share

His income dropped to $280K, then $240K (he was already burned out from trying to get bigger dividends he had to do more call, which was not sustainable. Yeah, many private groups make these kind of dead-end deals)

What happened next? He did not scale back his lifestyle because he was optimistic about his future. I don’t have the space here to list his expenses but what I remember after a very emotional and stressful session was that his parents were aging and he had to help financially. His sister-in-law had a business that he helped with some capital, which became a recurring theme. All these decisions are made with good intentions, but they add up. He leased a really nice car and could not figure out how to back out of that deal.

The real lesson: This story isn’t about judgment. It’s about prevention. Every physician should see this and think: “Could this happen to me with just 3-4 different decisions?”

Because here’s the truth: The distance between financial security and financial disaster for a high-earning physician is about five bad decisions over twenty years. That’s it.

Your restraint is admirable. But I wrote this article for the physicians who haven’t shown that restraint yet—and who still have time to fix it before they’re staring at a retirement calculator at age 58.

The $35K isn’t absurd. It’s terrifyingly more common (than you think) among physicians who started making big money without a financial plan. If this article makes even one physician audit their spending before it’s too late, it was worth writing—and worth your discomfort reading it.

As someone who spends at 30k per month, let me help with this: $2500 per month goes to an aging parent on one side, $2000 to an aging parent on the other. 3.5k per month goes to a vacation home mortgage and expenses, although it has appreciated enough over time that that will be eventually recovered. Travel is a big one as our 6 children and 6 grandchildren live all over the place, and flights, airport parking etc are $5000 per month. Life insurance is a big one, at 2k per month, health for myself is only $600 per month but it’s $1500 for my wife. I’ll stop there, but we are not driving fancy cars and our primary residence is only worth 330k, hardly a mansion. I retired with over 6 million NW and 60k in pension/ss, which will probably cover it: once the elderly parents have passed it should work out, but we might have to sell the vacation house when we are older.

This should be required reading for every resident – and required re-reading every year of residency and beyond! I appreciate the comments about spouses being involved in all finances – that goes for us, too! Many of us are married to high-earners who manage their own (and sometimes our) finances and find out too late that they were terrible at it.

Thank you! You’re absolutely right—this should be mandatory reading starting in residency, before the income jump happens and the mistakes become expensive.

Your point about spouses needing to be involved cuts both ways, and it’s critical. I’ve sat with too many people who discovered their high-earning spouse was: – Flying blind with no actual plan – Paying 2% in fees to an advisor who was just collecting checks – Invested in their buddy’s restaurant/startup/crypto scheme – Carrying three whole life insurance policies they didn’t understand – Making $400K but somehow living paycheck to paycheck

Financial competence doesn’t correlate with income or intelligence. A physician making $500K can be just as clueless as anyone else—sometimes more so, because the high income masks the problems until it’s too late.

Being involved doesn’t mean you need to manage everything. It means you know where the accounts are, understand the plan, can access everything if needed, and serve as that crucial second set of eyes. Your spouse’s overconfidence plus your informed questions might prevent a catastrophic mistake.

Money is a team sport. Whether you’re the earner or the spouse, staying informed and involved isn’t optional—it’s survival.

You can attach an ins package for your spouse. take a 4% W/D on your money. dont increase your standard of living to just be like everyone else. avoid the race to nowhere and stay away from out of state tuition. your kids will do well anywhere they go if they apply themselves: they got the intellect and drive from their parents not private school or private universities. #8548. Crew Review: High-Yield Checking With Built-In Budgeting for Families

Managing money as a household is harder than it looks. Most people use a regular checking account at a big bank, then juggle a separate budgeting app, maybe a savings account somewhere else, and possibly a kids’ debit card on top of that. It’s a lot to keep track of.

Crew is a fintech app that tries to put all of that in one place. It combines a high-yield checking account, built-in budgeting tools, and family banking features – all inside a single app. The goal is to help you organize your money, automate your budget, and earn more interest without switching between apps.

In this Crew review, we cover what it is, how it works, who it’s best for, the key features, pricing, and what real users are saying. If you’re looking for a smarter checking account that does more, this review gives you the full picture.

Crew is a fintech app that tries to put all of that in one place. It combines a high-yield checking account, built-in budgeting tools, and family banking features

• High-yield checking • Debit cards available for kids• Unlimited budgeting pockets• Cash deposits and mobile check deposit• No monthly fees or minimum balances

• App-only banking with no desktop login• No physical check writing

Crew is a financial technology (fintech) company based in Lehi, Utah. It was founded by Gentry Davies and Steve Domino, who previously worked at Divvy, a business expense platform acquired by Bill.com. The app launched publicly and has been growing steadily since 2023.

Crew is not a bank. Banking services are provided by Bangor Savings Bank, which is FDIC-insured. Your deposits are held at Bangor Savings Bank, so they are protected up to federal insurance limits – $250,000 for individual accounts and $500,000 for joint accounts.

The app is available on both iOS and Android. A web app is currently in beta.

Crew works well for a wide range of people, but it’s especially useful if you fall into one of these groups:

Crew offers a checking account that earns 2.95% APY on your full balance. This rate applies to every dollar you hold in the account – there’s no minimum deposit requirement and no tiered rate structure.

Why it matters: Most big bank checking accounts pay close to 0.01% APY. Earning nearly 3% on your everyday checking balance can add meaningful interest over time, especially for families keeping a few thousand dollars in their account at any given time.

Pockets are virtual “buckets” inside your single Crew checking account. You can create as many as you need – for example, one for bills, one for savings, one for a vacation fund, one for groceries.

Why it matters: You don’t need a separate savings account or multiple bank accounts. Pockets let you visually and mentally divide your money without moving it to another institution. You can also lock a pocket in “piggy bank mode” to avoid dipping into it.

Crew’s Autopilot feature lets you create rules that move money automatically based on triggers. Triggers can be events like a paycheck arriving or a balance dropping below a set level, or they can be time-based, like every Friday or the 1st of the month.

Why it matters: Automation removes the discipline requirement from budgeting. You set your rules once, and Crew handles the rest. For example, you can tell Crew to automatically send 10% of every paycheck to your giving pocket, $500 to bills, and keep the rest in checking — without touching the app every payday.

Crew supports joint accounts for couples and child accounts for kids. Each child gets their own Crew account with a debit card that has their name on it. Kids can log into the app with their own login to check their balance and track spending.

Why it matters: Most banking apps bolt on a kid’s account as an afterthought. Crew builds family banking into the core experience. Parents get real-time spending notifications, spend controls, and the ability to set automated allowances.

Parents can set up automatic recurring transfers to a child’s account. You define the amount and the schedule, and Crew handles the delivery.

Why it matters: Automated allowances teach kids about money while removing the “I forgot to pay your allowance” problem for parents. Kids learn what consistent saving looks like in practice.

Every account member gets a Mastercard debit card. You can switch which pocket your card draws from at any time inside the app – or update a transaction after the fact if you accidentally spent from the wrong pocket.

Why it matters: This setup means budgeting is “baked in” to your spending. Instead of tracking what you spent after the fact, you decide which budget category you’re spending from before or at the time of purchase.

You can use your Crew Mastercard at any ATM in the Mastercard, Maestro, or Cirrus networks. Crew does not have its own fee-free ATM network, but it reimburses ATM fees for up to 20 withdrawals per year.

Why it matters: The annual ATM fee reimbursement covers most casual cash users without adding much complexity.

Crew supports outgoing wire transfers. The fee depends on your total account balance.

Incoming wires and standard ACH transfers are processed as usual through the app.

Deposits held through Crew are insured through Bangor Savings Bank, a Member FDIC institution.

This is standard FDIC pass-through insurance. Crew’s website states that pass-through insurance is subject to certain conditions set forth in the deposit agreement.

Crew includes an AI-powered financial assistant called Penny. Penny can answer questions about your account, help you set up automations, and give you guidance on your financial situation.

Why it matters: Penny gives users a simple way to interact with their finances through natural language, without digging through menus.

One of Crew’s stronger selling points is its simple, low-fee structure. Here’s a clear breakdown:

Note: APY is variable and may change at any time. The 2.95% rate is the most recent published rate. Always check trycrew.com for the current rate before opening an account.

Opening a Crew account is quick. Most people complete it in under two minutes. Here are the steps:

To add a family member, go to the Family section of the app and follow the prompts to add a joint owner or create a child account.

No. Crew is a financial technology company, not a bank. Banking services are provided by Bangor Savings Bank, Member FDIC, which is a real, federally insured bank. Your deposits are held at Bangor Savings Bank, so they are FDIC insured up to federal limits.

The APY is variable, meaning it can change over time. It is not a limited-time promotional rate in the traditional sense; it applies to your full balance, with no minimum or expiration. However, Crew can adjust the rate when market conditions change. The rate has fluctuated over the app’s history (it was as high as 3.7% in early 2025). Referral sign-ups may qualify for a 0.5% APY boost for the first three months.

Cash deposit support has been in development. Some reviews noted it was not yet available at the time of writing, though the feature has been in the works. It’s worth checking the current app version or Crew’s website for the latest on cash deposits before signing up if this is important to you.

You need your legal name, date of birth, physical address, and a tax ID (typically your Social Security number). Most applicants complete the process in under two minutes.

Crew earns revenue in two ways: from the interest it earns on deposits held at Bangor Savings Bank, and from merchant fees when you use your Crew debit card to make purchases. This model is common among fintech companies and allows them to offer no-fee accounts while still generating revenue.

User feedback for Crew is largely positive, particularly among families and people who value built-in budgeting features.

Rating: 4.8 out of 5 stars (based on 179 reviews as of March 2026)

Positive trends from Google Play users include:

Crew’s iOS app carries consistently high ratings. Users describe it as well-designed and easy to navigate. Family features are frequently praised, with parents noting that kids enjoy having their own card and app login.

Reviewers across platforms repeatedly mention Crew as a genuine alternative to maintaining separate banking and budgeting apps. The combination of high-yield checking, automatic paycheck splitting, and child accounts in one place is the most-cited reason for switching from other banks or apps.

The most consistent piece of constructive feedback is that Crew is still a young product and some features – like the web app – are still catching up to the mobile experience.

Crew is a well-designed fintech product that combines several things that usually require multiple apps or accounts: a high-yield checking account, budgeting through pockets, spending automation, and family banking.

Overall, Crew fills a genuine gap. Most checking accounts don’t pay meaningful interest and don’t have built-in budgeting. Crew does both, and it adds family banking on top. For households looking to simplify their financial toolkit and earn more interest on everyday balances, it’s worth a serious look.

As always, make sure to read the deposit agreement and check the current APY at trycrew.com before opening an account, since rates are variable and can change.

This review is for informational purposes only and does not constitute financial advice. APY rates, fees, and features are subject to change. Always verify current terms directly with Crew at trycrew.com before making any financial decisions.

#8547. The Ultimate Life Coach

Almost  nineteen years into early retirement now, I’ve come to realize that the complete freedom of this lifestyle can be a double-edged sword.

You’ve already heard me raving plenty about the upside: having the freedom to raise a son from the day he was born to beyond his eighteenth birthday with no compromises. And then to put thousands of hours into everything else I value as well: family, health, friends, adventures, building stuff, and even writing the occasional blog post. No complaints about any of this.

But if I can indulge you to play me a brief Tiny Violin of First World Problems solo, even this perfect life comes with one flaw: I never have to do anything I don’t want to do.

To most people, this sounds like a dream come true. Especially if you combine total freedom with plenty of money, life is just a non-stop blissful playground of self actualization, right?

Well, maybe, but maybe not. In reality, the answer depends on who you are.

Freedom and money reveal a person’s true strengths and weaknesses, and the result is a spectrum with “Unlimited drugs and booze on the couch” at one end, and “Create and manage a series of nonprofit foundations which employ thousands of people to research and invest in medical advances and clean energy” at the other.

For most of my journey so far, I seem to have found the balance pretty naturally. My Dad job was very intense for the first decade, but somehow I also had time to build and restore quite a few houses in the neighborhood, take plenty of intense trips to interesting places, give some talks and make some videos, and still write a few hundred blog posts.

But in these last few years, I have started slowing down, and it has become more and more difficult to wrangle and focus myself to get these things to happen as often.

Instead of constantly bouncing around the construction site building cool things, or falling into laser focus on the keyboard finishing an article that I just had to share with you, I found myself retiring to the couch earlier and earlier each afternoon, seeking distraction on the phone and wishing I had the energy and focus to do those other more enjoyable things.

So I fought back, by learning more about health and wellness. Trying to study and train my way into more energy and focus and motivation. And you’ve seen some of the results here, in articles I’ve shared about daily habits, steering clear of excessive comfort, and more.

And all of these things really work, IF you take the knowledge and actually put it into action. And therein lies the problem:

I kept learning effective new things, and successfully incorporating them into my life. They would work for a while, but gradually my brain would invent various excuses to stop doing them consistently, leaving me with plenty of knowledge but far too little accomplishment to show for it.

Until finally, just a few months ago, I realized that I had been sabotaging my own progress by turning my biggest life advantage into a disadvantage:

I have been using my freedom too much – in order to avoid doing things that I didn’t feel like doing.

See, freedom is great if it frees you from leaving your children at 5am so you can drive an hour through a traffic jam to sit in an office building for nine hours. But that same freedom goes to waste if you then just plunk the kids down in front of a playlist of cheap cartoons while you lounge in the corner to scroll Facebook all day.

You need to use it to do things that are even more valuable than the job you just quit. And if you can’t do that, you might as well just keep the damned job.

This is what I was doing, while lying about it to myself. I would focus on the easy things which are still good for me, like taking care of the house or hanging out with friends who live nearby. But I avoid doing the harder things – which for me means the things that require more planning, energy or focus. Even though these are the things that allow me to lead the life I enjoy most.

Let’s use workouts as an easy example. I already know that on a minute-for-minute basis, this is the single most effective thing almost anybody can do with their time because it drastically improves every other area of life. But despite knowing this, I was still following this pattern:

“I want to get in a really good weight training workout today.But I don’t feel like doing a workout because it’s hard.So I’ll try to grease the wheels for myself so it’s easier to achieve. I’ll pick the perfect time of day when the weather is nice, and my energy level is high. I’ll set up my gym in advance the night before.And when that golden moment of perfect conditions hits,I’ll hit the gym!“

But between you and me, that moment didn’t always come. Some weeks I’d achieve it 2-3 times, some weeks I’d get “busy” and make excuses like “well at least I walked a lot today”. Some days I would complete a great workout, but when recording it in the journal I’d see that the previous one was over a week ago.

And the results of this lackluster effort were exactly what you’d expect: lackluster fitness.

Then something changed and I learned that there’s a much better way to get those workouts done. It’s by replacing the long, meandering, frankly wussypants dialog above with this one:

I want to work out today.I don’t feel like it.^^^ AHA!! I JUST CAUGHT MYSELF TRYING TO SELF SABOTAGE! ^^^I am now already putting on my shoes and walking to the gym.

I’m using workouts as an example because this is the behavior I managed to change most successfully, but the exact same technique applies to everything else that you or I want to do, but fail to do regularly.

The key is learning to watch over yourself like an Eagle and identify that exact moment of hesitation.

And then instead of using it as a trigger for excuses, you use it as a trigger for action.

It’s so counterintuitive at first, but then obvious in retrospect. Hesitance feels shitty in the moment, and it really can ruin your life if you listen to it too often. But the ultimate solution is usually to run directly towards, rather than away from, the stuff you don’t want to do.

So really, Hesitation can be the ultimate life coach.

As part of writing this article, I shared the idea around with friends to test it out first. And I was initially surprised to get mixed results. About half of them could relate with me: they felt they were underachieving in life and wanted to do more. The other half though I was crazy: these people feel they are already doing too much, raising multiple kids and managing multiple businesses and training for ironman triathlons in the mountains.

The overachievers go through life nicely buzzed but often stressed. When hearing them describe their schedules, I was absolutely not envious. At the same time, they weren’t impressed with my schedule either because it’s too easy. We could both benefit from making adjustments towards the center.

Impressive overachiever friends are one thing, but the thing that really flipped the switch for me was hearing a podcast interview with our planet’s most extreme example of driving yourself beyond your former limits, David Goggins.

I learned about his life story with a mix of awe and horror. Severely beaten as a child, he grew up with a looming wall of psychological demons and issues, but his reaction was the unique part: he has been driven to compulsively seek out and overcome extreme hardship, not just to unimaginable levels but hundreds of times beyond that.

From pushing through several near-death experiences just to qualify for a Navy SEALS career, to breaking his own legs, heart and lungs from the constant exertion of things like running 240 miles over four days without sleeping, to setting a world record of 4025 bar pull ups over 24 hours (shredding his hands to look like ground beef in the process), the man does things I would never have thought are even close to possible for a human.

And that flipped a switch for me, by putting my own incredibly easy, under-achieving life into perspective.

Because while I absolutely do not want any part of the Goggins life, and I would gladly live my life never having run more than 10 miles at a single stretch, I do find it incredibly helpful to learn that pretty much all of our barriers are entirely mental, not physical or placed upon us by the outside world.

Sure, we do have different starting points and different amounts of luck. But instead of thinking of life like this:

I now realize that things are more like this:

And that’s a really empowering way to think about life, that feels like the sky has opened way up.

So the podcast was just an introduction. I wrote down the particularly concise quote “You already fuckin’ know what to do.” on a piece of cardstock, stuck it to my bathroom mirror, and started acting on it immediately.

Suddenly, I was able to hit the gym every single day because I had two ways to approach it: wanting to put in a workout, and not wanting to put in a workout, either of which became a trigger to work out immediately.

And of course, once I finally put in the effort, it started working. Even though I’ve been sorta into this type of training since I was a teenager, I have mostly floated along on a plateau for years. But with this change in attitude, I gained ten pounds of lean weight over the first four months, returning to the strength and flexibility that I had at age 25, and every single joint in my body feels like it has been upgraded to a study, well oiled spring.

I also used the “catch yourself at the moment of hesitance” trick to get myself to run instead of walk more often (over 20 runs since I got back to Colorado last month), get over to the MMM-HQ coworking space for more work and socializing visits, and even to sit back down at the computer to write this post for you. While I’ve found that too much blogger work (and internet “success”) is a bad thing, there is still a right level that works for me. But it takes a lot of discipline to be willing to do it, because of all the other easier and more thrilling activities I could be doing with this same stretch of time.

For me, fully internalizing this one powerful piece of inspiring profanity has been transformative. But I still find that returning regularly to the well makes all this work even better. So I downloaded both of the Goggins audiobooks and worked through them in little chunks on my morning walks over the period of a month. Then I moved on to Peter Attia’s Outlive, and Jocko Willink’s Extreme Ownership.

While the intellectuals fret about the perils of “Bro Science” or the “Toxic Masculinity” of today’s tribe of health podcasters and question their motivation, I simply absorb the messages that work for me and discard the rest. Find people who make you reach a little higher, and feed on their energy.

And for me, being exposed to successful, strong, athletic people who squeeze a lot of work out of themselves is a big source of inspiration. It helps me do more with my day, which is exactly what works for me right now at this phase of life.

And I wish you more of what works for you too!

Some things that make me feel healthy, happy, and strong that I know I should do more of: weight training, mountain biking, backpacking in the mountains, keeping my house and garage workshop clean and organized, designing and building things, helping other people with home projects, cooking.

One thing I do that helps me stay focused on these things is turn off ALL notifications on my phone, then selectively turn on the few notifications I actually want to know about. I only get notified for text messages, voice mails, calendar reminders, and a few other things. There are often days when I get zero notifications on my phone.

This may not be for everyone, but I also don’t use any social media or read/watch hardly any news. I do watch youtube, but no facebook, instagram, twitter, tik tok, etc. For me all of these things feel like they are vying to “steal” my focus and make it harder to have a calm mind and energy to focus on the things I know I should be doing. I highly recommend people at least try this for a while and see if they feel different. You can always add things back in that you actually do miss. . . . is pure Stoicism, a topic you have touched on before.

That little voice in your head that says “I don’t feel like it” is what the Stoics called “an impression.” You have clearly learned to apply “prosoche” (mindfulness would be a good translation of this Greek word) to interrogate that impression. Then you applied natural wisdom (one of the Stoic virtues) to reach the logical conclusion that surrendering to that impression would not be in your best interest.

There is another Stoic echo in your rediscovered commitment to exercise. The Stoics strongly believed that it was crucial to constantly test oneself, whether that meant fasting, walking barefoot in the now, or undertaking difficult or unpleasant tasks.

So well done! You are proving an apt “prokopton” (one who is making progress to becoming a Stoic sage).

Glad to hear you’re picking up Extreme Ownership! As someone who is still in his working years, it’s made the way I think about getting work done much better. In software engineering, sometimes shit just goes wrong. Knowing that almost everything can be avoided by us engineers doing a better and robust job has improved the way I work and has made me _less_ stressed, because the work I do is better and more well thought out from the start. Even when something does go wrong, it’s just a learning experience that allows me to avoid those pitfalls in the future.

This book is even better for your social relationships though! Most of the time, you can be the ignition to a better relationship with someone. I’ve seen it many times where relationships you want drift away because neither side initiates social interaction enough with the other. “If they really care, they’d reach out.” Turns out, if you take ownership and reach out, you’ll see them a lot more and be happier as a result. The same thing applies for someone toxic in your life. Tired of this person bringing you down? Take ownership and remove yourself from the equation. (Obviously there are circumstances where this doesn’t apply, but you’ll know it when you see it).

Plus the narration of the audiobook is just great. Jocko has that Seal Team motivational way of speaking that makes you get your shit together!
