On both days I go to a weight training class for older adults. I like the work out, the instructors and my classmates. Oh yeah, and they play Beatles music.

I also get yearly DXA scans. Last year my scans were horrible and that motivated me to start regular strength training. This year I have improved and that motivates me to keep working out.

Not everything is mental unfortunately. I have all kinds of motivation and willingness to push myself, but no matter what I do, my body is just not in the condition that it was 10 – 15 years ago, and the aches and pains that result from pushing myself prevent me from doing anything more than walking at this point in my life. So, this advice is great if you don’t have any medical conditions preventing you from pushing yourself, however, I believe that there are many people out there like myself who are not built like Goggins.

I realise you have said you don’t swallow the whole Goggins creed, Mr. Moustache, but Goggins? In any measure? Really?

I am surprised you haven’t learnt by now that always pushing your limits, redlining your body, is not a formula for health, fitness and well-being; it is the road to injury and burnout.

There are countless examples of exercise fanatics who started off thinking, with Nietzsche, that ‘That which doesn’t kill me makes me stronger’. They end up realising that ‘That which doesn’t kill me can still cripple me’.

Just look at poor old Ronnie Coleman. https://youtu.be/kq0Sm4kAp4Y?si=_ma2zjT_WoWVi4wC

But after many injuries, all self-inflicted and therefore avoidable, I have developed a different philosophy: Progress over perfection; You won’t improve from something you can’t recover from; Little by little, step by step, work on your weaknesses and limitations; No brain, no gain.

Could your procrastination stem from thinking that exercise is a gruelling, penitential task? Why not just resolve to show up everyday and just do something — some mobility work, an easy jog, a few sets of easy pull-ups and hanging leg raises? Some days that will put you in the mood to push harder, go further— fine. Other days you can stop there — also fine. Just keep showing up and making deposits into the Bank (or ETF, or whatever) of Fitness. They will add up, and sometimes compound, just like money. Health and fitness is a long game, just like saving and investment.

There is definitely a time and place to test your mettle — generally in a competition or emergency. But suffering is not how you get fitter. ‘The ability to suffer during a workout is just one skill. Don’t over-focus on it. You also need to train a hundred other skills’.https://youtu.be/0h23IANIg6Q For most workouts, the goal should be to finish feeling better than when you started. Energised, not exhausted. If tired, sore, and injured are the side-effects, is it worth it?

Of course, who am I to say what will motivate you? But I know that when I changed my outlook from struggle-&-suffer to small, manageable steps, every day my hesitation vanished and I became keen to show up.

#8546. Debbie App: Can This App Really Help You Pay Off Debt Faster?

Debbie is a debt payoff app built around a truth most people already understand but rarely see addressed in finance tools: paying off debt is not just about numbers, it is about behavior. And if behavior is the real challenge, motivation matters more than spreadsheets.

Most personal finance apps track balances and interest rates and then stop there. Debbie goes a step further by rewarding people for making progress. When you do the right things consistently, you do not just see your debt go down. You actually get something back.

Many debt payoff journeys fail in the same place. Not at the beginning, when motivation is high, but in the middle, when progress feels slow, and life gets in the way. Debbie is designed specifically for that phase.

After connecting your credit cards, student loans, or other debts, the app creates a personalized payoff plan based on your balances and payment history. The plan is realistic and focused on consistency rather than extreme sacrifices.

As you make payments and reduce balances, Debbie rewards you for that progress.

• Cash rewards• Gift cards• Partner offers tied to financial milestones

These rewards are not meant to eliminate debt on their own. They exist to reinforce the habit of showing up and sticking with the plan.

Debbie gives users a clean dashboard showing:

This reduces the mental stress of juggling multiple accounts.

Unlike most personal finance apps, Debbie pays users for progress, which helps reinforce positive habits. Over $2,319,961.65 earned by people reaching their money goals.

This makes it beginner-friendly, even for people new to budgeting or debt payoff.

Debbie works best for people who need accountability and encouragement. If you already know what to do but struggle to stay consistent, this app fills an important gap.

• Rewards that reinforce good financial behavior• A clean, easy to understand interface• A focus on progress instead of perfection• Motivation during the hardest part of the journey

There are also a few limitations to keep in mind. Debbie is not a replacement for a full budgeting system, and the rewards alone will not move the needle if you are carrying very large balances. You still have to do the work. The app simply makes it easier to keep going.

You will also need to link your financial accounts, which is standard for most modern finance apps but worth noting.

Debbie is a strong fit for people who feel overwhelmed by debt, burned out on traditional budgeting apps, or frustrated that they are doing the right things but still don’t feel any momentum.

If you are already highly disciplined and managing everything with detailed spreadsheets, you may not need the additional reinforcement. For most people, though, motivation is the missing piece.

Yes. Debbie is a legitimate personal finance app built around a behavior-driven debt payoff model. While it won’t magically erase debt, it helps users stay engaged, which is often the biggest missing piece in successfully paying off debt.

If you’re exploring Debbie, there are several other financial wellness and money-saving apps worth considering. Each app offers a different approach to helping users improve their finances, build better habits, or earn rewards.

Acorns automatically invests your spare change by rounding up purchases to the nearest dollar. It’s designed for beginners who want a simple, hands-off way to start investing.

Rocket Money focuses on budgeting, subscription tracking, and lowering monthly bills. It can help users identify recurring charges and negotiate certain expenses on their behalf.

Qapital combines budgeting with automated savings goals. Users can create custom “rules” that move money into savings automatically based on spending habits or milestones.

YNAB is a budgeting app built around giving every dollar a purpose. It’s popular among people who want a more hands-on system for managing cash flow and paying off debt.

Paying off debt is rarely about knowledge. Most people already know what they should be doing. The real challenge is sticking with the plan month after month, even when progress feels slow.

Debbie helps solve that problem by rewarding progress, reinforcing positive habits, and making the journey feel less discouraging. It will not magically erase debt. But it can absolutely help you stay consistent long enough to change your financial life.

Practical advice to help you make money, save money and pay off debt, from a family that paid off $52,000 in 18 months.

My first patient was already dead. She arrived zipped in a vinyl bag, smelling of formaldehyde and phenol, and she taught me more anatomy in one semester than any lecturer managed in four years.

Somewhere between the first incision and the nervous jokes about her coral nail polish, I figured out that the human body runs stranger than the textbook admits. The mind bolted to it runs stranger still.

The years since have only confirmed the suspicion. Some of what I’ve seen belongs in a haunted house. The rest belongs in a haunted house with a billing department.

For Halloween this year, I’m recalling some of the odd things about being human you learn as a physician over the years.

Retirement is optional for the dead. Donated bodies pick up second careers the day their first one ends. At Wayne State University in Detroit, cadavers have ridden impact sleds for decades so engineers could learn what a steering column does to a sternum when a sedan meets a bridge abutment.

Seatbelts, airbags, and padded dashboards all carry the fingerprints of people who signed a donor form and then absorbed the kind of blow no living volunteer would accept. Count the people who walk away from highway crashes today, and a fair share owe a thank-you note to somebody in a body bag.

My cadaver spent her retirement teaching a roomful of first-years how a hand works. Meanwhile I spend Tuesday afternoons on hold with a prior authorization line. She was more productive, and she never billed.

Nothing in residency prepared me for the cadaver head course. Severed heads rested face up in disposable roasting pans, lined down a row of tables, while surgeons calmly rehearsed facelifts. I kept my coffee down, though it was close.

Consider the advantages. These patients won’t ask about downtime or bring up a cousin’s botched eyelid job, and the state board will hear nothing from them. Somebody should study their satisfaction scores.

Medicine has always practiced on the dead, and for a long stretch it practiced on dead people who never agreed to the arrangement.

Nineteenth-century anatomy schools bought corpses from grave robbers and asked few questions about provenance. In Edinburgh in 1828, William Burke and William Hare decided digging was too slow, murdered sixteen people, and sold the bodies to anatomist Robert Knox.

Britain answered with the Anatomy Act of 1832, which handed medical schools the unclaimed bodies of the poor. Reform, of a sort.

Physicians have spent centuries trying to pin down the second a person stops being a person. We have never once nailed it.

In 1905, a French doctor named Beaurieux stood beside the guillotine as a convict named Languille lost his head. Beaurieux called out the man’s name. By his own report, the eyelids lifted and the eyes fixed on him before closing, and the trick worked a second time before it quit for good.

Consciousness or reflex? Nobody could say then, and we can’t now.

Cleveland, 1970. Neurosurgeon Robert White transplanted the head of one rhesus monkey onto the body of another, and the head woke up and tracked people around the room. White spent the rest of his career insisting the operation could work in humans.

I met my own version of this riddle at the bedside of a brain-dead organ donor. He was warm and pink. His heart pumped, his kidneys made urine, and at one point a spinal reflex lifted his arm off the sheet, the move clinicians call the Lazarus sign.

The nurse beside me didn’t flinch. I did. Legally he had died hours earlier, and the procurement team was already en route.

Hospice taught me the rest. Dying unfolds over hours or days, a slow dimming no monitor captures cleanly, yet the death certificate demands a single timestamp. So we pick one and move on.

For several centuries, European apothecaries sold ground-up mummy as medicine. Physicians prescribed it for bruises, bleeding and a long menu of complaints, and when genuine Egyptian stock ran short, enterprising suppliers manufactured fresh “mummy” from whatever bodies they could find.

Folklore adds “mellified man,” a corpse supposedly steeped in honey for a century and sold by the chunk. Historians doubt he ever existed. I’ve seen supplement labels make bolder claims.

The dead, for all their weirdness, behave predictably. They stay where you put them. The living refuse that courtesy.

Beginning in the early 2000s, hundreds of children in Sweden withdrew into a state that looked like coma. Nearly all came from asylum-seeking families facing deportation.

They quit eating and talking, then quit opening their eyes, and some stayed that way for a year or longer while parents turned them in bed and nurses ran their feeding tubes. Swedish doctors named it uppgivenhetssyndrom. Resignation syndrome.

Scans came back clean, and so did the labs. Nobody found a virus, a toxin or a lesion. The condition clustered almost entirely inside Swedish borders, and many of the children surfaced slowly once their families won permission to stay.

That makes a lot of physicians squirm. The suffering is real, the paralysis is real, and the driver is a mind expressing despair in the shape its surroundings taught it to take.

I’ve watched a milder version play out in hospice more times than I can count. A patient holds steady for weeks, the family meeting goes sideways, and by the next morning he has stopped eating.

In the Kazakh village of Kalachi, starting around 2013, residents began dozing off mid-sentence. Some slept for days and woke with no memory of it. A shuttered Soviet uranium mine sat down the road, which made for a tidy villain.

Officials tested the air, water and soil, and the government eventually relocated much of the town. Plenty of clinicians point instead to a community watching its jobs and young people drain away, taking any sense of a future with them.

Le Roy, New York, ran a similar script in 2011. A cluster of high school girls developed tics, jerks and verbal outbursts that spread through the school and lit up the evening news.

Erin Brockovich showed up to investigate a chemical spill from a 1970 train derailment. Neurologists diagnosed conversion disorder, a label the families received with roughly the enthusiasm you’d expect.

I’ve delivered that diagnosis myself. The MRI was perfect, the legs still wouldn’t move, and the patient heard “it’s all in your head” no matter how carefully I phrased it. She left to find a doctor who would order another scan.

A toxin is a gift, because it blames no one. A functional diagnosis blames no one either, yet patients hear an accusation in it, and plenty of us deliver it like one. We fumble that conversation more often than we fumble a central line.

Among the Miskito people on Nicaragua’s Caribbean coast, young women fall prey to grisi siknis. They collapse, then bolt into the night, and later describe a dark stranger who came to carry them off.

Village healers treat it with rituals and herbs, and it hops from one community to the next like a bad cold.

Wealthy countries have their own spirits. In El Carmen de Bolívar, Colombia, in 2014, schoolgirls began fainting and convulsing after HPV vaccination. Videos of their episodes ricocheted across social media, and the country’s HPV vaccination rate collapsed.

Two years later, American diplomats in Havana reported headaches, dizziness and strange sounds, and the press settled on a mysterious energy weapon. Some neurologists argue for a more mundane explanation that nobody in Washington wanted to hear.

Our culture supplies the toxins, the radio waves and the MRI that might at last catch the culprit. The Miskito get a dark stranger, while our demons come with CPT codes.

Funerals are where the haunted house collides with your financial plan. The National Funeral Directors Association put the 2023 median cost of a funeral with viewing and burial at about $8,300, and a funeral with cremation at roughly $6,280. Your aunt’s flower budget comes extra.

Whole-body donation to a medical school typically covers transport and cremation and returns the ashes to family, often at little or no cost. Programs vary, so call the school before you count on it.

Your body could spend its retirement crash-testing airbags or showing some nervous first-year where the brachial plexus hides. Mine would be in good company. I still owe that woman with the coral nail polish.

Physicians spend years making sure the 401(k) has a beneficiary. Few of us spend ten minutes deciding who gets the rest of the estate, meaning the part with the liver in it. Put it in writing this Halloween, somewhere between the will and the trust, and let your remains keep earning after you clock out.

Shop from a written list, carry a basket or the smallest cart, and buy nothing that isn’t on the list. Supermarkets and big-box stores stack displays at the end of each aisle and line the checkout with candy to sell you more than you came for.

A quick stop for milk shows how the layout works. The dairy case often sits along the back wall, so the walk there can take you past the bakery and the end caps, the displays at the end of each aisle.

End caps sit right in your path, and a product on one sells far more than it does on its usual shelf, marked down or not. A display alone doesn’t mean a lower price. Pricier brands often sit at eye level, the shelf you see first, with cheaper ones above and below. Look up and down, and compare the unit price, the cost per ounce or count, where the shelf tag shows one. Checkout candy sits within reach while you wait in line.

Stores use pricing tricks too. A $4.99 price can feel closer to $4 than to $5, because your eye lands on the first digit. A “10 for $10” sign suggests you need to buy 10. Unless its small print says you must buy them all, one usually rings up at $1, so buy the number you need.

Four habits keep you buying only what you planned:

At the register, put back anything that isn’t on the list. If you still want it after a 24-hour wait, add it to next week’s list.

#8542. What Is Dollar Cost Averaging?

If the idea of putting money into the stock market makes you nervous, you are not alone. A lot of people hold back because they are afraid of buying at the wrong time.

Dollar cost averaging is a strategy that takes that worry off the table. Instead of trying to time the market perfectly, you invest a fixed amount on a regular schedule and let time do the heavy lifting.

In this article, we will explain how dollar cost averaging works, why so many long-term investors rely on it, and how to put it into practice starting today.

Dollar cost averaging (DCA) is an investment strategy in which you invest a fixed dollar amount in a specific asset at regular intervals, regardless of market conditions. Whether the market is up, down, or flat, you invest the same amount on the same schedule.

The result is that you end up buying more shares when prices are low and fewer shares when prices are high. Over time, this can lower your average cost per share compared to making a single lump-sum investment at the wrong moment.

Most people already practice dollar cost averaging without realizing it. If you contribute to a 401(k) every time you get a paycheck, that is dollar cost averaging in action.

The mechanics are straightforward. You pick an investment, decide on a fixed dollar amount, and choose a schedule. Every week, every two weeks, or every month, you invest that amount, no matter what the market is doing that day.

Because you are investing a fixed dollar amount rather than a fixed number of shares, your money automatically buys more shares when prices dip and fewer when prices climb. This built-in dynamic is what makes the strategy so useful for investors who want to build wealth steadily without spending hours watching the market.

For most people, low-cost index funds are the best vehicle for this strategy. They give you broad diversification across hundreds of companies in a single investment, and their expense ratios are far lower than actively managed mutual funds or target-date funds. That difference in fees compounds significantly over decades.

Say you decide to invest $300 every month into a low-cost S&P 500 index fund. Here is what three months might look like:

After three months, you have invested $900 and own 21 shares. Your average cost per share is $42.86. If you had invested all $900 in Month 1 at $50 per share, you would only own 18 shares. The dip in Month 2 actually worked in your favor because you had cash ready to put to work at a lower price.

This is the core idea. You stop worrying about whether today is a good day to invest and start focusing on building a consistent habit instead.

One of the biggest mistakes investors make is letting fear and excitement drive their decisions. They pile in when the market is hot and pull out when it drops. Dollar-cost averaging sidesteps all of that by turning investing into a routine, like paying a bill, that runs automatically on a schedule.

When markets fall, most people panic. With dollar cost averaging, a dip is simply an opportunity to buy more shares at a discount. If you stay consistent, you will naturally accumulate more of your investment when it is on sale.

You do not need a large lump sum to get started. Even small, consistent contributions can grow meaningfully over time thanks to compounding. A good starting point is to aim for at least 10% of your gross income going toward investments. If that feels like a stretch right now, start with whatever you can manage and increase it over time.

Consistency is the real edge in personal investing. Dollar cost averaging encourages exactly that. When you automate your contributions, investing happens in the background while you get on with your life.

Want a free tool to help you keep track of your investments? Check out Empower!

Dollar cost averaging is a sound strategy, but it is worth understanding its limits before you dive in.

If you are investing in a low-quality asset that trends downward over time, buying it consistently will not save you. That is why what you invest in matters just as much as how you invest. Sticking to broad, low-cost index funds gives you exposure to the overall market rather than betting on a single company’s performance. Investing heavily in individual stocks introduces a level of risk that most people do not need to take on.

Alternative investments should stay small

Things like gold, cryptocurrency, and other alternative assets can have a place in a portfolio, but they should stay well under 10% of your total invested assets. These assets tend to be far more volatile and speculative than a diversified index fund, and there is no reason to let them dominate your long-term strategy.

A lump sum can outperform in a rising market

Research has shown that if you have a large sum ready to invest, putting it all in at once tends to outperform dollar cost averaging over the long run, simply because markets go up more often than they go down. That said, most people do not have a large lump sum sitting around. For those building wealth paycheck by paycheck, dollar cost averaging is the practical and sensible path.

Getting started with dollar cost averaging does not require a financial advisor or a complicated setup. Here is a simple framework:

Dollar cost averaging is one of the most practical investing strategies available to everyday investors. It takes the guesswork out of market timing, helps you build a consistent habit, and naturally positions you to benefit from market dips over time.

The key is to pair this strategy with the right investments. Low-cost index funds are a strong foundation. They offer diversification, keep fees low, and have a long track record of rewarding patient investors. Avoid concentrating too much on single stocks or speculative alternatives, and keep contributing regularly regardless of what the market is doing on any given day.

If you stay the course and keep contributing, time becomes your greatest asset.

#8540. Hyatt Category 4 Free Night Certificate — Card Perk Sweet Spot

Savings rate, FI number, and the path to freedom.

Withdrawal plans, Roth ladders, and early access.

Index funds, asset allocation, and real estate.

Roth conversions, capital gains, and FI tax planning.

Career growth, side hustles, and entrepreneurship.

Beliefs, purpose, and financial psychology.

Exercise, nutrition, and mental wellness.

The simplest high-value card perk in travel rewards — no points math required

Picture this: you walk into a stunning hotel lobby — maybe it's the Hyatt Regency Kyoto, maybe it's the Andaz Maui at Wailea, maybe it's a chic Hyatt Centric in the heart of a city you've always wanted to explore. You hand over your World of Hyatt card at check-in, and the night is on the house. Not because you're a high roller. Not because you spent $50,000 on a credit card. Because you crossed a spending threshold you were hitting anyway, and Hyatt rewarded you with a free night certificate that covers any Category 1–4 property in the entire portfolio. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about travel rewards done right: identifying the moments where a credit card benefit perfectly intersects with your normal life, and extracting maximum value with minimum complexity. ## The Math That Makes This a No-Brainer Here's the value proposition in plain numbers. Category 4 Hyatt properties — places like the Thompson Nashville, the Hyatt Regency Maui, or the Andaz San Diego — regularly command **$200 to $400 per night** in cash. On peak dates, holiday weekends, or in premium markets, that number climbs even higher. Your free night certificate covers any of these properties at no additional points cost. None. Zero. This isn't a discount. It's a full, unrestricted free night at properties that charge real-world luxury rates. Why does this represent a genuine pricing inefficiency? Because Hyatt's Category 1–4 certificates are earned through a flat spending threshold — $15,000 on the World of Hyatt Credit Card in a calendar year — and can be redeemed at properties whose nightly rates vary enormously. A Category 4 certificate costs the same to earn whether you use it at a $150 roadside property or a $400 resort. The system rewards you for targeting the high end of the range every single time. For a household already putting everyday spending on a rewards card, $15,000 across a full calendar year is often an achievable benchmark. Groceries, utilities, insurance premiums, quarterly tax payments — it adds up faster than you think. And when it does, Hyatt drops a certificate in your account that can deliver **$300–$400 in hotel value** without spending a single additional point. In the World of Hyatt program — consistently rated the **best hotel loyalty program for value per point** — this certificate is one of the most quietly powerful perks on any hotel card in the market.

The core mechanism here isn't a transfer partnership exploit or a routing rule loophole. It's simpler and more durable than that: Hyatt's Category system creates a ceiling, not a floor. When you earn a Category 1–4 free night certificate, you're not locked into a $150-a-night budget motel. You're handed a key that opens any door in that range — and some of those doors lead to genuinely spectacular properties.

Hyatt operates on a fixed award chart, ranging from 3,500 points for a Category 1 night all the way up to 45,000 points for a Category 8 night. Unlike programs that use dynamic pricing (where award costs swing with cash demand), Hyatt's chart is static. A Category 4 property costs the same 15,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in February or New Year's Eve.

Your free night certificate functions exactly like those 15,000 points — but you earned it through card spending, not through a points balance. This means the certificate has a defined and predictable value: whatever a Category 4 property charges in cash on the night you use it is exactly what you're getting for free.

The pricing inefficiency exists because Hyatt assigns categories based on average nightly rates across the year — but peak-season rates at desirable Category 4 properties can blow well past that average. A Hyatt Regency in a major city might be Category 4 because its average annual rate qualifies, but on a conference weekend or holiday weekend, that same room might cost $350–$400. Your certificate captures that peak-season value without any upcharge.

While this sweet spot is certificate-based (no points required), World of Hyatt integrates beautifully with two major transferable currency programs:

This matters for your broader strategy. If you want to stack a certificate with a separate points redemption — say, booking multiple nights where the first is covered by the certificate and subsequent nights use transferred points — you have two strong, flexible on-ramps into the Hyatt ecosystem. Chase Ultimate Rewards is the workhorse of the FI community's travel rewards stack, and having Hyatt as an instant 1:1 partner makes it one of the most actionable transfer relationships in the game.

Hyatt charges no fuel surcharges on award redemptions — a meaningful distinction compared to some airline programs where surcharges can swallow most of your savings. Your certificate redemption is clean: one certificate, one free night, no surprise fees at checkout beyond standard resort fees (which, to be fair, do apply at some properties — more on that in Pro Tips).

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. As a World of Hyatt Credit Card holder, your card activity will naturally keep your account active, so expiry is rarely a concern for cardholders. But if you ever cancel the card, make sure you use your points and certificates before they age out.

Booking a World of Hyatt free night certificate is genuinely one of the easiest processes in all of travel rewards. Here's the complete walkthrough from certificate to check-in.

Log in to your World of Hyatt account at hyatt.com and navigate to your account dashboard. Under the "My Certificates & Awards" section, confirm your Category 1–4 free night certificate is present and note its expiration date. Certificates are typically valid for 12 months from issuance, so don't let it sit unused. If you don't see it and you've crossed the $15,000 annual spend threshold on your World of Hyatt Credit Card, allow a few days for it to post after your statement closes, or call Chase to confirm.

Go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search function. You can filter by World of Hyatt category — specifically, search for Category 4 properties in any destination you're targeting. Don't shortchange yourself by defaulting to a Category 1 or 2 property out of habit. The certificate works at any Category 1–4 property, so always target the top of the range. Look for properties with high nightly cash rates — this is where your certificate delivers the most value.

Once you've identified a target property, search your dates on hyatt.com and switch the search to "Use Points." Category 4 properties will show award availability for 15,000 points per night. If award availability shows for that date, your certificate will cover it. Hyatt's booking window opens 395 days in advance, so for peak travel dates — holidays, major events, popular travel seasons — you can and should book the maximum window out.

Proceed through the booking process. At the payment step, you'll see an option to "Apply Free Night Award" or select your certificate from your account. Select the Category 1–4 certificate. The system will apply it and your total cash charge drops to $0 for the room rate (plus taxes and any applicable resort fees).

Hyatt award availability at popular properties can be limited during peak periods. Your tactical options:

Hyatt operates on a fixed category system where each property is assigned a category from 1 to 8 based on the brand and location, not the current market rate. This creates a structural pricing inefficiency: a Category 4 property in a high-demand market like Maui or Kyoto charges the same certificate cost as a Category 4 in a mid-tier city. Your free night certificate works at all of them equally. Unlike hotel programs with dynamic pricing where the cost of a free night fluctuates with demand, Hyatt's fixed chart means you can target the highest-value Category 4 properties without paying more. The card's $95 annual fee is one of the lowest in the premium hotel card category, yet the certificate alone delivers $250 to $400 or more in value — a return that makes the math trivially easy for any FI-minded household.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's make this concrete with a real example that represents exactly how this certificate shines.

The Andaz San Diego is a boutique lifestyle hotel in the Gaslamp Quarter — rooftop pool, stylish rooms, walking distance to everything downtown. It's the kind of hotel that signals a real trip, not just a place to sleep. On a standard weekend night, cash rates run $250–$350 per night. During Comic-Con, a Padres playoff weekend, or a major convention, rates push past $400.

Cash cost: $300 (conservative weekend estimate) Certificate cost: 0 points, 1 Category 1–4 free night certificate Your out-of-pocket: $0 for the room rate

You earned this certificate by crossing $15,000 in annual spending on the World of Hyatt Credit Card — a threshold many households reach through regular everyday spending over 12 months. The certificate posts automatically, you search availability on hyatt.com, and you apply it at checkout in about five minutes.

You're not redeeming into a budget experience. The Andaz brand sits at the upper-upscale tier of the Hyatt portfolio. You check in through a host model (no formal front desk), settle into a room with thoughtful design, and wake up knowing that $300 night cost you nothing extra beyond your normal spending.

If you hold World of Hyatt elite status — Discoverist, Explorist, or Globalist — that status applies to certificate bookings exactly like paid stays. Room upgrade requests, early check-in, late check-out: all the same benefits apply.

In every case, your one certificate delivers more value than most points redemptions in any hotel program. And you earned it without touching your points balance.

Your certificate works identically at a $150/night Category 4 property and a $400/night Category 4 property. Always search for the properties with the highest cash rates in your target destination. Use hyatt.com's rate display to compare award availability against current cash pricing — this directly shows you the value you're capturing.

Hyatt's booking window opens 395 days in advance. For properties in high-demand markets — Maui, New York, Chicago during peak season — award inventory gets claimed fast. Set a calendar alert to search exactly 395 days before your target dates and book the moment the window opens.

Your certificate covers one night. If you're staying multiple nights, stack it strategically: apply the certificate to the highest-cost night (often a Saturday) and book the remaining nights with World of Hyatt points transferred instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards at a 1:1 ratio. This hybrid approach maximizes the value of every currency you're using.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of inactivity. As a cardholder, your spending activity resets this clock automatically. But if you ever pause card use, make a small Hyatt purchase — even a $1 on-property charge — to reset the timer and protect your balance.

Hyatt does not waive resort fees on award and certificate bookings at all properties. Before booking, check whether your target property charges a daily resort fee — these can run $25–$50/night and will appear on your final bill. Factor this into your value calculation, especially at resort properties in Hawaii or Las Vegas.

The $15,000 spend threshold should come from natural household spending, not manufactured purchases. In the FI community, we optimize around spending you're doing anyway — insurance premiums, tax payments, groceries, utilities. If you're buying things you don't need to hit the threshold, you're eroding the value of the certificate.

Certificates issued by Hyatt are typically valid for 12 months. Mark the expiration date in your calendar the moment the certificate posts. An expired certificate is $300+ in value that simply disappears — one of the most painful mistakes in travel rewards.

This sweet spot is built for the everyday FI household that's already spending $15,000 or more annually on a single credit card and wants to redirect that activity toward a meaningful travel benefit. You don't need a large points balance. You don't need to understand transfer partners or award chart math. You earn the certificate by spending, you apply it at checkout, and you get a free night at a genuinely nice hotel.

You need: the World of Hyatt Credit Card, $15,000 in annual card spending, and a World of Hyatt account. No minimum points balance required — this is a card perk, not a points redemption.

If your annual spending is significantly below $15,000 on a single card, this particular mechanism won't trigger. In that case, the World of Hyatt Credit Card still earns Hyatt points on spending and delivers a Category 1–4 certificate on each card anniversary — so it retains value, just through a different path. Also, if you're deeply committed to a non-Hyatt hotel program, the benefit is obviously less useful without a library of Hyatt properties in your regular rotation.

## Rated: Easy (4/5 Beginner Friendly) This is one of the most accessible sweet spots in the entire travel rewards ecosystem, and that's by design. The certificate mechanism removes the two biggest friction points in traditional points redemptions: **finding the right number of points** and **navigating complex transfer timing**. You earn the certificate passively through spending, it posts to your account automatically, and the booking process on hyatt.com is as intuitive as booking any other hotel stay. ## What Makes It Easy - **No transfer required** — the certificate lives in your World of Hyatt account, ready to apply at checkout - **Fixed pricing** — Category 4 is Category 4 everywhere in the world; no dynamic pricing surprises - **Simple availability search** — hyatt.com's award search is clean and straightforward ## The One Genuine Challenge: Availability at Popular Properties The only real friction point is award inventory at high-demand Category 4 properties on desirable dates. Hyatt limits how many award rooms it releases per night, and popular properties in destinations like Hawaii or New York fill quickly. **Three ways to beat this:** 1. Search 395 days in advance when fresh inventory releases 2. Build a shortlist of 3–5 Category 4 properties in your target region so you have backup options 3. Stay flexible on dates — midweek nights almost always have more award availability than weekends If you can approach this with even modest date flexibility, you will find great options. The Hyatt portfolio at Category 4 is large and geographically diverse, and there is almost always a compelling property available somewhere you'd actually want to go. For anyone new to travel rewards, this certificate is the perfect first redemption — low complexity, high reward, and a genuinely memorable hotel stay to show your household what this strategy can deliver.

Log in to hyatt.com and check My Certificates and Awards after your card anniversary. Note the expiration date — certificates are typically valid for 12 months. If it does not appear within a few weeks of your anniversary, contact Chase.

Search hyatt.com for Category 4 hotels in your target destinations. Compare the cash rate against the free certificate value. Target properties where cash rates exceed $300 per night — these deliver the highest return on your $95 annual fee.

Hyatt opens its booking window 395 days in advance. For popular Category 4 properties in Maui, New York, or Kyoto, set a calendar reminder and book the day the window opens. Apply your certificate during the booking process on hyatt.com.

Use the free night certificate for the most expensive night of your stay (typically weekends or peak dates), then book remaining nights with World of Hyatt points at 15,000 points per Category 4 night. This combination stretches your overall lodging value significantly.

Category 4 includes well-known properties like the Andaz Maui at Wailea, Hyatt Regency Kyoto, Andaz San Diego, Hyatt Centric locations in major cities, and many Thompson hotels. The full list is available on hyatt.com by filtering the award chart. Category 4 is the sweet spot tier where property quality is high but the award cost remains accessible.

The World of Hyatt credit card automatically issues a Category 1-4 free night certificate each year on your card anniversary. A second certificate is earned after you spend $15,000 on the card in a calendar year. No special action is required beyond holding the card and meeting the spending threshold for the bonus certificate.

Yes. The free night certificate is valid for any available standard room at a Category 1-4 property, including weekends and holidays. There are no blackout dates. However, standard room availability may be limited during peak periods, so booking early is recommended.

The certificate expires 12 months after issuance and cannot be extended or refunded. If you know you will not use it, consider booking a refundable reservation at a Category 4 property to hold the value, then cancel and rebook if your plans change. Do not let it expire unused — the value easily exceeds the annual fee.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Hyatt Category 4 free night certificate is the most accessible sweet spot in travel rewards. You do not need to understand transfer partners, award charts, or complex booking strategies. You hold the World of Hyatt credit card, the certificate arrives on your anniversary, and you redeem it at a hotel where cash rates run $250 to $400 or more per night. The $95 annual fee pays for itself three to four times over with a single use. For FI-minded households that consolidate $15,000 or more in annual spending on one card, the second certificate doubles the value. This is the card perk that turns skeptics into believers — simple math, real savings, no tricks required.

#8539. What Are Mutual Funds?

If you have ever looked at your 401(k) options or browsed a brokerage account, you have almost certainly seen mutual funds on the list. They are one of the most widely used investment vehicles in the country, and for good reason. But not all mutual funds are built the same, and understanding the differences can have a real impact on how much money you actually keep over time.

This article breaks down what mutual funds are, how they work, the different types you will encounter, and what to watch out for when deciding whether one belongs in your portfolio.

A mutual fund is a pooled investment vehicle. When you invest in a mutual fund, your money is combined with money from thousands of other investors. A fund manager then uses that pool of capital to buy a collection of assets, which might include stocks, bonds, or a mix of both, depending on the fund’s objective.

Each investor owns shares of the mutual fund, and those shares represent a proportional stake in everything the fund holds. When the underlying assets increase in value, your shares go up. When they fall, your shares go down.

Mutual funds are priced once per day, after the market closes, based on the total value of all the assets inside the fund. This is called the net asset value, or NAV. Unlike stocks, which trade throughout the day at constantly changing prices, mutual fund transactions are always settled at the end-of-day price.

When you buy shares of a mutual fund, you are not picking individual stocks or bonds yourself. Instead, you are hiring a fund manager, or a team of them, to make those decisions on your behalf. The fund follows a stated investment objective, and the manager selects holdings that align with that goal.

For example, a fund that aims for long-term growth might hold primarily large-cap U.S. stocks. A fund focused on income might hold a mix of dividend-paying stocks and bonds. The fund’s prospectus, a document you can access before investing, spells out exactly what the fund is trying to do and how it plans to do it.

Investors buy and sell mutual fund shares directly through the fund company or through a brokerage account. You can invest a specific dollar amount rather than buying a whole number of shares, making them accessible to investors at just about any level.

There are thousands of mutual funds available, but most fall into a handful of broad categories.

These funds invest primarily in stocks. They can be further broken down by the size of the companies they hold (large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap), the style of investing (growth vs. value), or the geography (U.S. only, international, or global). Stock funds carry more risk than bond funds but also offer greater long-term growth potential.

Bond funds hold debt securities issued by governments, corporations, or municipalities. They are generally considered less volatile than stock funds and are often used to add stability to a portfolio. However, they also tend to produce lower returns over long periods.

These funds hold a combination of stocks and bonds within a single fund. The allocation varies by fund, but the idea is to provide both growth and income while smoothing out some of the volatility of a pure stock fund.

Money market funds invest in short-term, low-risk debt instruments. They aim to maintain a stable value and are often used as a place to park cash. The returns are modest, and they are not a long-term wealth-building strategy.

Index funds are a specific type of mutual fund that tracks a market index, such as the S&P 500, rather than relying on active stock picking. Because they are passively managed, they tend to have much lower fees than other types of mutual funds. Over the long run, they have consistently outperformed most actively managed alternatives after costs are taken into account.

This distinction is one of the most important things to understand about mutual funds, and it directly affects your returns.

An actively managed fund employs a portfolio manager who researches investments, makes judgment calls, and trades frequently to outperform the market. This sounds appealing. Who would not want a professional trying to beat the market on their behalf?

The problem is that most actively managed funds do not beat the market over the long run, especially after fees are factored in. Study after study over multiple decades has shown that the majority of active fund managers underperform a simple index fund over a ten-year period. Yet they charge significantly more for the attempt.

A passively managed fund, like an index fund, does not try to beat the market. It simply tracks it. The holdings change only when the underlying index changes. Because no active management is required, the fees are a fraction of those charged by actively managed funds.

For most long-term investors, a low-cost index fund is the better choice. The math is straightforward: lower fees mean more of your return stays in your pocket, and that difference compounds significantly over decades.

Fees are one of the most overlooked factors in investing, and they deserve your full attention. Here are the main ones to know.

The expense ratio is the annual cost of owning a fund, expressed as a percentage of your investment. A fund with a 1.00% expense ratio costs you $10 per year for every $1,000 you have invested. That may sound small, but over 30 years of investing, that difference compared to a fund charging 0.05% can amount to tens of thousands of dollars.

Some mutual funds charge a sales commission, called a load, either when you buy (front-end load) or when you sell (back-end load). A front-end load of 5% means that only $950 of every $1,000 you invest actually goes into the fund. There is no reason to pay a sales load when thousands of excellent no-load funds are available.

These are marketing and distribution fees charged by some funds. They are baked into the expense ratio and can add up. A fund with a high 12b-1 fee is often a sign that the fund is spending money on sales and marketing rather than managing your investment.

When you invest in a mutual fund, you immediately own a small piece of every asset the fund holds. A single investment gives you exposure to hundreds or even thousands of companies, which spreads your risk far more effectively than buying individual stocks ever could.

For investors who do not want to research individual securities, mutual funds hand the decision-making over to professionals. This is especially relevant for bond funds and specialty funds, where the research involved is more complex than evaluating stocks.

Most mutual funds have low minimum investment requirements, and many allow you to invest in dollar amounts rather than whole shares. This makes them a practical option for investors who are just getting started or working with a limited budget.

Mutual funds in the United States are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Fund companies are required to disclose their holdings, fees, and performance data regularly. That transparency makes it relatively easy to compare options and know exactly what you are getting into.

Fees can erode your returns significantly

This is the biggest issue with many mutual funds, particularly actively managed ones. High expense ratios and sales loads reduce your effective return every single year. Over a long investing horizon, that drag is substantial. Always check the expense ratio before investing in any fund.

Because mutual funds are priced once daily at market close, you cannot buy or sell during trading hours at a live price. For long-term investors, this is rarely a concern. But it is worth understanding how mutual funds differ from ETFs in this regard.

When a mutual fund sells holdings at a profit, it distributes those capital gains to shareholders at the end of the year. Even if you did not sell any of your own shares, you may owe taxes on those distributions. This is less of an issue in tax-advantaged accounts like a 401(k) or IRA, but it is something to keep in mind for taxable brokerage accounts.

It is possible to hold too many mutual funds that overlap in their holdings, leaving you with a bloated, redundant portfolio. Owning five different large-cap U.S. stock funds does not give you five times the diversification. It mostly just gives you five sets of fees.

With thousands of mutual funds available, narrowing down your options does not have to be complicated. A few straightforward criteria will get you most of the way there.

Mutual funds are among the most practical investments available to everyday investors. They make it easy to build a diversified portfolio without needing to research and manage individual securities. For most people, the primary vehicle for building wealth over time is a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account.

That said, not all mutual funds are worth your money. Actively managed funds and those with high sales loads or steep expense ratios consistently underperform lower-cost alternatives over the long run. The evidence strongly favors low-cost index funds as the core of most investors’ portfolios.

The most important step is to start. Aim to invest at least 10% of your gross income consistently, keep your costs low, stay diversified, and give your money time to grow. The mechanics of which specific funds you choose matter far less than the discipline of contributing regularly over many years.

Practical advice to help you make money, save money and pay off debt, from a family that paid off $52,000 in 18 months.

#8537. Should I Come Out of Retirement?

More than 60% of respondents in a 2026 Goldman Sachs survey of 5,106 working and retired Americans said they had taken work outside their primary job, most out of necessity rather than a wish for extra spending money. Nearly 70% had delayed a major financial goal.

Retirement is increasingly becoming a touchy topic for many, especially those of us who are used to a certain level of stability.

The news only makes matters worse. On Friday, October 30, we saw Nasdaq’s biggest 1-day drop since June 5, setting the internet ablaze with speculation. The index closed 7.8% below its October 6 record, though it was noted that the S&P 500 was only a few percent below its own record.

Then there’s inflation. Annual inflation reached 3.7% in September, up from 3.4% in August. Pair that with continuing international conflicts on several fronts, and you’ve got the perfect storm of insecurity.

A National Institute on Retirement Security survey found that 80% of Americans say that the nation faces a retirement crisis and 61% worry they won’t be financially secure in retirement.

The respondents blamed inflation (73%) and market volatility (62%) as contributing factors, and 76% feared Social Security cuts if Congress fails to act.

A New York Life survey of more than 2,000 adults found that 34% had already delayed retirement or planned to, and 46% of them expected to push it back 5 years or more. Their top reasons were a lack of savings (46%) and inflation (45%).

Those who have already retired aren’t immune to these insecurities. The Goldman Sachs sample included 1,494 retirees aged 45 to 75. A market drop may also hurt more when you’re drawing from a portfolio than when you’re adding to it.

So, wondering if you should go back to work feels like a warranted question. Plenty of retirees take the leap back. Doctors go back too, though plenty of them say they don’t miss it. In a recent r/emergencymedicine thread, retired ED physicians were split on the question.

One, 3 years out, said he doesn’t miss it at all and still has the occasional nightmare. Another quit at 61 with no plan, misses the people and belonging to the group and keeps looking for work without luck.

1.5 million retirees reentered the workforce by March 2022.

We spend decades planning for the day we stop working. Then some of us stop, and a year or 2 later we’re checking job boards or answering calls from our old group. If that sounds like you, this article is for you.

Let’s take a look at the reasons many doctors feel the urge to un-retire, what going back to work in 2026 entails and the logistics of it all.

In case you missed it: Micro-retirements aren’t a shortcut to FIRE

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

Money is the top reason many retirees choose to go back, so let’s start there. A recent survey found that 48% of working retirees said they needed the income, while 45% said they worked for social and emotional benefits.

Divide 1 year of spending by your portfolio. An example in T. Rowe Price’s example illustrates a 62-year-old with $900,000 who spends $65,000 a year.

That’s a 7.2% withdrawal rate. She has a 64% chance of not outliving her money if she retires at 62, a 91% chance at 65 and a 97% chance at 67.

Now let’s imagine a physician-specific version.

Say you have $2,500,000 and spend $150,000 a year before taxes. That’s a 6% withdrawal rate. A part-time job paying $60,000 would trim your withdrawals to $90,000, which is 3.6%.

You lower your rate by 2.4 percentage points without changing how you live. Of course, taxes will reduce that paycheck so ask your planner for a clearer outline.

One retired doctor said he saved about 30% of his take-home pay in his last years of full-time work, and his spending ended up around half of his colleagues’.

He could walk away any day, and his group knew it. That kind of freedom is helpful even after you return because you’re able to negotiate better when you don’t actually need the job.

Before you take a job, figure out whether the problem is your portfolio or your spending. If your withdrawal rate looks fine but spending still makes you uneasy, a concrete spending plan may help more than a paycheck. Ask your planner to set a monthly amount you can spend without second-guessing.

Working longer also helps in 2 other ways. You can delay account withdrawals as well as Social Security. Benefits grow 8% for every year you wait past full retirement age until you reach 70, while claiming at 62 cuts them by almost 30%.

Continuing to work also gives you more time to contribute to your retirement accounts. If your new employer offers a 401(k) or 403(b), the 2026 limit is $24,500, plus an $8,000 catch-up at 50 and older or $11,250 at ages 60 to 63.

It depends on whether you’ve claimed it and how old you are. If you haven’t claimed, going back to work is straightforward and your eventual monthly SS check will continue to increase.

If you claimed before full retirement age (FRA), the earnings test applies. In 2026, Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480 if you’re under FRA all year.

In the year you reach FRA, the limit rises to $65,160, and the agency withholds $1 for every $3 above it. Only earnings before the month you reach FRA count.

If your part-time schedule pays more than $24,480, expect withholding. The money isn’t gone for good, though. Social Security recalculates your benefit at FRA to credit the months it withheld.

Only wages and self-employment earnings count, so investment income doesn’t trigger withholding. Once you reach FRA, working doesn’t reduce your benefit.

You’ll also keep paying Social Security taxes on your paychecks. Higher earnings can also make more of your benefit taxable, so ask your tax preparer to estimate that too.

What if you changed your mind after claiming early? If you claimed before FRA, you have 12 months to withdraw your application. You must repay what you received, and Social Security then treats your record as if you never claimed at all.

Coverage before 65 costs far more in 2026 than it did in 2025 since the enhanced ACA subsidies expired on December 31, 2025.

KFF reports that a 60-year-old with a $65,000 income now pays an average of $10,389 more per year, or $865 per month. The subsidy cliff is also back which means above 400% of the poverty level (which is $62,600 for a single person in 2026), you lose the premium tax credit entirely.

On top of that, the ACA allows insurers to charge adults in their 60s up to 3 times what they charge adults in their 20s.

So a job with group health coverage may save you thousands of dollars a year because it skips the marketplace and the income cliff.

A working physician said that if he left medicine early, he’d take a flexible management job of about 25 hours a week mostly for the group insurance and the 401(k) match.

If you’re considering the same, ask HR what hours are required for benefits and when coverage starts, since each plan sets its own cutoff.

Medicare changes much of the picture. If you delayed Part B because you had coverage through your own or your spouse’s current job, you get an 8-month special enrollment period after that job or coverage ends.

If you miss it, you’ll have to pay 10% more for each full 12-month period you could have had Part B, for as long as you keep it. COBRA and retiree coverage don’t count for that exemption.

Keep in mind that Medicare generally pays first if the employer has fewer than 20 employees. So a small practice’s plan may pay second and you’d still need Part B.

Learn more: 11 Retirement Planning Mistakes That Haunt High-Earning Physicians

Don’t count on getting your old job back.

An AARP survey of more than 3,500 people ages 50 and older found that 74% believe their age will be a barrier to getting hired, and 64% of workers 50 and older have seen or experienced age discrimination at work. That stigma is even worse for women.

Another AARP report found that 37% of workers 50 and older experienced subtle age discrimination during a job search in 2025, up from 30% in 2024. These surveys cover all fields, not only medicine, so ask recruiters in your specialty what they are seeing firsthand.

Think about what you want the next job to be. 24% of workers 50 and older planned a job change in 2025, so you won’t be the only one looking. If your retirement was driven mostly due to clinical work, teaching, consulting or chart review may suit you better than your old schedule.

We’ve already established that money drives about half of all unretirements. Boredom and a wish to help others drive many of the rest.

In an AARP survey, 18% of unretirees said boredom or a desire to stay active was their main reason for returning to work. For doctors, these sentiments start even before they leave.

In a Jackson Physician Search survey, 44% of physicians feared losing their sense of purpose in retirement and 39% feared boredom (money was still the top fear at 53%).

In CHG Healthcare’s 2024 survey, physicians who wanted to keep working felt that way because of a love of medicine (58%), social connections (57%) and concern for patients (39%). Others stated not feeling emotionally ready (47%), wanting to keep their lifestyle (35%) and fearing boredom or isolation (33%).

In Medscape’s 2025 retirement report, the top reason physicians gave for not retiring earlier was feeling they still had more to offer (62%), ahead of not having enough saved (45%). In the 2023 report, 46% expected retirement to feel like losing a part of their identity.

Retired and soon-to-retire ED physicians on Reddit offer a mixed bag of insights. One commenter who was 4 months from retiring expects to miss the ego boost of being a doctor. The one who quit at 61 with no plan misses colleagues and most of his patients, though not the fatigue of rotating shifts or the dread of sending home someone who should have stayed. Several said sleep and a normal daytime rhythm were the biggest change.

Retirement also changes what stresses you out. A 2025 Mayo Clinic review of physician well-being in retirement says that stress moves from work problems to personal ones, including professional identity, family, health and the loss of relationships.

The journal’s late-career paper urges physicians to plan for social and emotional needs along with finances. If you can’t picture your days without the work and the people, look at part-time options before you retire fully.

Give your first year in retirement a fair shake before you decide. People who leave long, consuming careers often describe a rocky start to retirement.

One user on Reddit said that it took about a year to stop feeling guilty about doing nothing. Another lasted 2 years, took a part-time job and has stayed 10 years. A third said the new job mattered to them mostly for the community, since all their friends still worked.

In case you missed it: The Nightmare Before Retirement: A Physician’s Cautionary Tale (2026 Edition)

If burnout pushed you out in the first place, the same job will push you out again. In 2026, burnout in healthcare is still running rampant.

Doximity’s May 2026 poll found that 82% of physicians say they’re overworked and 46% are considering early retirement because of it.

That number is up from 37% in 2025 and 21% in 2021. The jump is sharpest among women (54% in 2026 compared to 33% in 2023) and physicians ages 50 to 54 (56%, up from 35%).

Medscape’s 2026 burnout report corroborates this. 50% of male and 51% of female physicians say that their work causes their burnout, and 13%–14% are considering leaving medicine altogether.

In a MedCentral survey, 44% of physicians said they had considered leaving medical practice since the start of the year.

A recent AMA study in The Permanente Journal looked at doctors who had already left and found that 971 clinically inactive physicians were typically 48.1 years old when they left clinical practice. Their top reasons were the hassle factor (44.7%), stress (44.5%), unrealistic patient demands (41.1%) and lack of professional satisfaction (38.4%).

Most doctors don’t plan to go cold turkey, however. In CHG Healthcare’s late-career survey, 63% of respondents said they’d rather work less than not work at all and 94% had at least slight interest in locum tenens work.

26% of physicians from a Weatherby Healthcare survey say that they are interested in locum tenens work. That’s 7 points higher than last year and the highest in 10 years.

If the actual reason behind your retirement still rings true or any of the reasons stated above give you a pause, you may want to reconsider jumping back into the workforce. Unless financial insecurity is twisting your arm, there’s no point in going back to something that already burned you out.

Fortunately, there are many other work options for physicians that don’t involve selling your soul. Locum tenens and expert witness work are popular ways for physicians to keep working.

Learn more: Physician Side Gigs That Actually Pay in 2026

Rules vary by state so check what’s needed where you live. Florida requires a reactivation fee, proof of continuing medical education (CME) for each year the license was inactive or retired, a health history and a financial responsibility form.

Pennsylvania requires full Board review and possibly proof of competency. According to the AAMC some states require a reentry program after an absence that averages about 3 years.

The ED physician who quit at 61 let his board certification lapse and said he now wishes he’d kept it, because it might have opened insurance work.

Another retired ED doctor commented that he dreamed for 2 years about working shifts without a license or malpractice cover. The roles you want to work in may or may not require these credentials so check before you make up your mind.

Most carriers give retiring physicians tail coverage free or at low cost. But some carriers may cancel that tail or charge a premium if you resume practice because when you return to clinical practice and receive pay or compensation for clinical work, you violate the retirement condition under which the tail fee was waived. Check with your provider.

The AMA warns that some physicians’ retirement income may change if they take paid work. Check your pension plan before you accept a role.

Of course, there’s no universal right answer and no rulebook that says you must make one permanent decision.

Start by being honest about why you feel the urge to return. If it’s your portfolio that’s got you worried, earning an income may give you some much-needed breathing room.

If you miss the people, intellectual challenge or sense of purpose, you might find what you’re looking for in a very different role.

But if you’re simply uncomfortable with having more time than you’ve ever had before, give yourself a little longer before dusting off your resume.

Most importantly, don’t let a bad week in the market convince you that decades of retirement planning have failed. Nor should you feel obliged to return to medicine because you miss being a physician. It’s okay to miss parts of your career without wanting the whole thing back.

And no matter what you decide, don’t let your credentials lapse. Your medical license and board certification represent years of hard work and keeping them active preserves options you may not realize you’ll want later.

Even if you’re 100% certain you’ll never practice again, give your future self the benefit of the doubt. You don’t have to use those credentials, but you might one day wish you still had them.

Also read: The Idea of “Retiring to” Something

It depends on your finances, personal goals and reasons for retiring. Returning to work can provide income, health insurance and social connections, but it shouldn’t come at the expense of the retirement you worked so hard to achieve.

The most common reasons include financial insecurity, boredom, loss of purpose, social isolation and missing the intellectual challenge of their former careers.

Yes. Retired physicians can return to clinical practice, provided they meet their state medical board’s licensing and reactivation requirements. They may also need to address CME, board certification and malpractice coverage.

Yes, if you claim Social Security before full retirement age. In 2026, benefits are withheld if your earnings exceed $24,480, or $65,160 in the year you reach full retirement age. The earnings test no longer applies once you reach FRA.

Keeping your medical license active preserves the option to return to clinical practice without going through the full reactivation process. Check your state’s renewal requirements and consider maintaining board certification, too.

There’s no set waiting period. Give yourself time to adjust to retirement and understand what’s driving your desire to return. If finances aren’t forcing the decision, consider giving retirement at least a year before making a move.

This was a really thoughtful look at a question with no single right answer. The withdrawal-rate example was especially clear — seeing how part-time work could bring a 6% rate down to 3.6% makes the math feel much less abstract. I also had not realized how much the 2026 ACA subsidy changes could push someone back toward a job with group coverage. The advice to keep a license and board certification active, even when you are sure you are done, seems like wise insurance for your future self.

#8536. What Are Target Date Funds?

When you sign up for a 401(k) at work, there is a good chance that a target date fund shows up near the top of the investment options list. They are simple, widely available, and often the default choice for new investors. But simple does not always mean the best option for your situation.

In this article, we will break down what target date funds are, how they work, what they cost, and why a low-cost index fund strategy may serve most investors better in the long run.

A target-date fund is a type of mutual fund designed to serve as a single, all-in-one retirement investment. You pick the fund that most closely matches the year you plan to retire, and the fund handles everything else. If you plan to retire around 2050, for example, you would choose a fund labeled something like “2050 Retirement Fund” or “Target Date 2050.”

The fund holds a mix of stocks and bonds, and that mix automatically shifts over time as your target date gets closer. Early on, the fund is weighted heavily toward growth stocks. As retirement approaches, the portfolio gradually shifts toward bonds and more conservative holdings to reduce risk.

The appeal is obvious. You make one decision, contribute regularly, and the fund adjusts itself. For people who want to set it and forget it, that sounds like a dream. But there is more to the story.

Target date funds are known as “fund of funds.” Rather than holding individual stocks or bonds directly, they hold a collection of other mutual funds, typically a mix of domestic stock, international stock, and bond funds.

The fund manager adjusts the allocation over time according to a schedule called a glide path. When you are decades away from retirement, the fund might hold 90% stocks and 10% bonds. As you get closer to your target year, that ratio shifts until the fund is much more conservative, sometimes holding more bonds than stocks by the time you retire.

This rebalancing happens automatically inside the fund, which is one reason they are so popular in workplace retirement plans. You do not need to log in and make adjustments. The fund does it for you.

The glide path is simply the schedule that determines how the fund’s asset allocation changes over time. Think of it as the fund’s long-term plan for gradually reducing risk.

Different fund providers use different glide paths, and this matters more than most people realize. Some funds are more aggressive early on and pull back dramatically as retirement nears. Others maintain a higher stock allocation even into and through retirement, which some financial planners argue is actually smarter given how long retirement can last.

The important thing to understand is that the glide path is not customized for you. It is a one-size-fits-all formula based on your expected retirement year, nothing more. Your actual risk tolerance, health, spending plans, and other income sources are not factored in at all.

The biggest selling point is that target date funds require almost no ongoing attention. You pick one fund, contribute regularly, and walk away. For someone who has no interest in managing their investments, that convenience is genuinely valuable.

Because target date funds hold a mix of stock and bond funds, you get broad diversification across asset classes in a single investment. You are not putting all your money into a single sector or company.

Over time, a portfolio can drift away from its intended allocation as different assets grow at different rates. Target date funds handle this automatically, which is one less thing you have to manage yourself.

Target date funds are not without their drawbacks, and for many investors, those drawbacks are significant enough to look for a better option.

Because target date funds are funds of funds, they often carry two layers of fees: the expense ratio of the target date fund itself and the underlying expense ratios of the funds it holds. Even a seemingly small difference in fees can cost you tens of thousands of dollars over a long investing career. Low-cost index funds, by comparison, often charge a fraction of what target date funds do.

The glide path in a target-date fund is designed for the average investor retiring in a given year. But your situation is not average. You might have a pension, a working spouse, rental income, or a much higher risk tolerance than the fund assumes. None of that is reflected in how the fund manages your money.

When you hand everything over to a target date fund, you give up control over your allocation. If the fund has a heavy position in international stocks or bonds that you would rather avoid, there is not much you can do about it while staying in the fund.

Not all target date funds are created equal. The same target year fund from two different providers can have very different allocations, fee structures, and underlying holdings. Without digging into the details, it is easy to end up in a fund that does not match your actual needs.

This is where the comparison gets important. A target date fund is actively managed in the sense that a team of people decides how to allocate and rebalance it over time. An index fund, on the other hand, simply tracks a market index like the S&P 500. There is no active management involved, which is exactly why the fees are so much lower.

Decades of research consistently show that most actively managed funds underperform their benchmark index after fees. Target date funds are not immune to this problem. When you account for layered costs, many target-date funds trail what you would earn by simply holding a low-cost index fund over the same period.

A simple alternative that many investors use is called a three-fund portfolio: a U.S. total market index fund, an international index fund, and a bond index fund. You set your own allocation based on your age and risk tolerance, rebalance once a year, and pay minimal fees. It takes about 30 minutes a year to manage.

This approach gives you the same diversification as a target-date fund, with far more control and significantly lower costs. And as a general rule, the more of your return you keep rather than paying in fees, the better off you will be over time.

Target date funds are not the right choice for every investor, but there are situations where they make sense.

Even in these cases, it is worth checking the expense ratio. If your plan offers a target-date fund with an expense ratio above 0.50%, consider whether there are lower-cost index fund options within the same plan.

Target date funds solve a real problem: they make it easy for people who do not want to think about investing to still participate in the market. That convenience has real value.

But for investors who are willing to learn even a little bit about how to manage their own allocation, a portfolio of low-cost index funds will almost always be the better long-term choice. The fees are lower, the control is greater, and the returns tend to be better over time.

If you are currently in a target date fund, that is not necessarily a problem. But it is worth understanding what you are paying and whether a simpler, lower-cost approach might serve you better. Investing at least 10% of your gross income is the priority. Where exactly that money goes is the next question worth asking.
