#8533. Health Sharing vs. Traditional Health Insurance: Which Is Right for You?

By Deacon Hayes Updated November 14, 2026

If your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives. Health sharing plans have moved from a faith-based niche into a mainstream budgeting conversation. But before you switch, it’s worth understanding exactly what you’re trading away, not just what you’re saving.

A health sharing plan (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance company. There’s no insurance contract, and no company is legally on the hook to pay your claims.

Tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed. Michigan’s insurance regulator adds that HCSMs aren’t classified as insurance because they don’t assume risk and have no legal obligation to pay members’ costs.

Example: Zion HealthShare is a modern health sharing community that markets itself as a lower-cost alternative to ACA plans, with no provider networks and members paying an “Initial Unshareable Amount” (their version of a deductible) before larger bills become eligible for sharing.

Traditional health insurance is a regulated contract, an ACA marketplace plan, an employer plan, or a private major-medical policy. The insurer must pay covered claims, cover pre-existing conditions from day one, and include the ACA’s essential health benefits (preventive care, maternity, mental health, and more), a distinction healthinsurance.org explains in detail when comparing HCSMs with ACA-compliant coverage.

Solo Health is another option built for self-employed people. It’s a self-funded major medical health plan with a nationwide PPO network, and it works differently from both health sharing and ACA Marketplace coverage. Eligibility is based on a short health questionnaire. Read our full Solo Health review.

Employer-sponsored family premiums averaged $26,993 in 2025, and many 2026 ACA marketplace plans are seeing median premium hikes of 18–20% as subsidies shrink and medical costs climb. By comparison, health sharing contributions often run $150–$400 per person per month, roughly 30–50% less.

But that gap exists because health sharing plans aren’t required to guarantee anything. Traditional insurers already deny 19–20% of claims on average (some carriers reportedly higher), so even “real” insurance isn’t friction-free, but at least it comes with legal appeal rights and state oversight. A health share’s review process is informal and ministry-specific, with no equivalent legal backstop if a bill gets rejected.

It works best for generally healthy families who don’t qualify for meaningful ACA subsidies, are comfortable handling more paperwork and negotiating bills themselves, and want lower fixed monthly costs in exchange for taking on more risk. It’s a weaker fit for anyone managing a chronic condition, planning a pregnancy, or who needs the legal certainty of a regulated contract.

Health sharing can meaningfully lower your monthly healthcare costs, but the trade-off is real: you’re giving up the legal guarantee, essential-benefit mandates, and regulatory protection that come with traditional insurance. For a healthy family stretched thin by rising ACA premiums, it can be a reasonable bridge option. For anyone with ongoing medical needs, the savings usually aren’t worth the uncertainty.

Is a health sharing plan the same as a health insurance policy?No. It’s a voluntary cost-sharing arrangement, not a legally binding insurance contract.

Can I use a health sharing plan and still contribute to an HSA?Not based on the health share alone; you also need to be enrolled in a genuine HDHP to be HSA-eligible.

Will a health sharing plan cover a pre-existing condition?Usually only after a waiting period, which varies by organization, often 12 to 36 months.

Does the ACA’s individual mandate penalty apply if I only have a health share?No, the federal individual mandate penalty was eliminated starting in 2019, so this isn’t a factor either way.

Ian Ippolito, a former professional software developer, is an investor and serial entrepreneur. He founded Private Investor Club and The Real Estate Crowdfunding Review, where his five-part series on AI and investing begins here.

For years, I dismissed AI as hype. Then in February 2026, it finished in a few hours the Monte Carlo program for our family’s finances that had defeated it for months. Since then many have been surprised at how expensive and scarce AI is turning out to be. Here’s what I found, and how it’s changing where I invest.

(Disclaimer: I’m an investor sharing my personal opinion. I’m not your attorney, accountant or financial advisor, so consult your own professionals before making any financial decisions.)

Before starting companies, I worked as a professional software developer. Later I founded and sold vWorker (formerly Rent a Coder), an early online marketplace for hiring programmers.

Today I run Private Investor Club, where accredited investors share due diligence on private investments.

So when AI companies claimed their tools could write software, I tested the claim myself. In the fall of 2025, I used AI to help build a Monte Carlo simulation for our family’s finances: the kind of program that runs thousands of what-if market scenarios, which many of you have used to test your own retirement plans.

It was miserable. The AI forgot what it had done a few minutes earlier, ignored instructions and broke code that already worked. After a few months of workarounds, I gave up.

By December 2025, I expected AI to join the long list of technologies that never lived up to their hype. And I thought an ugly stock market correction was coming.

In February 2026, an acquaintance mentioned that Anthropic’s Claude Code had improved a lot, so I gave it one more try, fully expecting to be disappointed.

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

I handed it the half-finished Monte Carlo program. It finished the job in a few hours, and the code was clean and worked.

Then I gave it something harder. In 2024, my wife and I went shopping for a lot to build a home on, and quiet matters a lot to us. So I paid a talented overseas developer $3,500 to build a program that tracks airplane flights over different parts of town. He did excellent work in six weeks.

I gave Claude Code the exact same requirements. It built the whole program in about five hours, for roughly 69 cents’ worth of my $100 monthly subscription. It even caught an error in a data provider’s documentation that I had missed, and it added useful features I hadn’t asked for.

I spent decades learning to program. Watching a machine do that work faster and better than a very good human developer was both thrilling and a little sad.

When AI redoes a $3,500 programming job for 69 cents, it looks like a nearly free substitute for human workers. Plenty of executives had been saying exactly that for years:

The predictions had a real basis. AI is priced by the “token,” a small piece of text the AI reads or writes, and the price of each token really has collapsed. In early 2025, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman estimated that the cost of a given level of AI drops roughly tenfold every year (Three Observations).

But the newest AI models chew through far more tokens to finish each task. So the price per token can keep falling while the total bill keeps climbing.

The research firm Gartner now expects AI programming to end up costing more than the staff it was supposed to replace. In June 2026 it forecast that by 2028, companies will spend more on AI coding than the average developer earns, because models are consuming more tokens and vendors are moving to pay-per-use pricing (Gartner).

Even if tokens keep getting cheaper, AI runs on land, buildings, permits and electricity. And all four are getting scarcer.

Local communities are fighting new data centers:

Electricity is the other bottleneck. The consulting firm ICF forecasts that U.S. electricity demand will grow about 25% between 2023 and 2030 (ICF). Data centers are competing for that power with electric cars, heat pumps and new factories.

My view is that AI will stay scarce and expensive for a long time. Cheaper chips can’t conjure up power plants, transmission lines or a permitted data center overnight.

So I’m looking at two kinds of investments: the things AI can’t run without (the first three below), and the work AI still can’t do (the fourth). Physician on FIRE has covered the public-market side in Investing In The AI Revolution; my focus here is private deals.

In each area, I’ll start with the deals that didn’t make it through my due diligence, and then the ones that did.

1. The AI companies themselves. Every one of those runaway AI bills is income for whoever sells the AI.

I passed on two fast-growing startups, one claiming its revenue was multiplying about fourfold a month, because I thought the big AI developers, such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, could add what they do as a feature. I also passed on a fund aimed at mid-stage companies, which are riskier (though the winners can pay more).

Where I did invest is a fund focused on later-stage AI and robotics companies (ones already selling at scale, with more history to judge), and by extension several AI companies:

Ideal for: Physicians and high-income professionals looking to understand their tax-saving options before speaking with their CPA.

Sat, Nov 14  ·  1:00 pm ET  ·  10:00 am PT

2. The buildings and networks AI runs on. When billions of dollars of new data centers are blocked or delayed, the ones already approved, powered and operating become harder to replace.

I dropped one data-center sponsor I’d been interested in when it stopped answering my questions. And I passed on a communications-network fund because I had concerns about how its track record was put together, and many of its deals hadn’t been sold yet, so I couldn’t tell how well it had really done.

The one that passed is a fund that owns income-producing data centers leased to tenants with strong finances, on long leases with built-in rent increases. I intend to invest.

3. The energy that feeds them. Data centers need reliable power, whether it comes from natural gas, renewables or nuclear.

In oil and gas, I liked a fund that buys mineral rights, which collect a share of what wells produce without paying to drill them, and can be lower risk than drilling. I didn’t invest in the end, because of issues with answers and a higher minimum investment than I expected. And I’m continuing to look at multiple options here.

4. Businesses that AI has a hard time replacing. These are businesses whose essential work still needs a person on site:

And I wrote up each one I looked at, including what passed my due diligence and what didn’t, in the latest article in my AI series.

AI is the hottest label in investing right now, and sponsors are attaching it to everything. For the general questions to put to any private real estate sponsor, see Ten Questions I Run on Every Private Real Estate Deal. These are the AI-specific questions I add:

I went from AI skeptic to believer in 2026, and I expect AI to rank among the most economically important technologies of the coming years. And the prediction that it would be a cheap replacement for people hasn’t held up so far, as the companies that acted on it have learned from their bills.

For investors, I think that cost and scarcity point to opportunity. The places to look are the buildings, networks and power AI can’t run without, and the in-person work it still can’t do.

#8531. $656,000 of Frugal Things I Still Love Doing

“Until he got all rich and fancy so that he no longer understands the common person’s plight.

Stash probably doesn’t even practice any of these money-saving things he preaches any more!”

When I read things like this, I can’t help but laugh. Because on the one hand, when you put a bunch of personal life details online like this, being misunderstood is just part of the package. But on the other hand, if the critics could peek in and see our real lives – not just mine but those of all the Mustachians – they would have to give up their conspiracy theories and accept the fact that this stuff just works.

Because really, not much has changed when it comes to the basics. Like many MMM readers over the past twelve years, my total wealth level has increased pretty regularly.  But also like many of us, I haven’t felt the need to change very much about my spending because I was doing my best to live an enjoyable life in the first place.

How have so many people found such great success? I think we Mustachians have something that’s a bit more rare and special than standard financial advice, which is what makes it work so well:

Standard Advice: Slash your spending and make sacrifices until you reach a certain savings percentage, and beyond that it doesn’t matter, it’s all personal choice. More income? Great, that means you don’t have to sacrifice as much! FatFIRE for everyone!

Mustachianism: Cultivate a love of efficiency, creativity, self awareness, and self improvement. Use this knowledge to improve your life in all ways, including those which help you live better even as your monthly expense rate drops over time.

Well, I’ll give you some examples from my own present-day life. Things I do because I happen to enjoy them, which also happen to save a lot of money. Some of these are normal, some are silly and may end up in some future gossip magazine hit piece, but all of them happen to work for me, so the critics can be damned.

As I list each item, I’ll include an estimate of how much the activity saves me per decade, because you should always think at least in terms of decades. To make that calculation yourself, just use the “rule of 172” – take a monthly expense and multiply it by 172 to estimate how much it would compound into over ten years, if invested.

1) Fixing my own House (and everybody else’s too)

I’m a big believer in self-sufficiency, and working to build up the skills to manage the most important parts of your own life without depending on too many things (or people) that are outside of your control. In other words, one giant recipe for a happy life is simply to Become a Producer of the Things You Most Enjoy Consuming.

And in my case, I happen to love houses. I like living in beautiful, functional spaces and sharing them with friends. But most houses are ugly and poorly designed when you buy them, so I realized that I also love solving problems and redesigning old buildings to become new again. I enjoy this process so much that I spend most of my free time doing it – on both my own properties and the homes of friends.

And I love teaching other people to gain power over their own houses too. It’s amazing how great people feel as they lose their fear and dependence on outside contractors, and gain the ability to fix and maintain things with their own two hands.

Savings: An average of $20,000 per year = $287,000 per decade

You know what’s great? Having so much money that you can buy whatever you want – high quality things which get delivered to your front door the very next day.

You know what’s even better? Not buying some of those new things, and instead finding ways to share, repurpose and buy equally high quality items from other people who don’t need them any more. All while building up your own community and creating new friendships in the process.

Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, and even NextDoor all have Buy Nothing groups for most areas. In the MMM-HQ community, we run a Discord server with about 200 local people, who chat around the clock on a wide range of subjects. They help each other with major projects in one channel called #diyhowto, and give away and sell things on #forsale and #buynothing.

Although our private Discord group is my favorite, I also use Craigslist regularly, and probably save (and earn) a few thousand every year thanks to the habit:

We all know that Mr. Money Mustache’s biggest contribution to personal finance is to insist that bike transportation is the best way to get around. And I still feel this way. As we learned in The True Cost of Commuting, cars cost at least 50 cents per mile to operate, while bikes are much cheaper, mainly due to reduced depreciation and maintenance costs (which are even bigger than the gas savings).

I do still use bikes (or walking) for at least 95% of my local trips these days, but because I live in the center of a small city, my life is pretty local. So this still only adds up to about 2000 miles per year, a savings of “only” $14,000 per decade.

But when you choose active transportation, there’s much more to the picture than just cutting your car expenses. You’re changing everything about your physical and mental health picture for the better, which brings us to the next point of…

Although I’m no competitive athlete, whenever I see an option to make my body work a bit harder, I usually take it. Stairs instead of elevators, running the golf course instead of using a golf cart, moving my own furniture and appliances instead of calling a mover, shoveling snow and raking leaves instead of using a machine.

When I face a decision like this, I simply ask myself the question: “Well, Mustache. Do you want MORE health and fitness, or LESS?” Putting it in that context makes the answer obvious.  Every bit helps, because when it comes to your body, the rule is pretty much use it or lose it.

But how much money does this save? There’s no real way to calculate it exactly, but I like to think of it this way: The US average health care spending is about $13,000 per person per year. My lifetime costs due to illness or medication so far have been just about zero, plus I know I’ve had more energy and greater productivity due to being healthy. Let’s just put it very conservatively and set the estimated savings and benefits at $10k per year which means

5) Saving Energy by Running my home like a Glamping Retreat

Here’s where things get a bit silly, but my level of joy is actually at its greatest.

My personality type is probably a weird combination of an engineer, a carpenter, an artsy hippie, and a mad scientist. Oh, and a devoted homebody too. Because of this, my favorite activity most days is to just run around my house taking care of things and trying new little experiments and improvements.

Sometimes I’ll cut a few big holes on on the South side of the house and install sliding doors and big windows to allow nice sunbeams and passive solar energy to get into my house and give me free heat in the winters. Other times it’s just smaller things to save energy and live more at at one with the seasons of my area:

Even taken all together, these things are pretty small – the average combined gas and electric bill for my area is about $250 per month, while my usage adds up to about $75. So while we’re only saving about $30,000 per decade for what sounds like a lot of work to most people, I consider this to be the biggest win because I enjoy living in “MMM’s Energy Efficiency Playground” so much.

“Hey, we’re having a big back yard pool party next weekend to celebrate Amy’s graduation from kindergarten, can you make it?”

“OH NOOOO!!! We will be off in at Disneyland that whole week! We planned the trip months ago, I wish we could make it!

As I type this in the height of the summer season, I really feel this effect at its fullest: almost all of my friends are off on trips, and my guest suite here at home is almost constantly full. People are traveling a lot, and many of them sound like they wish they could spend a few more of their precious summer weeks and weekends at home.

I’ll let you in on a little secret: you can! The trick is saying, “no thanks” more often to plans that involve you being away, and “yes please” to things that let you stay at home. The benefits are numerous:

Estimated Savings: Even if you replace just two weeks of travel for a family of four, with equivalent time at home you might save $5,000 per year in direct costs and a further $5,000 per year in incidental benefits like the health and local friendships. This would work out to a shocking $143,000 per decade of wealth increase!

Of course, travel is generally a good thing for broadening the life experience of you and your kids. It’s worth spending on, lavishly at times. But the key is to balance it out and be discerning, keeping the most enriching trips and pruning a few off the bottom of the list. And remembering that home time is valuable and healthy too.

And Whoa! We’ve already built up a huge list and I feel like I was just getting started.

Taken all together, we’ve already detailed things that compound to $656,000 every decade, which already more than double the median wealth that most American seniors have as they cruise nervously into their retirement years – after over 40 years of work!

And now that I’ve been writing this blog for over ten years myself, I can safely say that over $656,000 of even my most recent worth increases are directly attributable to these simple habits. The same ones many of us have been enjoying and preaching about all along, both before and after our retirement dates.

If money is in genuinely short supply, you could go a lot further than the examples in this article. And indeed, there’s a lot more laid out in this blog or the MMM Boot Camp email series.

But one of the points of Mustachianism is that you usually don’t have to try all that hard. Just tweaking your lifestyle to be slightly less ridiculous and more efficient than average is usually all it takes.

In the comments: what are your quirks and frugal indulgences? The things you do now to save money, or things you still do even after it’s no longer about the money? I often wonder how widespread this frugality-just-for-fun is. But since we Humans are a naturally curious and problem solving species in our natural state, I suspect there are many more of us out there.

I think his first point “Fixing my own House” is invaluable advice for any homeowner in HCOL areas. I live in a very HCOL city (a conscious decision that currently is worth the tradeoff for me) and bought a modest “fixer upper” for well below my neighborhoods average home price during COVID.

Boy did I quickly hit the “find out” part of that decision. I’d never touched renovations or building or fixing a home / apartment beyond mounting bike racks on my rented apartments walls. I received insane quotes for electrical, plumbing, HVAC, and all the drywall repairs required for that kind of work. I did the math out for many of these projects based on the number of people and days the companies told me it would take and in many cases these companies were pulling in $300 per man-hour.

So I didn’t hire any of them. I spent an entire year learning the plumbing and electrical code for my city / state / country. I bothered the hell out of my city inspectors with questions. Made dozens of trips (sadly mostly via car) to the big box stores – eventually even started accounts with supply houses and lumber yards for better variety and deals.

In the two years I spent renovating the house, I’ve saved myself more than $300,000 (estimating the value of my time at $50/hour).

If anybody on here is considering buying a home, but isn’t willing to learn to do this stuff themselves, I think renting might be the more Mustachian decision if the alternative is paying for somebody else to do this work. I also don’t think there’s anything wrong with that.

Another good one is learning to replace capacitors yourself, with a multimeter you can check them, this is the most common HVAC failure point and an easy DIY job with lots of YouTube vids showing how to do it. Replacuparts on Amazon are cheap and have reviews to help ensure quality.

Thanks for the post MMM! Like those above, I resonated with your article. A lot of these were things I have “always just done” (like hang dry clothes) so a few more that “I just have always done”

(1) My grad school room mate and I loved new clothes but really couldn’t afford them. So we would challenge ourselves to keep our apartment as cold as we could tolerate in Ann Arbor, Michigan and “reward” ourselves in cost savings from our heating bill by buying a new sweater to keep us warm. That $50/month difference meant we were stoked by our new sweater and usually pocketed the savings the other months.

(2) Buy wool clothing. It’s more durable, needs to be washed less, and you can have a smaller wardrobe (which takes up less space, saving you money in storage/heating costs). Even better buy used wool clothing.

(3) Books. I love reading and go through upwards of 50+ books a year. Buying those new at a bookstore would be $30-$50 a month! Instead, I use Libby through my library and constantly have a multitude of books on hold. So yes, I need to wait, but honestly, it’s not that bad if you just had a great book come up that you’ve been waiting for. Slow gratification :)

(4) Shampoo / Conditioner. I’ve experimented a lot with this over the years. Especially for women, there is an expectation to have clean, styled, long hair. There just is. I have finally settled on washing hair 2-3x a week, using tiny amounts of shampoo and conditioner only when necessary means I can save 5 bottles of each a year.

(5) Buying the clearance veggies and cooking them that day. I’m also vegetarian. Both of these things save a TON of money, especially eating out (it’s about 10-15% less to be a vegetarian consistently when ordering out).

#8530. Solo Health Review (2026): Costs, Coverage, Pros & Cons

If you’re self-employed, finding affordable health coverage can be challenging. Traditional health insurance premiums can take a big bite out of your budget, especially when you’re paying for coverage without employer help.

Solo Health offers a different approach to health coverage designed specifically for entrepreneurs, freelancers, and self-employed business owners. Instead of purchasing a traditional individual health insurance policy, eligible business owners establish a self-funded major medical plan through their business.

But how does Solo Health work? Is the coverage comprehensive? And could it actually save you money? In this Solo Health review, we’ll break down the costs, benefits, potential drawbacks, and important details you should understand before enrolling.

Solo Health is a health coverage solution designed for self-employed individuals and business owners who want an alternative to traditional individual health insurance.

The company offers self-funded major medical plans that provide access to healthcare services through a nationwide PPO provider network.

Unlike a traditional insurance policy purchased through the Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace, Solo Health uses a business-based structure.

Your business establishes its own self-funded health plan to cover eligible medical claims.

According to Solo Health, its plans include:

One of Solo Health’s biggest selling points is major medical coverage specifically designed for self-employed people.

However, Solo Health is not a traditional ACA Marketplace insurance policy, and eligibility depends on a health questionnaire.

Solo Health operates differently from both traditional health insurance and healthcare-sharing programs. Instead of purchasing an individual insurance policy, your business establishes a self-funded health plan.

That self-funded plan pays eligible medical claims under the terms of your plan documents.

Here’s a simplified overview of how it works:

Preventive care is generally covered without meeting your deductible.

Prescription medications have their own coverage rules, including copays after the deductible.

Solo Health describes its product as a self-funded major medical health plan, not a healthcare-sharing ministry or a conventional individual insurance policy.

Eligible medical claims are paid through your business’s self-funded health plan.

While Solo Health provides major medical benefits, you should not assume it has all the same eligibility protections, regulatory requirements, or consumer safeguards as an ACA-compliant individual insurance policy.

For example, Solo Health requires applicants to complete a health questionnaire and meet its participation requirements. This differs significantly from ACA Marketplace plans, which generally cannot reject applicants because of preexisting medical conditions.

Before enrolling, make sure you understand the plan documents, coverage exclusions, and how the plan pays medical claims.

Solo Health offers several key medical benefits designed to protect members from both routine healthcare expenses and larger medical bills.

Here’s a closer look at what is included.

Solo Health covers eligible preventive healthcare services at 100%, with no deductible required.

This can be particularly helpful for self-employed individuals who want to stay on top of their health without paying the full cost of every preventive appointment. However, diagnostic tests or treatments performed during a preventive visit may be billed differently.

Solo Health covers primary care physicians and medical specialists. Members can access participating providers through the MultiPlan PHCS network, now associated with Claritev.

You generally don’t need a referral to see a specialist. For most non-preventive visits, you’ll pay the applicable cost until you meet your deductible. After you meet your deductible, the plan covers eligible medical services at 100%, subject to plan terms.

One of the most important reasons to have health coverage is protection against unexpected medical emergencies. A serious accident, hospitalization, or surgery can result in tens of thousands of dollars in medical bills.

According to the company, emergency services are processed as in-network regardless of which hospital provides the care.

Certain planned hospital admissions and surgeries require prior authorization.

Solo Health covers eligible mental health and substance use treatment. This can include outpatient therapy and other qualifying services. However, limits apply.

For example, Solo Health limits outpatient mental health therapy to 40 visits per covered individual each year. Some mental health treatments may also require prior authorization. If you regularly use mental health services, review these limitations before enrolling.

Solo Health includes prescription benefits administered through FairosRx. Preventive medications in Tier 1 are covered at $0. For other covered medications, members generally pay the discounted cost until they meet their deductible.

Afterward, prescription copays apply based on the medication’s tier. Some specialty medications can still involve high out-of-pocket costs.

Solo Health also lists maternity and newborn care among its covered benefits. This can include eligible prenatal services, childbirth, and medical care for newborns.

However, anyone planning to start or expand a family should review the plan’s maternity provisions, eligibility requirements, and applicable exclusions before enrolling. Don’t assume every pregnancy-related service will automatically qualify for payment.

One of the biggest questions when considering any health coverage option is how much you’ll pay. Solo Health offers three plan designs, each with a different deductible.

The main difference between these plans is how much you must pay toward eligible medical expenses before the plan pays most covered costs at 100%.

All three plans offer the same core coverage and provider network. The deductible you select influences your monthly payment. Generally speaking, plans with lower deductibles cost more per month, while plans with higher deductibles cost less.

Your actual monthly cost depends on factors such as your age, location, household composition, and eligibility. Because pricing is individualized, the best way to determine your cost is to request a quote directly from Solo Health.

Let’s say you choose the Solo Health plan with a $5,000 individual deductible. You would generally pay the applicable cost of eligible non-preventive healthcare services until you’ve spent $5,000 toward your deductible.

After that, the plan pays 100% of eligible medical expenses for the remainder of the plan year. However, prescription copays and potential out-of-network charges can still apply.

This is why it’s important to understand the difference between your deductible and your total possible healthcare expenses.

Solo Health advertises its deductible as the out-of-pocket maximum for eligible medical care.

This structure can make medical expenses easier to plan for.

However, the advertised maximum may not cover every expense you could incur.

Prescription copays, excluded services, and charges above the plan’s out-of-network reimbursement amount may result in additional costs.

When comparing plans, consider both your monthly payments and what you could reasonably afford if you had a major medical event.

Solo Health uses a six-tier prescription drug structure. Here is the company’s published schedule for covered medications after meeting the deductible.

Tier 1 preventive medications are available without meeting the deductible. For most other covered prescriptions, these copays apply after the deductible is satisfied. The plan also restricts certain expensive medications.

For example, the plan may exclude non-specialty medications that exceed specified price thresholds. If you take prescription medications regularly, check the company’s formulary to confirm whether your medications are covered and what they might cost.

A Health Savings Account (HSA) can be a valuable tool for managing healthcare expenses. HSAs can offer tax advantages when you contribute, invest, and use the funds for qualified medical expenses.

According to Solo Health’s published FAQ, the V2500 and V5000 plan designs are HSA-eligible, while the V10000 plan is not currently listed as HSA-eligible. However, HSA eligibility depends on federal tax requirements, not simply a plan’s marketing designation.

Before contributing, confirm that your specific coverage qualifies as an HSA-compatible high-deductible health plan under current IRS rules. This matters because deductible amounts alone don’t establish HSA eligibility.

Customer experiences can provide valuable insight when evaluating a healthcare company. However, a company’s advertised benefits differ from what customers experience when submitting medical claims.

Solo Health publishes information about its coverage, member services, and claims administration. It also offers concierge assistance and an online member portal.

Solo Health offers several features that may appeal to certain self-employed individuals.

Many freelancers and small business owners don’t have access to employer-sponsored health insurance. Solo Health is specifically designed for people in this situation.

Its business-based structure gives qualifying entrepreneurs another option to consider when shopping for health coverage.

Three deductible levels let members choose a plan that fits their financial situation. Someone with a larger emergency fund might prefer a higher deductible to reduce monthly costs.

Another person might prefer paying more each month in exchange for a lower deductible. The key is choosing a plan that fits both your budget and your ability to handle unexpected medical expenses.

Solo Health provides access to the MultiPlan PHCS network, which includes participating providers across all 50 states.

This may be especially valuable for entrepreneurs who travel frequently or work in multiple locations. Members can also seek out-of-network care, although additional financial risks can apply.

Unlike limited-benefit programs, Solo Health advertises coverage for major medical expenses such as hospital stays, surgeries, and emergency care.

It also includes preventive care, prescription benefits, and mental health services. The company states that there are no annual or lifetime dollar caps on covered medical benefits.

Solo Health’s business-based structure may offer tax advantages for eligible business owners. The company states that monthly plan costs are generally deductible as a business expense.

However, the tax treatment depends on your business structure and individual circumstances. Consult a qualified tax professional before assuming your payments will qualify for a deduction.

Eligible preventive services are covered at 100% from the beginning of coverage. This feature helps people prioritize preventive care while managing overall medical expenses.

While Solo Health has appealing features, it also has important limitations.

Solo Health requires applicants to have an eligible business with an active EIN. Applicants must also complete a health questionnaire.

If you don’t meet the company’s participation requirements, you may not qualify for coverage. This makes Solo Health less accessible than ACA Marketplace coverage, which generally offers guaranteed issue during applicable enrollment periods.

A $10,000 deductible may be manageable for someone with substantial savings. However, it could create financial hardship for someone living paycheck to paycheck.

Before selecting a high-deductible plan, make sure you have enough savings to handle unexpected healthcare costs. The lowest monthly payment isn’t necessarily the best financial decision if it exposes you to expenses you cannot afford.

Solo Health uses reference-based pricing for out-of-network services. This means the plan may reimburse a benchmarked amount rather than the provider’s full billed charge.

If the provider charges more than the plan allows, you could be responsible for the difference. This is sometimes called balance billing.

Although Solo Health offers support services to help members navigate medical bills, that does not necessarily eliminate the risk of additional charges.

Solo Health’s enrollment process includes health-related eligibility questions. This differs from ACA-compliant individual health insurance.

If you have ongoing medical conditions or a complicated medical history, review the eligibility requirements carefully.

Accurate answers are essential, and the company states that incomplete or inaccurate information can result in denial of coverage.

Although Solo Health advertises no annual or lifetime dollar caps on covered medical benefits, certain services have visit limits.

For example, outpatient mental health therapy is generally limited to 40 visits annually per covered individual. Some treatments also require prior authorization. Read the complete plan documents so you understand these limitations before enrolling.

Solo Health’s self-funded model may be unfamiliar to people who have only purchased traditional insurance.

The arrangement involves a self-funded business health plan, third-party administration, and a medical reimbursement policy.

Because this structure differs from a standard individual insurance policy, it is worth reviewing the legal and financial responsibilities involved.

How does Solo Health compare with a conventional ACA Marketplace plan?

Traditional ACA Marketplace insurance offers important consumer protections, including guaranteed coverage of preexisting conditions and standardized requirements for essential health benefits.

Solo Health offers a different structure that may appeal to qualifying business owners. However, these products are not interchangeable. For someone with ongoing medical needs, ACA-compliant coverage may provide greater predictability around eligibility and consumer protections.

For an eligible entrepreneur, Solo Health may be worth comparing based on its benefits, provider access, and total annual costs.

Another useful comparison is Solo Health versus healthcare-sharing organizations such as Zion HealthShare. Although both may appeal to people exploring alternatives to conventional individual insurance, they work differently.

Solo Health offers a self-funded major medical plan established through an eligible business.

Its structure includes formal plan documents, medical claims administration, and a self-funded plan structure.

Zion HealthShare is a healthcare-sharing organization. Members contribute monthly amounts to share eligible medical expenses within the community.

Healthcare-sharing programs are not insurance, and they don’t guarantee payment of medical expenses the same way an insurance contract does.

The better option depends on your needs. Solo Health may be more appealing to business owners who want a structured major medical plan with a nationwide provider network.

Zion HealthShare may appeal to people who are comfortable with the healthcare-sharing model and its guidelines. Don’t choose either based on monthly costs alone. Consider the eligibility requirements, exclusions, payment structure, and your financial exposure if you experience a major medical event.

Solo Health may be worth considering for:

It may be particularly appealing to someone who wants to explore a business-based health plan rather than purchasing coverage through the individual insurance market.

If you have significant ongoing medical expenses, compare your options carefully.

Solo Health offers an interesting alternative for self-employed individuals seeking major medical coverage outside the traditional individual insurance market. Its biggest advantages include multiple deductible options, access to a nationwide PPO network, preventive care benefits, and coverage for significant medical expenses.

For qualifying entrepreneurs, the business-based structure may also provide financial and tax-planning opportunities. However, there are important trade-offs. Applicants must meet health eligibility requirements, higher deductibles can create substantial out-of-pocket costs, and out-of-network billing can become complicated.

I recommend comparing Solo Health with at least two other coverage options before deciding. Look beyond the monthly payment and calculate what you might spend over an entire year, including deductibles, prescription costs, and potential out-of-network expenses.

The goal isn’t simply to find the cheapest health plan. It’s to find coverage that protects your health and your finances when you need it most. Eligible self-employed business owners may want to explore Solo Health.

In 1980, a benefits consultant named Ted Benna figured out how to use Section 401(k), a little-known provision Congress added to the tax code in 1978, to build the first 401(k) plan. It quickly became a favorite among companies looking to offer employees more retirement benefits.

Today, it is still the cornerstone of retirement planning in America. Even physicians who often have a 403(b), 457(b), or defined benefit plan available too, usually max out their 401(k) first.

Recently, Benna has made headlines for calling out his invention, the 401(k), for disproportionately rewarding the wealthy. He may have a point. But I still think the 401(k) is the best retirement account most workers can get, and that it’s still worth it for doctors.

Also read: Beyond the 401(k): Why Physicians Are Turning to Defined Benefit Plans

In a recent Bloomberg interview, Benna argued that the modern 401(k) has grown too complicated and too costly, and that it benefits wealthier savers more than middle- and lower-income workers, the people who arguably need it most.

Affluent employees can afford to max out an account and reap the tax break on top. Benna believes low-income workers either lack access to a plan or can’t afford to contribute if they do.

Research seems to agree. Researchers at Vanguard, Yale and MIT found that about 44% of employer matching dollars go to the top 20% of earners at their companies.

And the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics has reported that while 70% of private-sector workers have access to a defined contribution (DC) plan such as a 401(k), only 49% participate. That means roughly 3 in 10 workers who could use a plan but don’t.

Source: BLS. Alt text: BLS chart showing 70% of private-sector workers have access to a defined contribution plan and 49% participate, March 2026

Most physicians sit on the other side of this. Every specialty earns well above the national average. Doximity’s latest compensation report names pediatric infectious disease as the lowest-paying specialty, at $217,819. By comparison, the average American salary is $69,770.

The reason I bring this up here is so that physicians who run practices can make sure their employee 401(k) structures do not reflect these statistics. More on that below.

The 401(k) has been one of the most effective tools for building middle-class wealth the U.S. has ever had.

Household stock ownership went up from 32% in 1989, right before one of the best multi-decade stretches for stock returns on record, to 58% by 2022. Almost one-fifth of American households now hold a net worth above a million dollars— much of it held in home equity and retirement accounts like the 401(k)..

So even if the account rewards people who already earn enough to contribute, it still enables actual wealth-building for millions of ordinary workers who’d otherwise have little beyond Social Security waiting for them at retirement.

Access and participation are both on the rise largely thanks to policy changes. Many states now require employers without a retirement plan to enroll workers in a state-run IRA program. Employers can usually opt out by setting up their own plan, which is pushing more of them to offer a 401(k).

Small businesses, which employ close to half the American workforce, have historically skipped retirement benefits altogether. Tax credits and cheaper providers are changing that. Cerulli Associates projects that the number of 401(k) plans will grow 36% over the next five years, passing one million by the end of the decade.

Auto-enrollment deserves a lot of the credit for the jump in participation.

Under SECURE 2.0, 401(k) and 403(b) plans set up after December 29, 2022 must automatically enroll employees, starting with plan years that began in 2025. Older plans, businesses less than three years old and employers with 10 or fewer workers are exempt.

The effect is large. Vanguard found that plans with auto-enrollment had a 94% participation rate, compared with 64% for plans where employees sign up on their own.

Learn more: Year-End Tax Planning for Physicians. What To Do Before 2026 Is Over

For 2026, the IRS raised the 401(k) employee contribution limit to $24,500, up from $23,500 in 2025. Workers 50 and older can add a catch-up contribution of $8,000 on top of that, up from $7,500, bringing the total to $32,500 for savers in that age bracket.

A newer “super” catch-up of $11,250 lets savers ages 60 to 63 put away even more. It replaces the regular $8,000 catch-up for those years rather than stacking on top of it, bringing their total to $35,750.

re limited to 72,000for2026(80,000 with the age-50 catch-up, or $83,250 for ages 60 to 63), or 100% of eligible pay, whichever is lower. If your plan allows after-tax contributions, the room between your own contributions and that cap is what makes a mega backdoor Roth possible.

Important: starting in 2026, if your wages from the employer sponsoring your plan topped $150,000 in 2025, any catch-up contributions you make must go in as Roth (after-tax) instead of pretax. Two details matter for physicians:

If you’re weighing Roth against pretax for the rest of your contributions, here’s how to choose between a Roth and traditional 401(k). Full details are on the IRS catch-up contributions page.

Many employed physicians don’t have a 401(k) at all. Hospitals and academic centers usually offer a 403(b), which works almost the same way, with the same $24,500 limit and the same catch-ups.

Many also offer a 457(b), which has its own separate $24,500 limit. If you have both, you can defer up to $49,000 in 2026 before counting any catch-ups.

One caution: in a non-governmental 457(b), the money technically belongs to your employer until it’s paid out, so it’s exposed if the hospital runs into financial trouble. Here’s our full guide to 457(b) contributions.

If you own a practice with staff, plan design decides who actually benefits. A safe harbor 401(k) is the common choice. You make a required contribution for employees, either 3% of pay or a match of up to 4%, which vests right away.

In return, the plan skips the annual nondiscrimination tests that can otherwise cap what owners contribute. Under SECURE 2.0, small practices can also claim tax credits of up to $5,000 a year for three years toward startup costs, plus $500 a year for adding auto-enrollment.

Owners who want to save more than the 401(k) allows often pair it with a cash balance plan. And if you’re a solo practitioner with no staff, a solo 401(k) or SEP-IRA is usually simpler.

More than 80% of employers who sponsor a 401(k) offer some form of match, usually tied to how much the employee contributes. Some employers match dollar for dollar up to a set percentage of salary.

Others match 50 cents on the dollar up to a higher contribution threshold. The formula changes how much match each dollar you contribute actually earns, and that’s where dual-income households can come out ahead.

A brief published by the Center for Retirement Research (CRR) examined whether married couples coordinate contributions to capture both employer matches. Just over 40% of couples actively coordinate to maximize their combined match and roughly one in five couples leaves match money uncaptured.

In one example from the brief, a couple decides how to split $480 a month in savings between two accounts with different match formulas. Moving contributions toward the partner with the more generous 1-to-1 match, as opposed to splitting evenly, nets the household an extra $30 a month in employer money.

Stretched over 30 years at a 5% inflation-adjusted return, that $30 monthly difference compounds into roughly $25,000 in additional retirement savings, without either partner setting aside a single extra dollar of their own income.

Source: CRR. Alt text: CRR chart showing how couples split 401(k) contributions to capture employer matches.

Plenty of couples capture both matches without planning it, because each partner contributes enough on their own. That works fine.

Coordination matters when money is tight, like when one spouse is still in residency, working part-time or paying down loans hard. In those years, send your savings to the richer match first, then fill the other.

Say a resident earning $66,000 and her spouse earning $120,000 can save $600 a month between them. Her plan matches 50 cents per dollar on the first 6% of pay. His matches dollar for dollar on the first 4%, up to $400 a month.

Split evenly at $300 each, they collect $450 a month in match. If he puts in $400 and she puts in $200, they collect $500. That’s an extra $600 a year in employer money from the same $600 a month.

Compare match formulas with your spouse, figure out which account pays the better rate, and adjust the split.

Finally, if you’re wondering about how aggressively you should contribute, I’ll say that starting early beats chasing a better return.

In an example from Forbes, we see two 25-year-old savers earning identical salaries. One enrolls immediately at a 10% deferral rate with a 3% match. The other waits five years, then contributes 6% to capture the same 3% match.

The second saver’s fund even outperforms the first, returning roughly 8.9% annually versus 8.4%, partly from a private equity allocation meant to make up lost ground.

By 65, the early starter still ends up with roughly $3 million, compared with $2 million for the saver who waited. That $1 million gap comes from two things: five fewer years of compounding and a lower savings rate (9% of pay versus 13%). The higher return didn’t come close to closing it. If you’re still in training, here’s what to set up now.

As you can see, when it comes to retirement savings, your timing often matters more than any other variable.

A dollar contributed at 25 has decades to compound and no later contribution, however large, can fully make up for a late start. The 401(k) is also one of the few accounts you can start on day one without worrying much about what happens when you change jobs.

That’s because, as opposed to pensions and employer-funded bonus plans, the 401(k) is portable. Your own contributions are yours the moment they hit your account, and they go with you when you leave. Employer matches can be different. Many plans vest the match over time, either all at once after up to three years or gradually over up to six.

Leave before you’re vested and you lose the unvested part, so check your plan’s vesting schedule before you time a job change. You can roll it into a new employer’s plan or an IRA, and it will continue to compound without interruption.

Benna may not be happy with how his invention turned out, but for me, looking at how it has created a new class of millionaires, it is the one non-negotiable account in retirement planning for physicians and beyond.

Yes. A 401(k) invests in the market through mutual funds or target-date funds, so balances can drop during downturns. Over decades, though, contributions and compounding have historically outpaced short-term losses for most savers.

It depends. A 401(k) is portable, so you keep the balance and can roll it into a new employer’s plan or an IRA when you switch jobs. A pension pays guaranteed income for life, but most of the benefit builds in your later years with one employer, so people who change jobs often come out behind.

Yes. Directing more of a couple’s combined savings toward whichever spouse has the richer employer match captures free money that even splits often miss, sometimes adding thousands to household retirement savings with no extra out-of-pocket cost.

Yes, if your 2025 wages from the employer sponsoring your plan topped $150,000. Your catch-up contributions must go in as Roth. Partners paid through K-1 income aren’t affected.

You keep everything you contributed yourself, plus any match that has already vested. The unvested part goes back to the plan.

Nearly. Both have the same $24,500 limit for 2026 and the same catch-up rules. A 403(b) is offered by nonprofits like hospitals and universities, and some have fewer investment options.

Those who make more money can also save more money. Shocker.

Once you retire and accumulate enough to support the life you want, it’s likely your priorities will change. You won’t need to squeeze every last dollar of growth from your portfolio. You might be more focused on making what you’ve built last.

“The only purpose of money is to build the life you want.” What does it say about you if some of your happiest memories are those during which you didn’t have much money?

Happiness starts out higher when you’re young, dips in middle age and then goes back up in your older years. The thing about the happiness curve is you overestimate your future life satisfaction when you’re young and underestimate your future happiness when you’re in middle age. Both feelings are probably wrong but impossible to ignore.

Everybody wants to argue about what AI is going to do tomorrow. Which jobs will disappear? Which companies will lose? What happens to the people who get left behind? Those are fair questions. But what about the jobs that don’t exist yet? What about the industries nobody has invented? What about the opportunities we can’t even imagine today?

Renting comes with uncertainty. You might have to move, you’re subject to someone else’s rules, and you have less autonomy over your living space. Homeownership, meanwhile, is presented as stability, security, and a permanent place for your children to grow up. Sounds perfect. But where are the property taxes, maintenance bills, unexpected repairs, and time spent dealing with contractors? What about the opportunity cost of tying up a substantial portion of your net worth in a single, illiquid asset?

Retirees sometimes tap savings for one-off expenses. Withdrawing money from a traditional 401(k) or individual retirement account is not as simple as taking the amount you need, advisors say. There are tax implications to consider that go beyond owing taxes on the money you withdraw.

Many adult children are ignoring the old adage “don’t count your chickens before they hatch,” and conducting their finances based on an inheritance they may not receive. Baby boomers are sitting on a pile of wealth, and some researchers estimate they’ll have to pass about $124 trillion of that in what’s dubbed the “Great Wealth Transfer” to next generations through 2048. Others, though, warn potential heirs not to get their hopes up.

Financial silence creates immense, unnecessary suffering. The administrative scramble piled on top of deep grief is enough to break a family apart. So why do we wait until a crisis to have these conversations with our parents?

The holidays are just around the corner. A new inflation report just dropped. That means one thing: the Cost of Thanksgiving Discourse. The most expensive part of Thanksgiving is now less about the table and more about how you get there.

Even physicians who often have a 403(b), 457(b), or defined benefit plan available too, usually max out their 401(k) first. The 401(k) is the best retirement account most workers can get, and that it’s still worth it for doctors.

That habit got expensive in 2026. Itemizers now lose the deduction on the first 0.5% of AGI they give away, and top-bracket donors see the tax benefit capped at 35%. The write-off shrinks unless you change how the money leaves your account before December 31.

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Which move fits depends on whether you’ll itemize this year.

#8523. JAL Business Class via Multiple Transfer Partners

Savings rate, FI number, and the path to freedom.

Withdrawal plans, Roth ladders, and early access.

Index funds, asset allocation, and real estate.

Roth conversions, capital gains, and FI tax planning.

Career growth, side hustles, and entrepreneurship.

Beliefs, purpose, and financial psychology.

Exercise, nutrition, and mental wellness.

World-class Japanese hospitality at a fraction of the cash price via partner bookings

Picture this: you're settled into your own private suite at 37,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific. The door closes. A flight attendant in a crisp JAL uniform offers you a warm towel and asks how you'd like your appetizer served. The flat bed is already made with a proper duvet. Outside the window, the sun is setting over the ocean. You're nine hours into a 12-hour flight to Tokyo, and you feel more rested than you did when you boarded. This is JAL's Sky Suite — one of the most celebrated business class products in the world — and with the right travel rewards strategy, your family can experience it for a fraction of what everyone else is paying. Here's the math that stops people cold: a round-trip business class ticket from San Francisco to Tokyo on JAL typically retails for **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's not a typo. Premium transcontinental fares are genuinely that expensive, and most people simply accept that they'll never sit up front on a 12-hour flight across the Pacific. But the ChooseFI community knows better. That same seat — the same flat bed, the same Champagne, the same Sky Suite cocoon — is available for **60,000 miles** when booked through Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage. At a retail value of $5,000 to $10,000, you're looking at **8.3 to 16.7 cents per point** in value. For context, most travel rewards experts consider anything above 1.5 cents per point a good redemption. This one can be up to *eleven times* that benchmark. The pricing inefficiency exists because partner award programs — like Alaska and American — use fixed award charts that were negotiated years ago, before JAL's hard product became one of the most sought-after cabins in the sky. JAL hasn't raised these partner pricing levels proportionally as cash fares have climbed. The gap between what you pay in points and what the market charges in dollars is enormous, and it's yours to exploit right now. This isn't a loophole that's about to close tomorrow. It's a structural feature of the loyalty system — one that rewards people who understand how to use their points strategically rather than burning them on domestic economy upgrades. For anyone on the path to financial independence, where every dollar and every point is treated with intention, this is exactly the kind of asymmetric opportunity worth understanding.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: JAL's own frequent flyer program is not where you want to book this award. This is the aha moment that separates casual points users from strategic ones.

JAL operates its own loyalty program — JAL Mileage Bank — but it charges significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often running $100 to $500 or more per ticket. When you book JAL business class through JAL Mileage Bank itself, those surcharges erode a substantial portion of your points value before you even leave the ground. The ChooseFI community's editorial guidance here is unambiguous: book JAL through partner programs to avoid this tax on your redemption.

There are two primary programs where you can book JAL business class at 60,000 miles round-trip on the transpacific route:

Alaska Mileage Plan prices JAL business class at 60,000 miles for a round-trip between North America and Japan. Alaska is a oneworld partner of JAL and honors JAL's genuinely strong award availability. Critically, Alaska does not pass through JAL's fuel surcharges to awards booked through Mileage Plan. This is a massive advantage.

American AAdvantage also prices the same route at 60,000 miles round-trip. Both programs use fixed award charts, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash fares do — a $10,000 ticket at peak cherry blossom season costs exactly the same points as a ticket in a slower travel month.

Neither Alaska Mileage Plan nor American AAdvantage is a direct transfer partner from the major US bank programs in the same way Chase or Amex partners work. However, you have real pathways:

For Alaska and American miles specifically, the strongest earning strategies involve:

Both Alaska and American use fixed award charts — meaning the price in miles is the same regardless of how high the cash price climbs. This is the structural inefficiency at work. A seat that retails for $10,000 during peak season still costs 60,000 miles. The chart doesn't care about demand; it just prices by region and cabin. As long as JAL releases availability — and they do — the gap between cash cost and points cost remains enormous.

JAL also allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award, which means you can potentially add a stop in Tokyo itself while continuing to another Japanese city, or fly into one city and out of another — all at no additional miles cost.

This is the cardinal rule of all travel rewards bookings: never transfer points until you have confirmed availability. Points transfers are generally irreversible.

Go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) to search for JAL award availability. Because BA is also a oneworld partner, their search tool shows you JAL award space. Search for your route (e.g., SFO to NRT) in business class. Any availability you see here is almost certainly bookable through Alaska or American as well. Look for "J" class availability, which represents business class award space.

You can also call Alaska Airlines at 1-800-252-7522 or American Airlines at 1-800-433-7300 and ask their agents to search JAL availability on your dates. Agents sometimes see space that doesn't show up online.

JAL's booking window opens 360 days in advance. For peak travel periods — Golden Week in Japan (late April to early May), cherry blossom season (late March to early April), and the summer holidays — availability disappears fast. Set a calendar reminder to search and book as soon as the window opens for your target dates.

For travel year-round outside those peaks, JAL is known for releasing strong business class availability, which is why this sweet spot earns a 4/5 on availability. You have real flexibility here.

Decide whether you'll book through Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage. Both charge 60,000 miles round-trip. The key differentiator: Alaska does not pass through fuel surcharges. If minimizing out-of-pocket costs is your priority, Alaska is the better choice.

For Alaska miles: Apply for the Bank of America Alaska Airlines Visa, earn the welcome bonus, and use shopping portals and partner promotions to top up. For American miles: The Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select or Barclays AAdvantage Aviator cards offer solid welcome bonuses. You'll need a minimum of 60,000 miles per person.

If you need to use the Capital One → JAL Mileage Bank transfer path, initiate the transfer from your Capital One portal. Transfers post in 1-2 days. Note that booking through JAL Mileage Bank directly will incur fuel surcharges.

For Alaska: Call 1-800-252-7522 or book online at alaskaair.com/partner-awards. Online booking of JAL awards through Alaska can be hit-or-miss; calling is often more reliable.

For American: Book at aa.com or call. American's website allows partner award searches, though calling often surfaces additional availability.

Once booked, confirm your ticket number, that the cabin shows as "Business" (not an upgrade), and request your preferred meal. JAL offers Western and Japanese meal options — request ahead. Your seat assignment on the 787-9 Sky Suite or 777-300ER Apex Suite can be made at booking.

The core arbitrage here is the difference between booking through JAL's own program versus booking through oneworld partner programs. JAL Mileage Bank imposes significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets — often $100 to $500 per ticket — which erodes the points value substantially. But Alaska Mileage Plan and American AAdvantage can book the exact same JAL-operated flights with zero fuel surcharges because they use their own award charts and pricing rules. You are flying on JAL's aircraft with JAL's crew and JAL's business class product, but paying through a partner program's more favorable pricing. This is the same structural mismatch that creates sweet spots throughout the oneworld alliance — the booking program's pricing does not match the operating airline's product quality.

Let's run the numbers on a specific scenario that thousands of ChooseFI members have used as a benchmark: San Francisco (SFO) to Tokyo Narita (NRT) in JAL business class, round-trip for two people.

A quick search on Google Flights or JAL's own website for this route in business class will typically show cash prices ranging from $5,000 to $10,000 per person — let's use $7,000 as a reasonable midpoint for this example. For two people, you're looking at a $14,000 cash outlay before you even think about hotels in Tokyo.

Booked through Alaska Mileage Plan: 60,000 Alaska miles per person, round-trip. For two travelers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles total, plus taxes and fees (which Alaska keeps minimal for JAL awards, typically under $100 for the pair).

The CPP math: $7,000 in value ÷ 60,000 miles = 11.7 cents per point — squarely in the middle of the 8.3-to-16.7-cent range and nearly 8 times what most people get burning points on domestic economy tickets.

On the 777-300ER, you may get the Apex Suite — a staggered configuration with direct aisle access from every seat and a similarly flat, private sleeping environment.

Beyond the hardware: JAL's service is routinely ranked among the best in the world. The meal service for a 12-hour transpacific flight is multi-course, the sake selection is curated, and the attention to detail in Japanese hospitality culture elevates the experience above what the points price alone suggests.

You'll also access the JAL First Class Lounge or JAL Business Class Lounge at Narita on the return — another perk included with your business class boarding pass. By the time you land in San Francisco after a flat-bed sleep and a proper breakfast service, you've experienced what most travelers save for a once-in-a-lifetime trip. With travel rewards, it can be your default way to cross the Pacific.

British Airways' award search at ba.com is one of the best tools for seeing oneworld partner availability without committing any miles. Use it to scout JAL space across multiple dates before you transfer a single point. It shows business class availability clearly and quickly.

JAL's award calendar opens 360 days in advance. For anyone targeting cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or Golden Week (late April to early May), you should be searching and booking at the 360-day mark, not 60 days out. These are the hardest windows to find availability. Outside peak Japan travel seasons, this is much more forgiving.

JAL Mileage Bank allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award. If you're booking through JAL Mileage Bank directly (accepting the fuel surcharges), you can fly into Tokyo and out of Osaka, for example, without additional miles. This is a genuine value-add for anyone planning a broader Japan itinerary — no backtracking required.

This is a small thing that makes a big difference. Request the Japanese meal option when booking. It's more authentic, better-suited to the overall experience, and — in the ChooseFI spirit of intentionality — it's why you chose this airline over a generic carrier.

This is the single most common and most painful mistake. Points transfers are almost always one-way and irreversible. Never, under any circumstances, transfer points to a program before you have verbal or written confirmation of the award space you intend to book.

As emphasized in the program overview: JAL charges significant fuel surcharges on awards booked through its own program — $100 to $500 or more. For transpacific routes, always book through Alaska or American to avoid these fees. The data is explicit on this point.

If you do earn JAL Mileage Bank miles directly, note that they expire 36 months from the date earned on a rolling basis. If you let a balance sit idle, you may lose miles before you've accumulated enough to book. Keep the balance active through small purchases or partner activity.

This sweet spot is best suited for couples and individual travelers who are targeting Japan specifically — whether it's a bucket-list trip, a first visit to Tokyo, or a multi-city Japan itinerary. The fixed 60,000-mile price per person means that families with young children will need to accumulate significant balances (60,000 miles per ticketed passenger), which pushes the complexity and earning requirement higher.

You need a minimum of 60,000 Alaska miles or 60,000 American AAdvantage miles per person to execute this redemption. For a couple, that's 120,000 miles — achievable with two well-chosen credit card welcome bonuses plus some additional earning through everyday spending or partner promotions.

This redemption is not ideal for beginners — it scores 2/5 on beginner-friendliness, and honestly, that's accurate. The booking path involves navigating partner award searches, understanding the difference between booking programs (Alaska vs. JAL Mileage Bank) and why it matters for surcharges, and potentially calling airlines rather than booking online. If you're on your first or second travel rewards card and still building your foundational understanding, this is one to put on a future list while you sharpen your skills.

For the FI-focused traveler who has been in the travel rewards ecosystem for a year or more, this is a landmark redemption. The CPP ceiling of 16.7 cents per point represents one of the highest-value uses of any points in a North American loyalty portfolio. If you believe in maximizing every dollar you earn and every point you accumulate — and the ChooseFI community does — this is the kind of redemption that justifies the entire system.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty**, and that rating is honest. It's not the most complex thing in the travel rewards world, but it has enough moving parts that going in without preparation can lead to frustration or costly mistakes. **What specifically makes it moderate:** First, the **earning path is not plug-and-play**. Unlike Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards, which transfer to dozens of partners instantly, Alaska miles and American miles are earned primarily through co-branded credit cards and flying. There's no one magic transferable currency that flows directly into these programs at full value. Second, **the booking process often requires a phone call**. Online partner award booking through Alaska and American works inconsistently. Many experienced travelers report that calling the airline's award desk surfaces availability that the website doesn't show — which is a normal part of the process but adds friction. Third, **fuel surcharge awareness matters**. Understanding *why* you book through Alaska or American instead of JAL Mileage Bank directly is a non-obvious nuance that could cost you real money if you don't get it right. **Three tips to overcome the challenge:** 1. **Use BA.com as your availability scouting tool** — it gives you a clean, visual look at JAL award space without committing any miles. 2. **Call Alaska or American directly** when online searches fail. Agents are well-versed in partner award booking and can often find and hold space while you confirm your miles balance. 3. **Build your miles balance before you start searching.** Having 70,000+ miles in hand (a small buffer above 60,000) before you begin reduces stress and gives you flexibility on dates. If you've already completed one or two simpler travel rewards bookings and understand the basics of award searches, this is well within reach. The effort is real — and the payoff is a flat bed over the Pacific.

Go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) and search for your route in business class. Because BA is a oneworld partner, their search tool shows JAL award space. Search across multiple dates to find availability. Any space you see here is almost certainly bookable through Alaska or American as well.

Both charge 60,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges. Alaska miles can be earned through the Alaska Airlines Visa card or transferred from Marriott Bonvoy (3:1). AAdvantage miles can be earned through Citi cards or transferred from various hotel programs. Choose based on which miles you have or can earn most efficiently.

Only transfer points after confirming award availability on ba.com. For Alaska, earn through card spending or Marriott transfers. For AAdvantage, earn through Citi cards. Never transfer before confirming space — transfers are generally irreversible.

Call Alaska Mileage Plan or book on aa.com to ticket the JAL-operated flight. For Alaska, phone booking is required for partner awards. For AA, search on aa.com and book online if the JAL space appears. Confirm your JAL seat assignment on jal.com after ticketing.

JAL Mileage Bank imposes fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often adding $100 to $500 per ticket on transpacific routes. Alaska Mileage Plan and American AAdvantage book the exact same JAL-operated flights at the same 60,000-mile price but with zero fuel surcharges. You fly the same plane, same seat, same service — but pay significantly less out of pocket.

JAL opens its award calendar approximately 360 days in advance. For peak seasons like cherry blossom season (late March to early April) and Golden Week (late April to early May), you should begin searching the day the window opens. Off-peak dates are generally easier to find with 3 to 6 months of lead time.

Not directly, but you can use Chase points indirectly. Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards to British Airways Avios and book JAL through BA's oneworld partnership. However, BA charges fuel surcharges on partner awards, so this path is less favorable than Alaska or AA. The cleanest Chase path is to earn Alaska or AA miles through other means.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

JAL business class via Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage is the definitive sweet spot for anyone targeting Japan. At 60,000 miles one-way with zero fuel surcharges, you are booking a $5,000 to $10,000 cash experience for a fraction of the cost through a partner program pricing arbitrage. The key is searching ba.com for availability before transferring a single point, booking 360 days out for peak cherry blossom or Golden Week dates, and choosing between Alaska and AA based on which miles you can earn most efficiently. JAL's business class product — lie-flat seats, exceptional cuisine, and Japanese hospitality — delivers an experience that justifies the points spend and then some. This is the redemption that puts Japan within reach for every FI-minded traveler.
